_Why does scale transform hardware failure from rare exception to routine condition that systems must absorb continuously?_

A single accelerator can run for years between hardware failures. A thousand accelerators turn that same component risk into failures every couple of days, and ten thousand see failures every few hours, while shared power and network faults can interrupt many workers at once. Individual devices need not become less reliable for the fleet to experience failures routinely. A program on one machine can often stop and restart when a component fails; a distributed training job must also recover agreement among surviving workers about which progress remains valid. Restarting quickly is of little value if the restored state silently changes the computation. Preserving more state reduces the work at risk, but consumes storage bandwidth and memory while the job is healthy. Waiting longer between saves reduces that overhead while increasing the progress a failure can erase. Serving imposes a different consequence: users may abandon a request before recovery completes, and replacing a worker may leave the request's context unavailable. A response that arrives on time can still be unacceptable if recovery has discarded information needed to produce it. Engineers must therefore bound lost work and recovery delay while preserving the validity of training and the usefulness of service. The goal is continued useful execution despite repeated failures, with the costs and limits of recovery made explicit. In C³ terms, fault tolerance spends compute and communication on coordination so that component failures do not routinely become failures of the entire workload.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::
::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate mean time between fleet failures from component rates and estimate interruption frequency for large training clusters
- Classify hardware, software, silent-data-corruption, and slow-but-alive failures by detectability, blast radius, and recovery path
- Select checkpoint intervals that balance write overhead against acceptable lost work and recovery delay
- Design distributed checkpointing and elastic recovery plans for multi-terabyte model state across accelerator fleets
- Design serving redundancy, failover, and state-recovery policies under latency budgets and partial failures
- Select graceful degradation strategies that preserve useful service when models, features, regions, or capacity fail
- Evaluate detection timeouts, restart strategies, and fault-injection evidence against a per-failure recovery-time budget

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fault-tolerance-reliability-rates
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FLEET RELIABILITY RATES — PERSISTENT (single source of truth)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: PERSISTENT. Per-GPU and fleet failure rates derived from canonical
# │          MTTF/fleet constants. Consumed by the failure-rate footnote
# │          [^fn-fits-failure-rate] and the Fallacies and Pitfalls section
# │          (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-fallacies-pitfalls-74b8).
# │
# │ Goal: Derive lambda, FIT, and fleet failure cadence from one constant set so
# │       every quoted reliability number is traceable and cannot drift.
# │ Show: GPU FIT, lambda_hour, fleet FIT total, fleet failure rate, hours between.
# │ How:  lambda = 1/MTTF; FIT = 10^9/MTTF; fleet rate = N/MTTF; interval = 1/rate.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_math, fmt_time, sci_latex

class FleetReliabilityRates:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    fleet_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    lambda_gpu = 1 / gpu_mttf_h  # per-GPU failure rate (per hour)
    gpu_fit = BILLION / gpu_mttf_h  # failures per 10^9 device-hours
    fleet_fit_total = fleet_gpus * gpu_fit  # aggregate FITs across the fleet
    fleet_rate_per_h = fleet_gpus / gpu_mttf_h  # fleet failures per hour
    hours_between = 1 / fleet_rate_per_h  # mean hours between fleet failures

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(gpu_fit * gpu_mttf_h - BILLION) < 1, "FIT definition: FIT x MTTF must equal 10^9")
    check(abs(hours_between * fleet_rate_per_h - 1) < 1e-9, "interval must be reciprocal of fleet rate")
    check(0 < fleet_rate_per_h < fleet_gpus, "fleet failure rate must be positive and below the GPU count")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    _fleet_tex = fmt(fleet_gpus, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _mttf_tex = fmt(gpu_mttf_h, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _fit_tex = fmt(gpu_fit, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    gpu_mttf_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    gpu_mttf_prose_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    fleet_gpus_str = fmt_count(fleet_gpus, label="GPU")
    fleet_fit_str = fmt(fleet_fit_total, precision=0)
    hours_between_str = fmt_time(hours_between, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    gpu_mttf_sym_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True)  # margin caption
    gpu_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word", attributive=True)
    gpu_fit_str = fmt(gpu_fit, precision=0)
    node_gpus_str = fmt(Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node, precision=0)  # series-system example
    hours_between_sym_str = fmt_time(hours_between, "hour", precision=0)  # margin caption
    fit_eq_math = fmt_math(rf"\text{{FIT}} = {_fit_tex}")
    lambda_eq_math = fmt_math(rf"\HourlyComponentFailureRate = {sci_latex(lambda_gpu, precision=1)}")
    fleet_rate_eq_math = fmt_math(f"{_fleet_tex}/{_mttf_tex} = {fmt(fleet_rate_per_h, precision=1, commas=False)}")
```

```{python}

class FaultToleranceIntroRecap:

    )
    check(2.3e12 < gpt3_ckpt_bytes.to(byte).magnitude < 2.6e12, "175B resumable checkpoint must be about 2.45 TB")
    check(1.0 < vit_ckpt.to(GB).magnitude < 2.0, "ViT-Large checkpoint row is a single-digit-GB 'middle ground'")
    check(100 < idle_cost_per_min < 1000, "one idle minute of the 10,000-GPU cluster costs hundreds of dollars")
    check(3e5 < daily_cost < 7e5, "opening hook: an idle day of the 10,000-GPU cluster costs about half a million dollars")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_bpp_str = fmt(ckpt_bpp.magnitude, precision=0)

    gpus_example_str = fmt(gpus_example, precision=0, commas=True)
    rate_str = fmt_usd(rate, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    daily_cost_str = fmt_usd(daily_cost, scale="M", precision=1, commas=False)
    idle_cost_per_min_str = fmt_usd(round(idle_cost_per_min, -1), precision=0, commas=False)
    vit_ckpt_str = fmt_memory(vit_ckpt, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    recsys_table_str = fmt_text(fmt_memory(recsys_table, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False), "+")
```

Imagine a `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpus_example_str`-GPU cluster midway through a three-month training run for a new foundation model. The parallel training plan and the communication layer beneath it have done their job, and thousands of devices exchange gradients through AllReduce, AllGather, and AllToAll as if they were one machine. Then the arithmetic of scale catches up. A GPU fails every few hours, and if the system cannot absorb that ordinary physical event, synchronized training halts while compute worth about `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.daily_cost_str` a day sits idle. **Fault tolerance**\index{Fault tolerance!definition} is the system property that lets distributed execution continue making useful progress when components fail, degrade, or disappear. In the fleet stack of @fig-fleet-stack, fault tolerance occupies the Reliability & Control row of the Distribution band, where it protects the progress that parallelism and communication produce.

That fragility is the direct consequence of successful synchronization. Every collective in @sec-collective-communication assumed that all ranks in its process group arrive, and each dependent consumer waits for every contribution. One stalled device can therefore stop progress in its synchronous training group, even while unrelated jobs continue elsewhere in the fleet. Fault-tolerant ML systems preserve progress by detecting failure, checkpointing recoverable state, restarting or elastically reshaping jobs, and treating hardware churn as normal execution rather than an exceptional path. That reliability envelope covers both halves of the fleet's work. Training needs recovery that preserves weeks of accumulated progress, while serving needs redundancy, failover, and graceful degradation that preserve a latency contract, and both draw their spare capacity from a shared fleet pool.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How the scheduler holds spare capacity for failed jobs and prepositions replacement nodes while a missed heartbeat is confirmed is developed in @sec-fleet-orchestration-failure-rates.
:::

Not every failure announces itself. A component can stop outright, slow down while still answering liveness checks, or keep running while it computes wrong values. The quiet cases pair low detection rates with a high blast radius, because the system keeps running on state it should no longer trust. The recovery target here is therefore trustworthy execution: preserving valid training progress and restoring a service after its infrastructure or software fails. A restored model can still make poor predictions on changed inputs even when every component executes correctly. Evaluating that behavioral robustness requires a separate contract for model quality under distribution shifts and adversarial inputs, developed in @sec-robust-ai. The distinction lets us use model-quality signals to diagnose a fault without treating every quality regression as evidence of failed hardware.

Because failures cannot be eliminated at this scale, fault-tolerant systems verify completion rather than assume it, treat failure as a normal code path, exercise recovery continuously, and account for partial failures that naive error handling may not anticipate. These techniques draw on decades of distributed systems research, but ML workloads change the economics. Training checkpoints are large but can be sized from the model and optimizer state, while some optimization algorithms tolerate bounded numerical perturbations without requiring bitwise replay. That tolerance must be established for the training method; stochasticity does not make arbitrary corruption or inconsistent recovery safe. A recovery design can exploit approximate execution only while preserving its declared convergence and quality requirements. Making failure a routine part of operation starts with knowing how often failures arrive, and the mathematics that follows makes the shift from *rare exception* to *routine occurrence* precise.

## The Mathematics of Inevitable Failure {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-mathematics-inevitable-failure-93ef}

A single data-center GPU can run for years without a hardware fault, yet a synchronous job spanning ten thousand of those same GPUs is interrupted every few hours. System reliability engineering explains why individual device longevity erodes so quickly when thousands of components must stay healthy at the same time [@birolini2017]. Each component has a failure rate $\ComponentFailureRate$,[^fn-fits-failure-rate] measured in failures per unit time. When $\ComponentFailureRate$ is constant, the probability that a single component survives without failure until time $\TimeInstant$ follows an exponential distribution,[^fn-poisson-failure-rate] as in @eq-single-component-reliability:

[^fn-poisson-failure-rate]: **Poisson process**\index{Poisson process!failure modeling}: A statistical model for events occurring independently at a constant average rate. In this model, event counts follow a Poisson distribution and waiting times follow an exponential distribution, giving the survival function $\ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}$. With independent identical component hazards, the probability of at least one failure in a 10,000-component cluster is $1 - e^{-\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}$. The aggregate hazard $\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate$ scales linearly with component count; the failure probability is nonlinear in both $\RequiredComponentCount$ and $\TimeInstant$, approaching $\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant$ only when that product is small.

[^fn-fits-failure-rate]: **Failure rate ($\ComponentFailureRate$)**\index{Failure rate!FITs}: Expressed in FITs (Failures In Time), where 1 FIT equals one failure per billion device-hours. A data center GPU with a `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_attr_str` mean time to failure has `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fit_eq_math`, corresponding to `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.lambda_eq_math` failures/hour. That seems negligible for one device but becomes dominant at fleet scale: a cluster with `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str` accumulates `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_fit_str` FITs from GPUs alone, translating to an expected GPU failure every `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between_str`.

$$ \ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant} $$ {#eq-single-component-reliability}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The independence, exponential-lifetime, and Poisson results this failure arithmetic rests on are developed in @sec-appdx-reliability-foundations-probability-tools.
:::

The expected time to failure of this component equals $1/\ComponentFailureRate$. In this book's convention, mean time to failure (MTTF)\index{MTTF!per-component failure rate}\index{MTTF!vs. MTBF}\index{Mean time to failure|see{MTTF}} names a single component's expected time to its first failure. MTBF\index{MTBF!system failure rate}\index{MTBF!component vs. system} names the repairable system's expected operating time between successive failures, excluding recovery downtime. Under the constant-rate exponential model used here the two coincide numerically, and the fault-tolerance model uses MTTF for per-component constants and MTBF for composed system rates. Data center GPUs often use planning MTTF values in the tens of thousands of hours, with field behavior depending on operating conditions, cooling effectiveness, manufacturing variation, and workload stress.[^fn-gpu-mtbf-reliability] @Sec-appdx-reliability-foundations-component-rates catalogs the reference per-component FIT and MTTF values (GPU, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), network interface card (NIC), power supply, PCIe switch, optical cable, ToR switch) that anchor these $\ComponentFailureRate$ and FIT figures. A reader can substitute the constant for any device and reproduce the rates used throughout the fault-tolerance analysis.

[^fn-gpu-mtbf-reliability]: **GPU MTTF variation**\index{GPU!MTBF variation}\index{MTBF!GPU field variation}: This chapter uses `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_prose_str` as a planning constant for current data center GPUs (A100 and H100 class), not as a guarantee for every deployed GPU. Published fleet studies from Google TPUv4 pods and Meta GPU clusters report that field reliability depends on topology, cooling, workload, and operational practice [@zu2024tpuv4; @kokolis2025; @dubey2024llama]. The planning constant therefore anchors the arithmetic, while operators should substitute measured fleet rates when they have them.

When multiple independent components operate in a system where any single failure causes system failure, @eq-system-reliability-product formalizes how system reliability becomes the product of individual component reliabilities:

$$ \SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = \prod_{i=1}^{\RequiredComponentCount} {\ComponentReliability}_i(\TimeInstant) = \prod_{i=1}^{\RequiredComponentCount} e^{-\ComponentFailureRate_i \TimeInstant} $$ {#eq-system-reliability-product}

For $\RequiredComponentCount$ identical components with individual failure rate $\ComponentFailureRate$, @eq-system-reliability-n-components gives the identical-component simplification:

$$ \SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant} $$ {#eq-system-reliability-n-components}

The system failure rate becomes $\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate$, and @eq-system-mtbf expresses how the system MTBF scales inversely with component count. This inverse scaling explains why per-device reliability that looks excellent in isolation erodes at cluster scale:

$$ \SystemMtbf = \frac{1}{\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate} = \frac{\ComponentMttf}{\RequiredComponentCount} $$ {#eq-system-mtbf}

The consequence is a gap between failure cadence and job length. At `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str`, the GPU-only calculation gives an expected interval of `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between_str`, so a training run measured in weeks accumulates dozens of expected failures and one measured in months accumulates hundreds. These are planning averages, not a schedule of incidents; a shorter job can finish without failure even when its expected failure count exceeds one. Once the expected time between failures falls below the length of the job, fault tolerance becomes part of the execution budget for long-running fleet work. Applied to the landmark training runs of @sec-vol2-introduction-scale-moment, whose accelerator counts grew by about four orders of magnitude between 2012 and 2024, the same per-device planning rate puts the largest of them, with more than ten thousand GPUs, below a 10-hour system MTBF. Recovery therefore becomes an active scheduling constraint rather than a reliability feature.

### Composing component reliability {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-quantitative-analysis}

The GPU-only calculation of @eq-system-mtbf supplies the scale intuition; a real training system then composes GPUs, HBM, links, power supplies, storage paths, and redundancy into one failure budget. Component rates are usually quoted in the FIT units introduced with the failure rate, so the `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_attr_str` GPU contributes `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_fit_str` FIT to whatever system contains it. The new question is how different component rates compose, and the composition rule depends on the redundancy structure and the independence assumptions. For series systems\index{Reliability!series system}\index{Series system!reliability calculation} (for example, a node where all `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs must work), failure of any component fails the whole. With independent constant-rate failures, the reliabilities multiply as in @eq-system-reliability-product, so the rates add even when the components differ:
$$\SystemMtbf = \frac{1}{\sum \ComponentFailureRate_i}$$
Under this additive failure-rate law, the system failure rate grows linearly with component count while system MTBF falls in inverse proportion. Every unredundanted component on the critical path adds its FIT contribution directly to the denominator.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-nines-reliability
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class NinesReliability:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    availability_pct = 99.99
    single_gpu_success = availability_pct / 100

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    downtime_min_year = (1 - single_gpu_success) * HOURS_PER_YEAR * MINUTES_PER_HOUR
    cluster_prob = single_gpu_success**n_gpus
    fleet_mtbf = FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between * hour
    fast_mttr = 5 * minute
    slow_mttr = 30 * minute
    fast_availability = (fleet_mtbf / (fleet_mtbf + fast_mttr)).to("").magnitude
    slow_availability = (fleet_mtbf / (fleet_mtbf + slow_mttr)).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < cluster_prob < 1, "Probability must be in (0,1)")
    check(cluster_prob < 0.5, "Cluster survival must be low at scale")
    check(0 < slow_availability < fast_availability < 1, "Faster repair must improve availability")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0)
    availability_str = fmt_percent(availability_pct / 100, precision=2, commas=False, style='prose')
    downtime_min_str = fmt_time(downtime_min_year, 'minute', precision=1, commas=False, style='word')
    cluster_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(cluster_prob * 100) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    fleet_mtbf_str = fmt_time(fleet_mtbf, hour, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    fast_mttr_str = fmt_time(fast_mttr, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    slow_mttr_str = fmt_time(slow_mttr, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    fast_availability_str = fmt_percent(fast_availability, precision=2, commas=False, style="prose")
    slow_availability_str = fmt_percent(slow_availability, precision=2, commas=False, style="prose")
```

The same product governs instantaneous availability, a different quantity from the survival function $\ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant)$. Availability $\SteadyStateAvailability$ is the probability that a component is up at a randomly chosen instant, counting repairs, whereas $\ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant)$ is the probability that it has not yet failed by time $\TimeInstant$. If each GPU is independently up with probability $\GpuAvailability$, all $\RequiredComponentCount$ are up together with probability $(\GpuAvailability)^\RequiredComponentCount$, which is the reliability gap of @eq-reliability-gap. For the chapter's `{python} NinesReliability.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster, a per-GPU availability of `{python} NinesReliability.availability_str` (only `{python} NinesReliability.downtime_min_str` of downtime per year) leaves about a `{python} NinesReliability.cluster_pct_str` chance that every GPU is up at the same instant. That power erodes even highly reliable hardware once $\RequiredComponentCount$ reaches fleet scale, so software must handle failures automatically.

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-scale-transforms-failure .callout-perspective title="Scale transforms failure"}

A cluster of `{python} NinesReliability.n_gpus_str` GPUs turns a per-GPU MTTF of `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.gpu_mttf_prose_str` into a system MTBF of `{python} NinesReliability.fleet_mtbf_str`. For a repairable system, steady-state availability\index{Availability!MTBF and MTTR} is $\SteadyStateAvailability= \MeanTimeBetweenFailures/(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures+\MeanTimeToRepair)$, where mean time to recovery (MTTR)\index{MTTR!availability impact}\index{MTTR!recovery interval}\index{Mean time to recovery|see{MTTR}} is the recovery interval. Cutting MTTR from `{python} NinesReliability.slow_mttr_str` to `{python} NinesReliability.fast_mttr_str` raises availability from `{python} NinesReliability.slow_availability_str` to `{python} NinesReliability.fast_availability_str`. This stationary two-state model assumes unconstrained repair capacity and complete outage; correlated incidents, repair contention, and degraded operation require direct measurement [@birolini2017]. Systems must engineer recovery, not merely improve components.

:::

Engineering faster recovery is one response to that arithmetic; redundancy is the other. For parallel systems\index{Reliability!parallel system}\index{Parallel system!redundancy calculation} providing redundancy, suppose that any surviving component can satisfy the required service. With independent failures and no repair during the observation interval, the system survives until every component has failed:
$$\SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{\RedundantComponentCount} (1 - {\ComponentReliability}_i(\TimeInstant))$$

Series composition is the training job's problem, because a synchronous step needs every participant. Parallel composition is the serving fleet's lever, and it returns when interchangeable replicas protect a latency contract. Both rules, however, describe whatever the model calls a component, and the fault rate assigned to that component depends on which protections sit inside it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ UNPROTECTED-HBM SOFT-ERROR BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Goal: Show why unprotected HBM at cluster scale corrupts memory every tens of seconds.
# │ How: 250 FIT/Mbit x (1,024 x H100 HBM) megabits -> aggregate FIT -> mean time to first error.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_time

class HbmSerBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ser_fit_per_mbit = Systems.Reliability.Hbm.soft_error_fit_per_mbit
    cluster_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    hbm_per_gpu = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    total_mbit = (cluster_gpus * hbm_per_gpu).to(bit).magnitude / 1e6
    aggregate_fit = float(ser_fit_per_mbit) * total_mbit
    failures_per_hour = aggregate_fit / BILLION  # FIT = failures per 1e9 device-hours
    time_to_error_s = SEC_PER_HOUR / failures_per_hour
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(10 <= time_to_error_s <= 60, "Illustrative raw-error interval should be tens of seconds")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    fit_per_mbit_str = fmt(ser_fit_per_mbit, precision=0, commas=False)
    time_to_error_str = fmt_time(round(time_to_error_s), 'second', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    cluster_gpus_str = fmt(cluster_gpus, precision=0, commas=True)
    hbm_per_gpu_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(hbm_per_gpu, unit=GiB, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#lhs-fault-tolerance-archetype-a-gpt-4-llama-3-memory-soft-error .callout-lighthouse title="Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Memory soft-error scale"}

Composition makes the distinction between raw faults and job interruptions essential. Memory soft-error rates are quoted per megabit of storage rather than per device, so the exposure grows with memory capacity. As an illustrative raw-bit-error budget, assume `{python} HbmSerBudget.fit_per_mbit_str` FIT per megabit across `{python} HbmSerBudget.cluster_gpus_str` GPUs with `{python} HbmSerBudget.hbm_per_gpu_gb_str` each, the size of the Archetype A reference cluster. The resulting interval between raw memory errors is roughly `{python} HbmSerBudget.time_to_error_str`. This is not a measured job-failure interval. Error-correcting code (ECC) protection can correct covered error patterns before they affect computation, while detected uncorrectable errors and escaped corruption require different recovery paths. At that raw rate, unprotected memory in the reference cluster would corrupt training state many times per hour, so ECC is a precondition for large-scale training rather than an option. A fleet reliability budget therefore needs the residual job-interrupting and silent-corruption rates under its actual protection scheme; raw bit-error rates alone cannot establish whether memory, logic, or interconnect dominates.

:::

These raw bit-error rates justify ECC, but they are not the interruption rates that set checkpoint cadence; the worked cascade that follows uses device MTTF values that already include the effect of that protection. The cascade also treats its GPU, PCIe, power, and network contributions as separate categories, so a measured whole-node rate that already includes those paths cannot be added to them again.

### Cluster MTBF calculation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-worked-example-cluster-mtbf-calculation-9255}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fault-tolerance-mtbf-cascade
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLUSTER MTBF CASCADE — WORKED EXAMPLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-worked-example-cluster-
# │          mtbf-calculation-9255. Drives the Steps 1-3 display equations and the
# │          closing narrative (every 3.9 h, 6.2/day, ~43/week).
# │
# │ Goal: Reproduce the worked MTBF cascade from canonical MTTF/fleet constants so
# │       every quoted rate is traceable and cannot drift.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor — checkpoint analysis reuses the worked cluster MTBF.
# │ Show: lambda per subsystem, total, system rate, cluster MTBF, failure cadence.
# │ How:  lambda = 1/MTTF; network shared across the node's GPUs; power enters only
# │       through series (non-redundant) PSUs, 0 for the DGX H100's 4+2 supply;
# │       system = N*total. Narrative cadence follows the displayed rate (0.2583)
# │       for self-consistency.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_rate, fmt_time

class FailureCascadeExample:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    fleet_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    gpu_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    pcie_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.PcieSwitch.mttf_hours)
    psu_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.Psu.mttf_hours)
    nic_mttf = float(Systems.Reliability.Nic.mttf_hours)
    gpus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node
    series_psus = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.series_psus  # 0: 4+2 redundant supplies
    psus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.psus_per_node
    psu_redundancy = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.psu_redundancy
    psus_required = psus_per_node - psu_redundancy
    ref_gpus = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference.system.total_accelerators

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    l_gpu = 1 / gpu_mttf
    l_pcie = 1 / pcie_mttf
    l_power = (series_psus / gpus_per_node) / psu_mttf  # 0 for the DGX H100's 4+2 supply
    l_net = (1 / gpus_per_node) / nic_mttf
    l_total = l_gpu + l_pcie + l_power + l_net
    l_system = fleet_gpus * l_total
    l_system_disp = round(l_system, 4)  # rate as displayed (0.2583)
    mtbf_h = 1 / l_system_disp  # narrative follows the displayed rate
    per_day = 24 * l_system_disp
    per_week = 24 * 7 * l_system_disp
    weekly_failures = round(per_week)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(0 < l_gpu < 1, "per-GPU failure rate must be a small positive value")
    check(l_power == 0, "DGX H100 PSUs are 4+2 redundant: no single-PSU term in the series sum")
    check(2.0 < mtbf_h < 5.0, "10k-GPU cluster MTBF should be a few hours")
    check(per_week > per_day > 1, "weekly failures must exceed daily, both above one")
    check(9 < fleet_gpus / ref_gpus < 11, "prose says 'roughly ten times' the reference cluster")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    fleet_gpus_str = fmt(fleet_gpus, precision=0)
    ref_gpus_str = fmt(ref_gpus, precision=0)
    gpu_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    pcie_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(pcie_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    psu_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(psu_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    nic_mttf_hours_str = fmt_time(nic_mttf, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    gpus_per_node_str = fmt(gpus_per_node, precision=0)
    psus_per_node_str = fmt(psus_per_node, precision=0)
    psus_required_str = fmt(psus_required, precision=0)
    psu_redundancy_str = fmt(psu_redundancy, precision=0)
    _gpu_d = fmt(gpu_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _pcie_d = fmt(pcie_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _psu_d = fmt(psu_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _nic_d = fmt(nic_mttf, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _fleet_d = fleet_gpus_str.replace(",", "{,}")
    _npn = gpus_per_node_str
    lambda_gpu_eq_math = fmt_display_math(rf" \GpuFailureRate = \frac{{1}}{{{_gpu_d}}} = {l_gpu*1e5:.1f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} ")
    lambda_pcie_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \PcieLinkFailureRate = \frac{{1}}{{{_pcie_d}}} = {l_pcie*1e5:.1f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_power_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \PerGpuPowerFailureRate = \frac{{\SeriesPsuCount}}{{{_npn}}} \times \frac{{1}}{{{_psu_d}}} = \frac{{{series_psus}}}{{{_npn}}} \times \frac{{1}}{{{_psu_d}}} = 0 \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_net_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \PerGpuNetworkFailureRate = \frac{{1}}{{{_npn}}} \times \frac{{1}}{{{_nic_d}}} = {l_net*1e5:.3f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_total_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \PerGpuTotalFailureRate = ({l_gpu*1e5:.1f} + {l_pcie*1e5:.1f} + {l_net*1e5:.3f}) \times 10^{{-5}} = {l_total*1e5:.3f} \times 10^{{-5}} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    lambda_system_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf" \SystemFailureRate = {_fleet_d} \times {l_total*1e5:.3f} \times 10^{{-5}} = {l_system:.4f} \text{{ failures/hour}} "
    )
    mtbf_eq_math = fmt_display_math(rf" \SystemMtbf = \frac{{1}}{{{l_system_disp:.4f}}} = {mtbf_h:.2f} \text{{ hours}} ")
    mtbf_hours_str = fmt_time(mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    mtbf_hours_2dp_str = fmt_time(mtbf_h, "hour", precision=2, commas=False, style="word")
    failures_per_day_str = fmt_rate(per_day, "failures/day", precision=1, commas=False)
    weekly_failures_str = fmt_count(weekly_failures, precision=0, label="failure")
```

Consider a training cluster designed for large language model development, roughly ten times the `{python} FailureCascadeExample.ref_gpus_str`-GPU Archetype A reference cluster, with the following specifications:

- `{python} FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus_str` NVIDIA H100\index{H100!cluster reliability}\index{NVIDIA!H100} GPUs
- Individual GPU MTTF: `{python} FailureCascadeExample.gpu_mttf_hours_str`
- Each GPU connected to host via PCIe (MTTF: `{python} FailureCascadeExample.pcie_mttf_hours_str`)
- Each node contains `{python} FailureCascadeExample.gpus_per_node_str` GPUs fed by `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psus_per_node_str` power supply units (MTTF: `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psu_mttf_hours_str` each) in `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psus_required_str`+`{python} FailureCascadeExample.psu_redundancy_str` redundancy, so the node keeps full performance with any `{python} FailureCascadeExample.psu_redundancy_str` of them failed
- Network infrastructure per node (NIC, cables): MTTF `{python} FailureCascadeExample.nic_mttf_hours_str`

Each GPU operates within a failure domain that includes the GPU itself, its PCIe connection, and a proportional share of the node's shared power and network infrastructure. Dividing a node-wide subsystem rate by the `{python} FailureCascadeExample.gpus_per_node_str` GPUs in the node prorates one shared failure source across those GPUs, so that multiplying the per-GPU total by all `{python} FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus_str` GPUs in the final step counts each node's shared hardware once per node rather than eight times. Power enters the sum only through supplies whose single failure stops the node, counted as $\SeriesPsuCount$ in the power equation. With the node's supplies in redundant sets, no single unit qualifies, so the power term below is zero in this first-order calculation. The approximation omits the residual risk that additional independent failures exhaust redundancy before repair. A fault upstream of the chassis, such as the loss of the circuits feeding it, can also take down the whole node. That risk belongs to the correlated failures treated later in this chapter. The four subsystem rates follow from their MTTF values:

`{python} FailureCascadeExample.lambda_gpu_eq_math`

`{python} FailureCascadeExample.lambda_pcie_eq_math`

`{python} FailureCascadeExample.lambda_power_eq_math`

`{python} FailureCascadeExample.lambda_net_eq_math`

Because the subsystems sit in series, their rates add to a per-GPU total:

`{python} FailureCascadeExample.lambda_total_eq_math`

Multiplying that total by the cluster size gives the system failure rate, whose reciprocal is the cluster MTBF:

`{python} FailureCascadeExample.lambda_system_eq_math`

`{python} FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_eq_math`

Under the model, the cluster experiences a failure every `{python} FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_hours_str` on average. The expected failure cadence is `{python} FailureCascadeExample.failures_per_day_str`; a training run lasting one week has an expected count of `{python} FailureCascadeExample.weekly_failures_str`. Actual incident times vary, but the expected loss is large enough that recovery must be part of normal execution planning.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The step-by-step composition of per-component failure rates into a fleet-wide system MTBF, reusable for any node design or cluster size, is developed in @sec-appdx-reliability-foundations-mtbf-cascade.
:::

The cluster MTBF scaling\index{Cluster!MTBF scaling} in @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling isolates the GPU-only baseline across cluster sizes. The full-system calculation is lower once PCIe and network failure domains are included. The same 10,000-GPU cluster therefore carries three MTBF values in this chapter. Each later calculation names the one it uses: the GPU-only `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between_str` of this table, the full-system `{python} FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_hours_str` of the cascade above, and the two-to-three-hour cadence that somewhat larger production runs report below. Two running scenarios carry the rest of the chapter. The `{python} FailureCascadeExample.ref_gpus_str`-GPU Archetype A reference cluster sizes per-node state, restore paths, and the elastic and straggler examples, while the `{python} FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus_str`-GPU cluster of the cascade sets failure cadence and checkpoint intervals. The full-system MTBF is the default input; a calculation that uses the GPU-only value says so, usually because it compares cluster sizes on the common basis of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling, and its failure count is then a lower bound.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: cluster-mtbf-scaling-table
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLUSTER MTBF SCALING TABLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling — GPU-only MTBF and failures-per-day rows
# │          across seven cluster sizes.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute each row's cluster MTBF and expected failures per day from the
# │       single canonical per-GPU MTTF constant, so the whole table reproduces
# │       the 1/N scaling law and cannot drift from the registry.
# │ Show: Per-row cluster MTBF (hours, plus a days parenthetical for the long-MTBF
# │       rows) and expected failures per day.
# │ How:  cluster_mtbf = MTTF / N; failures_per_day = 24 * N / MTTF.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import day, hour
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_text, fmt_time

def _mtbf_h(v):
    # integer-like rows display as whole hours; fractional rows keep one place
    return fmt_time(round(v) * hour, hour, precision=0, commas=True, style="word")

def _mtbf_cell(v):
    # show the days parenthetical only where the cluster MTBF is at least a day
    hrs = _mtbf_h(v)
    if v >= 24.0:
        days = fmt_time(round(v / 24.0) * day, day, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
        return fmt_text(hrs, " (", days, ")")
    return hrs

def _fpd_cell(v):
    if v < 0.01:
        return fmt(v, precision=3, commas=False)
    if v < 1.0:
        return fmt(v, precision=2, commas=False)
    if float(round(v, 1)).is_integer():
        return fmt_int(int(round(v)))
    return fmt(v, precision=1, commas=False)

class ClusterMtbfScaling:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    sizes = [8, 64, 512, 1000, 4000, 10000, 25000]

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    cluster_mtbf_h = []
    failures_per_day = []
    for _n in sizes:
        cluster_mtbf_h.append(gpu_mttf_h / _n)
        failures_per_day.append(24.0 * _n / gpu_mttf_h)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(cluster_mtbf_h[3] - 50.0) < 1e-9 and abs(cluster_mtbf_h[5] - 5.0) < 1e-9, "1,000-GPU MTBF must be 50h and 10,000-GPU MTBF must be 5h")
    check(abs(failures_per_day[5] - 4.8) < 0.01, "10,000-GPU failure rate must be 4.8 failures/day")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    gpu_mttf_hrs_str = fmt_time(round(gpu_mttf_h) * hour, hour, precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    n0_str, n1_str, n2_str, n3_str, n4_str, n5_str, n6_str = [fmt_int(_n) for _n in sizes]
    mtbf0_str, mtbf1_str, mtbf2_str, mtbf3_str, mtbf4_str, mtbf5_str, mtbf6_str = [_mtbf_cell(_v) for _v in cluster_mtbf_h]
    fpd0_str, fpd1_str, fpd2_str, fpd3_str, fpd4_str, fpd5_str, fpd6_str = [_fpd_cell(_v) for _v in failures_per_day]
```

| **Cluster size (GPUs)**              |            **Individual GPU MTTF**             |             **Cluster MTBF**            |     **Expected failures per day**      |
|:-------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------:|
| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n0_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf0_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd0_str` |
| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n1_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf1_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd1_str` |
| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n2_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf2_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd2_str` |
| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n3_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf3_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd3_str` |
| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n4_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf4_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd4_str` |
| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n5_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf5_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd5_str` |
| `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n6_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.gpu_mttf_hrs_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf6_str` | `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.fpd6_str` |

: **Cluster MTBF Scaling**: GPU-only mean time between failures falls in inverse proportion to cluster size, transforming failures from rare events to continuous operating conditions at scale. Additional host, power, storage, and network failure domains reduce system-level MTBF further. {#tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: published-failure-rates
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PUBLISHED FAILURE RATES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The Kokolis/Llama 3 paragraph below and @fig-published-failure-rates.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the published fleet MTTF evidence to Literature so the prose and
# │       the figure quote the same measured and projected values.
# │ Show: 16,384-GPU projected MTTF (1.8 h); Llama 3 405B snapshot of 419
# │       unexpected interruptions over 54 days on 16,384 H100s (~3.1 h MTTF).
# │ How:  Literature.FleetOperations.Kokolis*; Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_*;
# │       Models.Language.Llama3_405B.training_accelerators_ref; MTTF = days*24/count.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature, Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_time

class PublishedFailureRates:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    kokolis_16k_mttf_h = float(Literature.FleetOperations.Kokolis16KGpuProjectedMttfHours)
    llama_gpus = Models.Language.Llama3_405B.training_accelerators_ref.magnitude
    llama_interruptions = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_UnexpectedInterruptions)
    llama_days = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_SnapshotDays)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    llama_mttf_h = llama_days * 24 / llama_interruptions

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(float(Literature.FleetOperations.Kokolis16KGpuJobGpus) - llama_gpus) < 1, "Kokolis projection and Llama 3 run must share a job size")
    check(1.5 < kokolis_16k_mttf_h < 2.0 and 2.5 < llama_mttf_h < 3.5, "prose brackets the cadence at 'roughly two to three hours'")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(kokolis_16k_mttf_h, "hour", precision=1, style="word", attributive=True)
    llama_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(llama_mttf_h, "hour", precision=1, style="word", attributive=True)
    llama_mttf_str = fmt_time(llama_mttf_h, "hour", precision=1, style="word")
    llama_gpus_str = fmt(llama_gpus, precision=0)
    llama_interruptions_str = fmt(llama_interruptions, precision=0)
    llama_days_str = fmt(llama_days, precision=0)
```

Production measurements confirm the $1/\AcceleratorCount$ trend of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling and show that the GPU-only line is optimistic. Plotted on log-log axes, measured MTTF values and fitted projections from Meta's clusters follow the slope of the $50{,}000\,\text{h}/\AcceleratorCount$ line across more than three orders of magnitude in job size but sit below it. The gap arises because a job can be interrupted by far more than its GPUs (@fig-published-failure-rates). The @kokolis2025 study of Meta's Research SuperCluster reported measured MTTF values for observed RSC job sizes and projected a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` MTTF for `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU jobs. That projection lands next to the Llama 3\index{Llama-3!failure report} run previewed in @sec-vol2-introduction-scale-moment (war story \ref{ws-fault-tolerance-llama3-failure-cadence} follows its recovery). That run recorded `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_interruptions_str` unexpected interruptions across a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_days_str`-day snapshot on `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str` H100 GPUs, which gives an observed MTTF of about `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_str`. Together, the measured Llama run and Kokolis projection put `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU training on a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours, bracketed by the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` projection and the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_attr_str` measurement. This evidence turns the idealized $1/\AcceleratorCount$ relation into an engineering constraint that determines checkpoint frequency, recovery architecture, and infrastructure investment.

::: {#fig-published-failure-rates fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Published Failure Rates from Production Clusters**: Measured MTTF values and fitted projections from Meta's RSC clusters [@kokolis2025] plotted with Llama 3 training measurements [@dubey2024llama] against the theoretical 1/N curve. At 16,384 GPUs, the Kokolis projection and the Llama 3 empirical measurement bracket a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours (the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` projection and the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_attr_str` measurement), confirming that fault tolerance is a mathematical necessity, not an edge case. Data sources: Kokolis et al., arXiv:2410.21680; Meta, arXiv:2407.21783." fig-alt="Log-log scatter plot of mean time to failure in hours versus GPU count with a dashed theoretical 50,000 hours over N line. Filled blue dots mark measured Meta RSC values at 8 and 1,024 GPUs, hollow blue dots mark projections at 16,384 and 131K GPUs, and a dark diamond marks the Llama 3 measurement of 3.1 hours. A short light red band at 16,384 GPUs spans 1.8 to 3.1 hours, labeled failure every 2 to 3 h. Dotted gray reference lines mark 1 day, 1 week, and 3 months."}

## Failure Taxonomy {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-taxonomy-e78c}

A network partition that clears in seconds and a permanent GPU failure both interrupt a training step, yet retrying the first succeeds while retrying the second wastes cluster time on dead silicon. Silent memory corruption that produces wrong gradients demands a different defense again from a node crash that stops responding altogether. While the MTBF calculations quantify *how often* interruptions arrive, which sets checkpoint intervals and spare-pool sizes, choosing the right recovery action requires distinguishing *what kind* of failure has occurred. In standard reliability terms, a fault is the underlying defect or disturbance, an error is the corrupted internal state it produces, and a failure is the externally visible misbehavior that the training or serving system must handle [@avizienis2004basic].

No single label captures all of these differences. Reliability decisions require three orthogonal axes [@constantinescu2008; @lamport1982byzantine]: persistence (transient, intermittent, or permanent), manifestation (fail-stop, degraded, or value-corrupting), and failure scope (one device, one node, a rack or power domain, or the whole job). Two manifestations need names because liveness checks cannot see them. A **gray failure**\index{Gray failure!definition} is a component that stays alive but runs slowly or erratically, so it keeps answering the liveness checks that would flag a crash while every peer that waits on it slows down. **Silent data corruption (SDC)**\index{Silent data corruption!definition} goes further, producing wrong values with no error at all. Because the three axes are independent, a single fault sits on all three at once: a transient disturbance can manifest as either a detected crash or silent corruption, while a permanent switch failure can remain confined to one rack or partition an entire job. Each axis governs a different operational choice. Persistence determines whether a fault clears on its own or requires hardware quarantine and replacement (@sec-ft-fault-persistence-response). Manifestation separates crashed ranks from slow stragglers (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distinguishing-stragglers-failures-285d) and from Byzantine value corruption, while scope determines when a single shared hazard can defeat naive redundancy.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEASURED INTERRUPTION ROOT CAUSES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Paragraph opening the failure taxonomy and
# │          @fig-llama3-interruptions.
# │
# │ Goal: Show which failures a large training run actually meets.
# │ Show: GPU components 268 of 419 (~64%), software bugs 54, network 35,
# │       host components 21; six detected silent data corruptions.
# │ How: Counts from Literature.Series.Llama3Interruptions, cross-checked
# │      against Literature.TrainingRuns totals.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature, Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent

def _by_category(rows):
    out = {}
    for r in rows:
        out[r["category"]] = out.get(r["category"], 0) + r["interruption_count"]
    return out

def _component(rows, name):
    return next(r["interruption_count"] for r in rows if r["component"] == name)

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class InterruptionCauses:
    """Root causes of unexpected interruptions in Llama 3 405B pretraining."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    rows = Literature.Series.Llama3Interruptions.entries
    total_ref = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_UnexpectedInterruptions)
    days = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_SnapshotDays)
    gpus = Models.Language.Llama3_405B.training_accelerators_ref.magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    total = sum(r["interruption_count"] for r in rows)
    cats = _by_category(rows)
    gpu_share = cats["GPU"] / total
    faulty_gpu = _component(rows, "Faulty GPU")
    hbm = _component(rows, "GPU HBM3 Memory")
    software = _component(rows, "Software Bug")
    sdc = _component(rows, "Silent Data Corruption")

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(total == total_ref, f"Table 5 counts must sum to the registry total {total_ref}, got {total}.")
    check(0.6 <= gpu_share <= 0.7, f"Prose says GPU components caused about two-thirds, got {gpu_share:.2f}.")
    check(cats["GPU"] > cats["Dependency"] > cats["Network"] > cats["Host"], "Prose orders GPU > software > network > host.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    total_str = fmt_int(total)
    days_str = fmt(days, precision=0)
    gpus_str = fmt(gpus, precision=0)
    gpu_count_str = fmt_int(cats["GPU"])
    gpu_share_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(gpu_share, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    faulty_gpu_str = fmt_int(faulty_gpu)
    hbm_str = fmt_int(hbm)
    software_str = fmt_int(software)
    network_str = fmt_int(cats["Network"])
    host_str = fmt_int(cats["Host"])
    sdc_str = fmt_int(sdc)
```

Production logs show which of these failures a large run actually meets. During a `{python} InterruptionCauses.days_str`-day period of Llama 3 405B pretraining on `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpus_str` H100 GPUs, Meta traced each of `{python} InterruptionCauses.total_str` unexpected interruptions to a root cause [@dubey2024llama]. Grouped by cause in @fig-llama3-interruptions, GPU components account for `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpu_count_str` of them, about `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpu_share_pct_str`, led by `{python} InterruptionCauses.faulty_gpu_str` faulty GPUs and `{python} InterruptionCauses.hbm_str` HBM memory failures. Software bugs caused `{python} InterruptionCauses.software_str`, network switches and cables `{python} InterruptionCauses.network_str`, and the remaining host hardware, from NICs to power supplies, `{python} InterruptionCauses.host_str` between them. Only `{python} InterruptionCauses.sdc_str` interruptions were attributed to silent data corruption, and that count includes only corruption that was caught. Most fault-tolerance effort therefore goes to frequent, detectable accelerator failures, while the rare silent ones demand a different kind of defense.

::: {#fig-llama3-interruptions fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Root Causes of Training Interruptions**: The 419 unexpected interruptions recorded over 54 days of Llama 3 405B pretraining on 16,384 H100 GPUs, by root-cause component and colored by category. GPU components dominate; silent data corruption appears only where it was detected. Counts are from Table 5 of @dubey2024llama; one percentage in that table (Faulty GPU) disagrees with its count, so shares here are computed from the counts." fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of 18 root-cause components sorted by count, colored by category. Faulty GPU leads with 148 interruptions, then GPU HBM3 memory 72, software bug 54, network switch or cable 35, host maintenance 32, GPU SRAM memory 19, and GPU system processor 17. The remaining components each caused 7 or fewer, including NIC 7, NCCL watchdog timeouts 7, silent data corruption 6, and GPU thermal interface and sensor 6."}

### Transient failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-transient-failures-57b4}

A transient fault clears without physical repair, but the state it corrupts can persist after the disturbance ends, forcing recovery to retry or validate affected work before relying on that state. In large-scale training systems, temporary disruptions range from network packet loss\index{Transient fault!network packet loss}, where dropped packets are recovered by transport retransmission, to memory bit flips\index{Memory!bit flip} triggered by cosmic-ray-induced single-event upsets.[^fn-seu-soft-error] Timing disturbances can be equally disruptive without corrupting bits directly. Under temperature spikes, thermal throttling\index{Thermal throttling!performance degradation} reduces compute throughput without halting execution. Software timeouts\index{Software timeout!resource contention} fire when transient contention delays a collective beyond its allotted window.

[^fn-seu-soft-error]: **Single-event upset (SEU)**\index{SEU!error rate}: From particle physics, where "upset" denotes a nondestructive state change. Cosmic rays and alpha particles from chip packaging can flip bits in memory and logic; the observed rate depends on altitude, process technology, packaging materials, shielding, and workload [@ziegler1996; @baumann2005]. ECC memory corrects single-bit errors but cannot handle every multi-bit upset in the same word, leaving a residual silent-corruption risk that compounds across the terabytes of state in large-scale ML training.

Transient faults are particularly difficult to diagnose in ML training when they leave no explicit error signal. If hardware protection and the computation itself do not mask a memory bit flip during gradient computation, the corrupted value propagates into later updates while training continues. Large-scale SDC studies document such escaped corruption in production processors, and DRAM field studies confirm that memory errors occur frequently enough to require fleet-level monitoring [@dixit2021silent; @sridharan2015; @schroeder2009]. In ML training, that undetected corruption surfaces as degraded gradients, anomalous loss curves, or rollback-worthy checkpoints rather than an explicit crash.

How the system responds to a transient failure therefore depends on whether the fault announces itself. Errors that raise explicit exceptions can be handled through bounded retry logic, whereas silent corruption requires end-to-end validation. Checksums catch altered bytes in storage or transport, cross-rank digests expose disagreement across a supposedly identical reduced buffer, and statistical or replay checks test whether the computation itself remains plausible. Because a rank that computes the wrong local gradient and then checksums those wrong bytes will pass an ordinary transport check, only independent recomputation, invariants, or model-level evidence can expose the error.

### Fail-stop failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failstop-failures-5cdd}

In synchronous distributed training, a single participant that goes silent stalls the entire group's next update. A conventional AllReduce cannot complete until every rank supplies its input, so one dead GPU in a 10,000-GPU job can leave the other 9,999 accelerators waiting at the barrier until recovery begins. Smaller communication groups limit the immediate dependency, although pipeline or data-parallel stages soon propagate the stall across the rest of the job. Such **fail-stop failures**\index{Fail-stop failure!characteristics}\index{Fail-stop failure!detection and recovery} occur when a component ceases operation outright and stops responding to requests. A GPU hardware failure\index{GPU!hardware failure} renders an individual accelerator unresponsive, and a host node crash\index{Node!crash} terminates all training processes on the machine. A network partition\index{Network partition!fault tolerance} severs communication between a healthy node and the cluster, and a storage failure\index{Storage!failure} blocks workers from reading or writing checkpoint shards.

A stopped component gives a clearer symptom than one that keeps returning plausible but incorrect values. Yet a stopped rank announces itself only through silence, so detection rests on timeouts that must separate an outright crash from a slow or isolated host, such as a GPU still writing a large checkpoint while the collective waits. Once a timeout flags the missing participant, the recovery system replaces or restarts it and restores the most recent valid checkpoint; @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-mechanisms-efed sets that timeout threshold once the full recovery-time budget is in view.

### Byzantine failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-byzantine-failures-8a24}

Where a fail-stop component ceases to participate, a value-corrupting component can keep running while returning incorrect results. A GPU may return wrong gradients without raising an error, a link may deliver a corrupted packet whose error pattern the CRC happens not to cover, or a worker may compute different results for identical inputs and state. Byzantine failures\index{Byzantine failure!classification} allow arbitrary behavior, including inconsistent messages to different participants [@lamport1982byzantine]. ML systems can encounter this broader failure model through silent data corruption\index{Silent data corruption!mechanism} or adversarial corruption. Numerical instability\index{Numerical instability!Byzantine failure} and determinism violations\index{Determinism!violation} also require validation when they break the execution contract, but ordinary rounding differences or intentionally stochastic outputs are not themselves evidence of a faulty worker. The recovery concern is a participant whose accepted contribution can corrupt shared state without a visible crash.

The two models leave different evidence (@fig-failure-types). A fail-stop worker such as W2 falls silent, and its missing heartbeats make it suspect. A Byzantine worker such as W6 keeps sending messages on schedule, so it passes every liveness check while the values it sends are wrong.

::: {#fig-failure-types fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Fail-Stop vs. Byzantine Failures**: In the fail-stop model (left), a failed worker simply ceases to send messages, which a timeout flags as suspect without distinguishing a crash from delay or isolation. In the Byzantine model (right), a failed worker continues to participate but sends incorrect data (for example, corrupted gradients reported as valid), which can poison the global model state if not detected by redundant validation." fig-alt="Two panels divided by a dashed line, each showing four worker message streams along a time axis with a liveness column at the right. Left, fail-stop: W1, W3, and W4 emit regular violet heartbeat ticks and get green checks; W2's ticks stop at a red X, a bracket labeled silence runs to a violet diamond labeled timeout, and W2 gets a red X for liveness. Caption text reads silence is the evidence. Right, Byzantine: W5 to W8 send amber gradient squares on the same schedule and all four get green checks, but partway along W6's row its squares turn red. Text reads on time, but wrong."}
![](images/svg/failure-types.svg)

:::

In an ML fleet, the most common source of value corruption is not an adversary but hardware that changes a value without raising an error, the silent data corruption already met among transient failures. Its physical causes, the training signals that expose it, and the verification and hot-spare defenses that contain it are developed together in @sec-ft-sdc-verification, after the hardware faults that produce it. Whatever its source, a Byzantine contribution violates a contract that liveness checks never test. Ordinary data-parallel workers process different batches and need not produce identical local gradients; the required contract is that each contribution correctly represents its assigned computation. A single Byzantine worker can violate that contract and corrupt the averaged gradient, potentially causing training to diverge or converge to a poor solution.

Redundant computation supplies one form of evidence against Byzantine failures. Workers repeating a computation from matching inputs, state, and random-number streams can compare results under a stated numerical tolerance. Statistical outlier detection and invariants provide additional evidence without fully repeating the computation. Each method has a coverage limit. Agreement can miss shared faults, while a statistical anomaly can arise from legitimate data variation. Detection overhead must therefore be evaluated together with the faults the method can expose.

Byzantine-resilient distributed training algorithms exist but impose significant overhead. Krum [@blanchard2017machine] keeps the single worker gradient whose nearest neighbors lie closest to it and discards the rest, while coordinate-wise trimmed mean [@yin2018byzantine] drops the largest and smallest values in each coordinate before averaging what remains. Both compute aggregates that stay robust to a bounded number of Byzantine workers, but they require more communication and computation than simple averaging. Without such protection, corrupted gradients can push the optimizer toward an unreliable model state while the training job appears healthy. Reliability must therefore protect semantic correctness rather than process liveness alone.[^fn-byzantine-consensus-overhead]

[^fn-byzantine-consensus-overhead]: **Byzantine-resilient ML**\index{Byzantine-resilient ML!algorithmic overhead}\index{Byzantine fault tolerance!ML overhead}: Named after Lamport's 1982 "Byzantine Generals Problem," these algorithms (Krum\index{Byzantine fault tolerance!Krum algorithm}, trimmed mean\index{Byzantine fault tolerance!trimmed mean}, and signSGD, which aggregates only the signs of gradient coordinates by majority vote) tolerate a bounded fraction of corrupted workers, with the exact bound depending on the rule and its assumptions. Krum's original analysis requires $2\ByzantineClientCount + 2 < \KrumClientCount$ for $\ByzantineClientCount$ Byzantine workers among $\KrumClientCount$, while coordinate-wise median and trimmed mean rest on different robustness assumptions, so the tolerated fraction depends on the aggregation rule, dimensionality, and statistical model. For $\KrumClientCount$ workers, Krum requires pairwise distance computations over worker gradients, so overhead grows quadratically with worker count and directly competes with the throughput gains of data parallelism [@blanchard2017machine].

### Correlated failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-correlated-failures-95e8}

The reliability calculations in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-mathematics-inevitable-failure-93ef assume independent failures, yet real systems depart sharply from this assumption when common physical or operational dependencies take down multiple components at once. Within a single node, a power fault that exhausts the chassis's redundant supplies\index{Correlated failure!power supply}, such as the loss of its feed circuits, removes every GPU in the chassis. Across a cluster, a top-of-rack network switch failure\index{Correlated failure!network switch} isolates all attached nodes, while a cooling system failure\index{Correlated failure!cooling system} can trigger thermal shutdowns down an entire row of racks. Shared software and operational dependencies widen the blast radius further. A software bug\index{Correlated failure!software bug} in an updated CUDA driver can crash processes across nodes whenever they exercise the affected code path, and operator error\index{Correlated failure!operator error} during cluster reconfiguration can render an entire fleet unreachable.

Correlated failures violate the independence assumption underlying @eq-system-reliability-n-components. A model that counts only independent device failures omits shared hazards and their potentially larger blast radius; incident frequency and the number of affected devices must be modeled separately. Correlated failures can also defeat redundancy strategies. Three replicas of a model provide no protection against a shared power failure if all three run on the same power domain.

Defending against correlated failures\index{Correlated failure!failure domain protection} requires classifying each failure by its scope, the failure domain\index{Failure domain!ML infrastructure} it takes down, and ensuring that redundancy spans independent domains. Common failure domains in ML infrastructure range from a single GPU to an entire data center region, and each calls for its own mitigation (@tbl-failure-domains). These domains nest, so a physical disruption scales upward from one eight-GPU node to a rack and then to a multi-rack power and network envelope (@fig-failure-domains).

| **Failure domain**     |                   **Impact scope**                  | **Typical recovery time** |   **Mitigation strategy**    |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------:|:-------------------------:|:----------------------------:|
| **Single GPU**         |                        1 GPU                        |      Seconds (spare)      | Hot spare, elastic training  |
| **Node (power/OS)**    | `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs |          Minutes          | Checkpoint, node replacement |
| **Rack (ToR switch)**  |                     32--64 GPUs                     |      Minutes to hours     |    Cross-rack redundancy     |
| **Power domain**       |                    100--500 GPUs                    |           Hours           |     Multiple power feeds     |
| **Data center region** |                       All GPUs                      |       Hours to days       |   Geographic distribution    |
| **Software version**   |               All GPUs running version              |     Minutes (rollback)    |       Staged rollouts        |

: **Failure Domains in ML Infrastructure**: Understanding failure domain boundaries enables placement of redundant components across independent domains, preventing correlated failures from defeating redundancy strategies. {#tbl-failure-domains}

::: {#fig-failure-domains fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Hierarchy of Failure Domains**: Failure domains are often nested or overlapping. A GPU failure affects one device. A node failure affects `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs. A rack switch failure affects 32--64 GPUs (each rack is drawn with only two of its four to eight nodes). A power distribution unit (PDU) failure may affect multiple racks. The red rack shows one such correlated failure: a single top-of-rack switch fault removes every GPU it contains, while the neighboring rack is untouched, which is why replicas must span independent domains (for example, different racks or rows)." fig-alt="Nested rectangles: a data center labeled blast radius all GPUs contains a power and network domain spanning several racks, which contains two racks, each drawn with two of its eight-GPU nodes. The left rack is outlined in red, labeled ToR switch fails and 32 to 64 GPUs, and all its GPU squares are red; the right rack is labeled unaffected and its GPUs are blue."}
![](images/svg/failure-domains.svg)

:::

The containment hierarchy in @tbl-failure-domains and @fig-failure-domains explains why replica placement must match the fault being tolerated: placing replicas within the same domain provides zero protection against that domain's failure mode. The highlighted rack in @fig-failure-domains contains nodes that share a top-of-rack (ToR) switch, so that switch's loss can disconnect every attached node from the job. A neighboring rack with a separate switch can remain reachable during that event even if both racks share a power domain, yet that same placement does not protect against loss of their shared power source. Redundancy must therefore cross the relevant failure boundary, not merely occupy different devices.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The failure domain and its physical nesting from node to rack to building are established in @sec-compute-infrastructure-node-health-reliability-56a6.
:::
