## Software Faults {#sec-ft-software-faults}

A team spends three months testing a large language model (LLM) against complex prompt-level failure cases, only to realize that its preprocessing script kept only the last 512 tokens of each input, silently discarding the system prompt on long requests. The example exposes an ordinary source of ML failure that algorithmic testing can miss. A logic error in a data loader or prompt assembler can preserve valid tensor shapes while changing the computation's meaning, allowing the pipeline to continue without a crash.

Software faults require a different recovery lens from hardware failures. Hardware faults enter from silicon, electrons, and physical wear; software faults enter through design choices, dependency versions, and pipeline glue. The fault-tolerance problem shifts from replacing a failed component to identifying which valid-looking transformation corrupted data, gradients, or predictions. Every boundary between framework, library, runtime, and distributed system is a place where such a transformation can hide.

### Software fault properties and propagation {#sec-ft-software-fault-properties}

A single tensor reference leaked on every training iteration lets a correctly sized job drift toward the device memory limit over hundreds of steps and then crash with an out-of-memory error far from the code that leaked it. Across ML frameworks, software faults of this kind span logic errors, resource leaks, concurrency bugs, and integration mismatches that propagate across system boundaries. Race conditions in asynchronous updates can lose or overwrite parameter updates, and deadlocks[^fn-deadlock-pipeline-stall] leave workers waiting on messages that never arrive. Because many of these faults surface only under high load, on particular hardware, or with a specific pairing of a high-level framework and a low-level numerical library such as cuDNN, root-cause analysis must treat the model code, the runtime, and its dependencies as one versioned artifact.

[^fn-deadlock-pipeline-stall]: **Pipeline deadlock**\index{Deadlock!pipeline parallelism}: In pipelined training, a deadlock can form when stage 1 waits for a free buffer to send activations to stage 2 while stage 2 waits for stage 1 to accept its backward gradients. Neither stage can proceed, and because every other stage depends on them, the whole job stalls with no error raised, which a collective timeout eventually converts into a detectable failure.

### Software fault detection and prevention {#sec-ft-software-fault-detection-prevention}

The prompt-truncation bug from the opening example and the memory or synchronization bugs above should never survive unchallenged into a multi-week run. Because many software faults leave the pipeline running while corrupting inputs or gradients, each verification gate must establish which invariant holds and which recovery action is safe when it fails. A unit test catches the tokenizer boundary before launch, an integration replay verifies that a recorded batch reproduces the expected shapes and state on known-good hardware, and a fault-injection test verifies that a corrupted buffer or lost worker triggers rollback before tainting committed state.

Several of these gates also test the recovery machinery itself before an incident relies on it. A restore drill verifies a checkpoint manifest, the record that names every saved shard and the training step they share (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-checkpointing-5dcc). A membership fault-injection test kills or partitions a worker and checks that, once replaced, the stale process can no longer write state the job will trust under the epoch, lease, and fencing rules of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-recovery-procedures-002d. Every recovery drill is judged against two bounds formalized in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-restart-fundamentals-0ac2: how much completed work a failure may lose and how long recovery may take before useful execution resumes. Across all six gates, each test earns its place through the operational decision it authorizes (@tbl-software-faults-summary-ft).

| **Reliability evidence**       | **Invariant exercised**                                                            | **Decision enabled**                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| **Boundary unit test**         | Tokenizer limits, tensor shapes, masks, and step metadata remain valid             | Reject the change before distributed execution            |
| **Deterministic replay**       | A recorded batch produces equivalent state on known-good hardware                  | Separate input or software defects from suspect hardware  |
| **Checkpoint restore drill**   | A committed manifest restores every shard and resumes at its named step            | Accept the generation as satisfying the recovery contract |
| **Membership fault injection** | A killed or partitioned worker loses ownership and cannot write after replacement  | Validate ownership handoff and communicator rebuild       |
| **Corruption injection**       | A changed shard, reduced buffer, or checkpoint fails the intended verifier         | Block the optimizer step or roll back before propagation  |
| **Dependency rollback test**   | A versioned runtime and artifact set can return to the last known-good combination | Authorize automated rollback instead of manual repair     |

: **Reliability Evidence and Recovery Decisions**: Tests earn operational value when each one establishes an invariant and authorizes a specific rejection, rollback, isolation, or restore decision. {#tbl-software-faults-summary-ft}

These safeguards matter only when each gate targets a concrete corruption path. A test that checks only whether the tokenizer runs is too weak; it must assert that system prompts, labels, masks, and sequence-length metadata survive preprocessing with the intended semantics. Integration replay then follows one recorded batch through loading, sharding, collation, and model input construction. Fault injection tests whether the detector fires before the protected commit and whether recovery stays within the named bounds on lost work and recovery time for the injected fault. Restore drills, stale-writer rejection, and corrupted-shard rejection therefore provide evidence that generic build success cannot supply, and @sec-ft-fault-injection-tools-frameworks exercises those claims directly once the recovery paths themselves have been built. Before building those paths, however, a fleet must decide how much protection each workload is worth.

## The Cost of Failure {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-economic-framework-fault-tolerance-investment-e032}

Losing an uncheckpointed day on a 10,000-GPU foundation-model run burns hundreds of thousands of dollars in accelerator time, whereas losing an hour on a small vision job costs a few hundred dollars and a failed update in an online recommender costs live revenue rather than batch rework. Hardware, silent corruption, and software together set how often a fleet fails, but the work a failure destroys determines what each incident costs. A defense is worth buying only where it removes more of that expected loss than it adds in standing overhead.

### Failure cost by workload {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-modeltype-diversity-failure-impact-8ec0}

Three workload properties set the price of a training interruption: the burn rate of the cluster running the job, the footprint of state that must be saved and reloaded, and how sensitive model quality is to lost or reordered updates. Those three factors separate multi-terabyte foundation models and continuous recommenders from smaller vision, speech, and scientific workloads (@tbl-failure-impact-by-model).

| **Model type**                  | **Typical training duration** |                        **Checkpoint size**                        |      **State sensitivity**      |                              **Failure cost**                             |
|:--------------------------------|:-----------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------------------:|:-------------------------------:|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------:|
| **Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3)** |        Weeks to months        |    `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` (175B)    |  High (position in data order)  | `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.daily_cost_str` compute per 24 hr loss |
| **Vision (ViT-Large)**          |           1--3 days           |          `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.vit_ckpt_str`         |   Medium (augmentation state)   |                           \$10--50K per day loss                          |
| **Archetype B (DLRM at Scale)** |           Continuous          | `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.recsys_table_str` (embeddings) | Very High (embedding freshness) |                          Revenue impact per hour                          |
| **Speech (Whisper-scale)**      |           3--7 days           |                              5--10 GB                             |              Medium             |                          \$50--200K per day loss                          |
| **Scientific (AlphaFold)**      |         Days to weeks         |                             10--50 GB                             |     High (exploration state)    |                               Research delay                              |

: **Failure Impact by Model Type**: The cost of training failures varies dramatically by model type, driven by training duration, checkpoint overhead, and the value of accumulated training state. The Archetype A cost is one lost day on the chapter's 10,000-GPU cluster; the vision, speech, and scientific rows give illustrative ranges rather than measured values. These differences demand model-specific fault tolerance strategies. {#tbl-failure-impact-by-model}

Large language model training illustrates how a costly allocation magnifies each hour of lost progress. The chapter's `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpus_example_str`-GPU cluster at approximately `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.rate_str` incurs `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.daily_cost_str` in compute costs per day. A job checkpointed only once a day can lose up to a full day of progress to one failure, which costs `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.daily_cost_str` in wasted compute plus schedule delay. At the checkpoint interval derived in @sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly, the same failure costs minutes of rework instead of a day. The checkpoint overhead is correspondingly large. At the `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.ckpt_bpp_str`-byte-per-parameter resumable format that the checkpointing analysis uses (BF16 weights, FP32 master weights, and two FP32 Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) moments), the 175B-parameter running example writes `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` at every save.

### Investing in protection {#sec-fault-tolerance-investing-protection}

Every GPU cycle, network byte, and storage drive dedicated to checkpointing, standby nodes, or verification is a resource that is not training the model, yet skimping on protection leaves a multi-million-dollar run exposed to day-long rollbacks. Rational investment in fault tolerance therefore weighs what a failure destroys against what the defense costs to run.

When a failure strikes, its bill extends well beyond the GPU-hours burned on steps that must be replayed. Repeating lost work delays the delivery of the trained model, ties up accelerators that could have run other jobs, and pulls engineers away from research to diagnose faults and nurse manual restarts. On the other side of the cost account, prevention carries a continuous overhead even when the cluster is healthy. Checkpoint storage scales with model size and save frequency, and checkpoint writes compete for memory and network bandwidth. Hot spares and automated recovery controllers consume standing infrastructure, and fault-tolerant coordination adds software complexity that must be maintained and debugged.

Optimal investment balances these two curves against cluster scale. For a small job on a few GPUs where hardware failures are weeks apart, infrequent checkpoints and manual restarts are cheaper than standing recovery infrastructure. On thousands of GPUs where failures arrive several times a day, frequent checkpoints, automated failover, and elastic resizing pay back their overhead many times over. The checkpoint interval derived in @sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly applies this exact marginal balance to a single decision variable, choosing the cadence where the cost of one more save equals the expected rework it prevents.

@Eq-ft-total-cost presents a simplified economic model for expected cost per training run:

$$ \TotalTrainingRunCost= \BaseTrainingComputeCost+ \mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount] \times \FailureEventCost+ \FaultToleranceCost$$ {#eq-ft-total-cost}

where $\BaseTrainingComputeCost$ is the base compute cost, $\mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount]$ is the expected number of failures during training, $\FailureEventCost$ is the cost per failure, and $\FaultToleranceCost$ is the cost of fault tolerance mechanisms. The cost per failure includes wasted compute plus overhead.

@Eq-ft-investment-criterion formalizes when fault tolerance investment is justified:

$$ \frac{\partial \FaultToleranceCost}{\partial \FaultToleranceInvestment} < -\frac{\partial (\mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount] \times \FailureEventCost)}{\partial \FaultToleranceInvestment} $$ {#eq-ft-investment-criterion}

where $\FaultToleranceInvestment$ represents investment in fault tolerance mechanisms and the base compute cost is held fixed. The negative derivative on the right is the marginal reduction in expected failure cost. Additional protection reduces total expected cost while this reduction exceeds its marginal cost; an interior optimum equates the two when the cost functions have a suitable minimum.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: hot-spare-breakeven
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HOT-SPARE BREAK-EVEN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-economic-framework-
# │          fault-tolerance-investment-e032, worked instance of
# │          @eq-ft-investment-criterion.
# │
# │ Goal: Price one idle hot-spare node against the recovery time it must save
# │       on the chapter's 10,000-GPU cluster.
# │ Show: ~$384/day idle node; ~$2,100/day per minute shaved from each
# │       recovery at 6.2 failures/day; break-even ~11 s saved per failure.
# │ How:  spare cost = GPUs/node x 24 h x price; benefit per second saved =
# │       failures/day x fleet GPUs x price / 3600; break-even = cost / benefit.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Infrastructure, Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_time, fmt_usd

class HotSpareBreakeven:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    fleet_gpus = FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus
    failures_per_day = FailureCascadeExample.per_day  # full-system cascade cadence
    gpus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node
    price = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    spare_cost_day = gpus_per_node * 24 * price  # one node held idle all day
    value_per_min_day = failures_per_day * fleet_gpus * price / 60  # one minute shaved per failure
    breakeven_s = spare_cost_day / (value_per_min_day / 60)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(breakeven_s < 60, "at fleet scale a spare should pay back within a minute saved per failure")
    check(value_per_min_day > spare_cost_day, "one minute saved per failure must outweigh one idle node")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    gpus_per_node_str = fmt(gpus_per_node, precision=0)
    spare_cost_day_str = fmt_usd(round(spare_cost_day), precision=0)
    value_per_min_day_str = fmt_usd(round(value_per_min_day, -2), precision=0)
    breakeven_s_str = fmt_time(round(breakeven_s), "second", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
```

One investment worked through the criterion shows what it decides. Let $\FaultToleranceInvestment$ be a hot-spare node held idle beside the chapter's `{python} FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus_str`-GPU cluster, so that a failed node's replacement no longer waits for the scheduler to find capacity. Its marginal cost is `{python} HotSpareBreakeven.gpus_per_node_str` GPUs idling all day, about `{python} HotSpareBreakeven.spare_cost_day_str` per day. Its marginal benefit is the recovery time it removes from each failure while every other GPU waits. At the cascade's `{python} FailureCascadeExample.failures_per_day_str`, each minute removed from every recovery is worth about `{python} HotSpareBreakeven.value_per_min_day_str` per day, so the spare pays for itself once it shortens each recovery by about `{python} HotSpareBreakeven.breakeven_s_str`, provided it is refilled before the next failure arrives some `{python} FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_hours_str` later. The same node beside an eight-GPU job, whose GPU-only MTBF in @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling is `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.mtbf0_str`, would sit idle far longer than it could ever save. Scale reverses the verdict on the same hardware, and three foundational principles distill how that shift guides design across the rest of this chapter.

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-three-rules-failure-at-scale .callout-perspective title="Three rules of failure at scale"}

1. *At scale, failures are continuous, not exceptional.* A `{python} FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus_str`-GPU cluster experiences a failure every `{python} FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_hours_str` on average. Systems must be designed expecting failure as normal operation.
2. *Checkpoint intervals have an optimum.* The Young-Daly interval (developed in @sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly) sets checkpoint frequency from write time and system MTBF under its stated assumptions, and it shrinks only with the square root of a falling MTBF.
3. *Training and serving have fundamentally different fault tolerance requirements.* A long training job can budget minutes for recovery while preserving accumulated progress; an interactive serving request may have only milliseconds left before its deadline. Those budgets motivate checkpoint recovery for training and ready alternate capacity for serving.

:::

These three rules organize the rest of the chapter: rules 1 and 2 govern long-running training jobs that must protect accumulated progress, rule 3 governs low-latency serving fleets that must protect live requests, and observability and fault injection verify that both recovery paths work under fire. Training resilience begins with the durable state that every restart or resize falls back on.

## Checkpointing and Progress Preservation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-restart-fundamentals-0ac2}

When a top-of-rack switch dies two weeks into the training run of a 175-billion-parameter model, the cluster loses 64 GPUs instantly. Because a large cluster experiences such interruptions routinely (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-analysis-scale-6b4b), it cannot restart multi-week jobs from scratch; training fault tolerance must preserve state, detect and classify the failure, and resume or resize the worker group. Checkpointing supplies the first of those three obligations, and every detection, restart, and elastic-resizing path later in the chapter depends on the durable snapshot it produces. The first design question is what that snapshot must contain to make a restart valid.

::: {#dfn-fault-tolerance-checkpointing .callout-definition title="Checkpointing"}

***Checkpointing***\index{Checkpointing!definition} is the periodic serialization of the complete training state (parameters, optimizer state, data loader position, and random state) to persistent storage at a recorded training step.

1.  **Significance**: It minimizes lost work after a system failure by trading checkpoint I/O against rework. Writing too often wastes accelerator time on storage traffic; writing too rarely risks replaying many completed steps after a failure. The Young-Daly interval\index{Young-Daly formula!square-root trade-off} developed in this section chooses the cadence that balances write cost against expected lost work.
2.  **Distinction**: A resumable checkpoint captures a consistent execution state, including optimizer state, random-number generator state, data position, and learning rate schedules. It can use full or incremental storage; bitwise replay additionally requires compatible deterministic execution.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that checkpointing is "just writing to disk." For large models it is a storage-system stress test, because the simultaneous write from thousands of GPUs can trigger a checkpoint storm (definition \ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}) that saturates the shared network and storage bandwidth $(\Bandwidth)$.

:::

A checkpoint is useful only if it resumes the recorded step consistently. In distributed training, every shard must belong to the same recoverable state; a collection of files from different steps does not preserve progress. For the interval model, assume that writing a checkpoint completes durably before it becomes available for recovery and that a failure discards the work performed since the last completed checkpoint.

Two recovery objectives turn those obligations into a contract. The recovery point objective (RPO) bounds acceptable lost progress, so checkpoint age and replication lag must fit within it. The recovery time objective (RTO) bounds the delay until useful work resumes, which covers detection, resource replacement, restore, and warmup. A 20-minute checkpoint interval cannot promise an RPO below 20 minutes without a more frequent durable log or replica, and asynchronous flushing can leave the last durable generation older still. A five-minute RTO is impossible if checkpoint reload alone takes eight minutes. These objectives apply to a stated fault model. Corruption discovered after several saves can require rollback beyond the newest durable checkpoint. The Young-Daly interval derived next minimizes expected waste; RPO and RTO impose service constraints that the expected-value optimum must still satisfy [@beyer2016sre].

### The Young-Daly checkpoint interval {#sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly}

When failures are expected during a job, the key engineering decision is how often to write that state, because every save costs I/O time and every unsaved step is work a failure can erase. The Young-Daly formula\index{Young-Daly formula!optimal interval}\index{Daly formula|see{Young-Daly formula}}[^fn-young-daly-formula] (principle \ref{pri-young-daly}) gives a first-order estimate of that balance through a square-root rule:

$$ \OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf} $$ {#eq-ft-young-daly-interval}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: young-daly-checkpoint-state
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESUMABLE CHECKPOINT STATE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly, the T_write paragraph below.
# │
# │ Goal: Size a resumable mixed-precision Adam checkpoint for a 70B model and
# │       for the 175B running example from one bytes-per-parameter anchor.
# │ Show: 14 bytes per parameter; ~1 TB (70B) and >2 TB (175B).
# │ How:  params x ReferenceStats.MixedPrecisionAdam.CheckpointBytesPerParameter.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt

class YoungDalyCheckpointState:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    ckpt_bpp = ReferenceStats.MixedPrecisionAdam.CheckpointBytesPerParameter
    params_70b = Models.Language.Llama3_70B.parameters
    params_175b = Models.Language.GPT3.parameters

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    ckpt_70b_tb = (params_70b * ckpt_bpp).to(TB).magnitude
    ckpt_175b_tb = (params_175b * ckpt_bpp).to(TB).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(0.9 < ckpt_70b_tb < 1.0, "70B checkpoint must 'approach a terabyte'")
    check(ckpt_175b_tb > 2.0, "175B checkpoint must 'exceed two terabytes'")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    ckpt_bpp_str = fmt(ckpt_bpp.magnitude, precision=0)
```

$\CheckpointWriteTime$ in distributed ML training is not the time to flush a small process state; it includes transferring model weights and optimizer state to durable storage. The reference format here stores BF16 weights, separate FP32 master weights, and two FP32 moment tensors per parameter for Adam. A single resumable checkpoint for a 70B-parameter model therefore approaches a terabyte at `{python} YoungDalyCheckpointState.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter; for the later 175B-parameter running example, it exceeds two terabytes. Of those `{python} YoungDalyCheckpointState.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter, the optimizer state[^fn-adam-state-memory] dominates the payload, exactly as in the storage sizing of the same resumable checkpoint in @sec-storage-checkpointing. The optimizer state rather than the model weights therefore sets most of $\CheckpointWriteTime$. Reducing $\CheckpointWriteTime$ requires a smaller payload or higher sustained write bandwidth, and $\CheckpointWriteTime$ is the central constraint that determines how tightly the checkpoint interval can be set before I/O overhead displaces productive training compute.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_fault_tolerance_margin_002.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Stacked checkpoint payload bar where BF16 weights occupy 14 percent and optimizer state, the FP32 master weights plus Adam moments, occupies 86 percent."}

*Optimizer state, not weights, dominates checkpoint size.*
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Checkpointing section — Adam state and shard sizing.
# │ Note: resumable checkpoint = 14 B/param (bf16 weights 2 + fp32 master 4
# │       + fp32 Adam moments 8); gradients and activations are not saved.
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim import *

class FaultToleranceCheckpointRecap:
    m = Models.Language.GPT3
    gpt3_ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(m.parameters)  # 14 B/param default
    gpt3_adam_bytes = (m.parameters.to(param).magnitude * 2 * BYTES_FP32).to(byte)  # m and v moments
    n_workers = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    aggregate_ckpt_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    ckpt_write = (gpt3_ckpt_bytes / aggregate_ckpt_bw).to(second)
    check(gpt3_adam_bytes < gpt3_ckpt_bytes, "Adam moments must be a subset of the checkpoint")
    check(22 < ckpt_write.to(second).magnitude < 27, f"GPT-3 checkpoint write should be ~24.5 s, got {ckpt_write.to(second).magnitude:.1f}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_params_b_str = fmt_params(m.parameters, scale="B", precision=0, commas=False)
    gpt3_ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_ckpt_bytes, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
    gpt3_adam_tb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_adam_bytes, unit=TB, precision=1, commas=False)
    gpt3_shard_gb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_ckpt_bytes / n_workers, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    ckpt_write_s_str = fmt_time(ckpt_write, second, precision=None, commas=False)
    aggregate_read_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(aggregate_ckpt_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
```

[^fn-adam-state-memory]: **Adam optimizer state**\index{Adam optimizer!state}\index{Adam optimizer!checkpoint memory}: Adam's per-parameter first-moment ($\AdamFirstMoment$) and second-moment ($\AdamSecondMoment$) estimates are two FP32 values, 8 of the `{python} YoungDalyCheckpointState.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter in the resumable checkpoint; with the FP32 master weights, optimizer-side state accounts for all but the 2 bytes of BF16 weights. For a `{python} FaultToleranceCheckpointRecap.gpt3_params_b_str` parameter model, the two moments alone reach `{python} FaultToleranceCheckpointRecap.gpt3_adam_tb_str`, which typically dominates checkpoint size and recovery time, making optimizer state the primary bottleneck in checkpoint I/O design.

To see the balance, consider an interval between saves. Doubling that interval approximately halves the checkpoint writes per unit of training, but a failure then loses twice as much work on average. Under the constant-rate, rare-failure approximation, failure occurs approximately uniformly within an interval, so the average lost work is half the interval. When write time is small relative to the interval, the wasted fraction from saving and replaying work is approximately the sum below. Detection, allocation, and restoration time require a separate recovery budget.

$$ \CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointInterval}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf} $$ {#eq-ft-checkpoint-waste}

Setting the first derivative to zero ($\frac{d\CheckpointWasteFraction}{d\CheckpointInterval} = -\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf} = 0$) directly yields the square-root minimum of @eq-ft-young-daly-interval. As clusters grow, system MTBF drops, so the optimal interval shrinks, demanding higher-bandwidth storage to keep $\CheckpointWriteTime$ small before checkpoint overhead consumes the cluster's compute capacity. Because the relationship is a square root, halving MTBF tightens the interval by only $\sqrt{2}\approx 1.4\times$, so doubling cluster size does not demand doubling checkpoint I/O bandwidth when checkpoint size and the other assumptions stay fixed. Substituting the optimum back into @eq-ft-checkpoint-waste gives a minimum waste of $\sqrt{2\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf}$. Because $\SystemMtbf$ falls as $1/\DeviceCount$ under independent failures, that optimized overhead grows as $\sqrt{\DeviceCount}$, and doubling the cluster raises it by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ even though the interval itself adapts.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The per-tier storage bandwidths that bound how quickly a checkpoint can be written are established in @sec-storage-hierarchy.
:::

[^fn-young-daly-formula]: **Young-Daly formula**\index{Young-Daly formula!history}: @young1974 derived the first-order optimal checkpoint interval, and @daly2006 independently refined it with tighter second-order bounds.

### Checkpoint interval from failure analysis {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-interval-failure-analysis-c28d}

The Young-Daly interval of @eq-ft-young-daly-interval needs two inputs, the system MTBF and the write time $\CheckpointWriteTime$, and the chapter's 10,000-GPU cluster supplies both as computed values. The worked cascade (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-worked-example-cluster-mtbf-calculation-9255) put full-system MTBF, including PCIe and network failures (the redundant power supplies add no term), at `{python} FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_hours_2dp_str`. For the write time, the 175B running example's `{python} FaultToleranceCheckpointRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` resumable checkpoint drains to shared storage at the sustained aggregate write bandwidth this chapter assumes for the cluster, `{python} FaultToleranceCheckpointRecap.aggregate_read_gb_per_s_str`, which takes `{python} FaultToleranceCheckpointRecap.ckpt_write_s_str`. Substituting these into the Young-Daly formula gives a candidate interval for this cluster, which must still satisfy its RPO and RTO.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: checkpoint-tradeoff-inputs
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHECKPOINT TRADE-OFF INPUTS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-checkpoint-tradeoff and its caption.
# │
# │ Goal: Feed the U-curve the same two inputs the Young-Daly notebook uses
# │       later, so the plotted optimum and the worked interval agree.
# │ Show: T_write ~24.5 s (175B, 14 B/param, registry write bandwidth);
# │       full-system MTBF ~3.87 h (GPU + PCIe + shared NIC, 10,000 GPUs);
# │       tau_opt ~13.8 min.
# │ How:  Same series-rate composition as the worked MTBF cascade (redundant
# │       PSUs add no term); tau_opt = sqrt(2 * T_write * MTBF_system).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_time

class CheckpointTradeoffInputs:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters)  # 14 B/param
    write_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    gpus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    pcie_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.PcieSwitch.mttf_hours)
    nic_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Nic.mttf_hours)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_write_h = (ckpt_bytes / write_bw).to(hour).magnitude
    rate_per_gpu = 1 / gpu_mttf_h + 1 / pcie_mttf_h + (1 / gpus_per_node) / nic_mttf_h
    mtbf_h = 1 / (n_gpus * rate_per_gpu)
    tau_opt_h = math.sqrt(2 * t_write_h * mtbf_h)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(22 < t_write_h * 3600 < 27, "175B checkpoint write should be ~24.5 s")
    check(3.5 < mtbf_h < 4.2, "full-system MTBF should match the worked cascade (~3.87 h)")
    check(12 < tau_opt_h * 60 < 15, "tau_opt should match the Young-Daly notebook (~13.8 min)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_write_s_str = fmt_time(t_write_h * 3600, "second", precision=1, commas=False)
    mtbf_h_str = fmt_time(mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False)
    tau_opt_min_str = fmt_time(round(tau_opt_h * 60), "minute", precision=0, commas=False)
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: young-daly-optimal-interval
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ YOUNG-DALY OPTIMAL INTERVAL (NOTEBOOK)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "The Young-Daly Optimal Interval" .callout-notebook
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the optimal checkpoint interval for a 10K-GPU cluster
# │       to minimize wasted work using the square-root rule.
# │ Show: tau_opt_min_str ≈ 13.8 min (2.45 TB, 14 B/param checkpoint), inline in notebook steps;
# │   mtbf_s_str and tau_opt_s_str support the arithmetic.
# │ How: tau_opt = sqrt(2 * T_write * MTBF_system); bare arithmetic for clarity.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics import calc_young_daly_interval

class YoungDalyOptimal:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_bytes = FaultToleranceCheckpointRecap.gpt3_ckpt_bytes  # 14 B/param resumable checkpoint
    mtbf = round(float(FailureCascadeExample.mtbf_h), 2) * hour  # worked cascade MTBF, at the 2 dp the chapter displays
    aggregate_ckpt_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    t_write = (ckpt_bytes / aggregate_ckpt_bw).to(second)
    tau_opt = calc_young_daly_interval(t_write, mtbf)
    overhead_pct = ((t_write / tau_opt) + (tau_opt / (2 * mtbf))).to("").magnitude * 100
    hourly_interval = 1 * hour
    hourly_overhead_pct = ((t_write / hourly_interval) + (hourly_interval / (2 * mtbf))).to("").magnitude * 100
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(12 < tau_opt.to(minute).magnitude < 15, f"Interval {tau_opt.to(minute).magnitude:.1f}m outside expected range")
    check(hourly_overhead_pct > overhead_pct, "Hourly checkpointing should waste more than optimal")
    check(abs(tau_opt.to(hour).magnitude / CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_h - 1) < 0.01, "notebook interval must match @fig-checkpoint-tradeoff")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_write_s_str = fmt_time(t_write, second, precision=None, commas=False)
    mtbf_h_str = fmt_time(mtbf, hour, precision=2, commas=False, style='word')
    mtbf_s_str = fmt_time(mtbf, second, precision=0, commas=False)
    tau_opt_s_str = fmt_time(tau_opt, second, precision=1, commas=False)
    tau_opt_min_str = fmt_time(tau_opt, minute, precision=1, commas=False)
    overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(overhead_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    hourly_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(hourly_overhead_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    seconds_per_hour_str = fmt_time(SEC_PER_HOUR, "second", precision=0, commas=False, per="hour")
    n_gpus_str = fmt(Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators, precision=0, commas=True)
```

::: {#nbk-fault-tolerance-young-daly-optimal-interval .callout-notebook title="The Young-Daly optimal interval"}

**Problem**: A `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster has an MTBF of `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.mtbf_h_str`. A full model checkpoint takes `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.t_write_s_str` to write. What is the optimal checkpoint frequency?

**Math**:
Apply the Young-Daly interval of @eq-ft-young-daly-interval (principle \ref{pri-young-daly}).

1. **Convert to common units**: $\SystemMtbf =$ `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.mtbf_h_str` $\times$ `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.seconds_per_hour_str` = `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.mtbf_s_str`.
2. **Substitute and solve**: With $\CheckpointWriteTime =$ `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.t_write_s_str` and $\SystemMtbf =$ `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.mtbf_s_str`, the formula gives $\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx$ `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.tau_opt_s_str`, or about `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.tau_opt_min_str`.

**Systems insight**: At this interval, the checkpoint overhead (time spent saving plus time spent recomputing) is minimized to approximately `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.overhead_pct_str`. Checkpointing every hour instead would lengthen the expected rework after each failure, wasting about `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.hourly_overhead_pct_str` of the cluster's capacity.

:::

The result connects measured or estimated interruption rates to checkpoint policy. At this interval, saving and expected replay together consume approximately `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.overhead_pct_str` of training time in the first-order model, half from writes and half from replay, because at the square-root optimum the two terms of @eq-ft-checkpoint-waste are equal. Plotting those two terms for this cluster shows how forgiving the optimum is (@fig-checkpoint-tradeoff). Write overhead falls hyperbolically and expected rework climbs linearly, so their sum has a shallow floor around `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. An interval slightly off the optimum costs little, while one several times too short or too long costs far more, which is why a rough MTBF estimate still yields a usable schedule. How far the estimate itself can be trusted depends on the simplifying assumptions behind it.

::: {#fig-checkpoint-tradeoff fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Checkpoint Trade-Off**: Checkpoint save overhead (dashed blue) falls as the interval lengthens, while expected rework after a failure (dashed red) rises; their sum (solid) is minimized at the Young-Daly interval. The curves use this chapter's 175B running example on its `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster, with a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.t_write_s_str` checkpoint write and a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.mtbf_h_str` full-system MTBF, which put the optimum near `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. The minimum is shallow, so an interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while a far shorter or far longer one costs a great deal." fig-alt="Plot of share of wall time wasted against checkpoint interval in minutes. A dashed blue save-overhead curve falls hyperbolically, a dashed red expected-rework line rises linearly, and a solid dark total curve has a shallow minimum marked with a green dot at about 14 minutes and 5.9 percent wasted. A dotted dropline from the minimum passes through an open circle where the two dashed terms cross, labeled terms equal. The background left of the optimum is tinted blue and labeled writes dominate; the background to the right is tinted red and labeled rework dominates. Each curve carries a direct label."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHECKPOINT TRADE-OFF (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-checkpoint-tradeoff.
# │
# │ Goal: Plot save overhead, expected rework, and their sum vs. interval for
# │       the chapter's 175B / 10,000-GPU example; mark tau_opt.
# │ Show: Three curves; optimum annotation near 14 min.
# │ How:  Inputs from CheckpointTradeoffInputs (no literals); book_style.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 3.5))

t_write = CheckpointTradeoffInputs.t_write_h
mtbf = CheckpointTradeoffInputs.mtbf_h
tau_opt = CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_h

tau = np.linspace(tau_opt / 6, tau_opt * 4, 300)
over_ckpt = t_write / tau
over_rework = tau / (2 * mtbf)
total_waste = over_ckpt + over_rework
waste_opt = t_write / tau_opt + tau_opt / (2 * mtbf)

x_min = tau * 60
x_max = tau_opt * 4 * 60

# Regimes on either side of the optimum: writes dominate (left), rework dominates (right).
ax.axvspan(0, tau_opt * 60, color=COLORS['BlueL'], alpha=0.35, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axvspan(tau_opt * 60, x_max, color=COLORS['RedL'], alpha=0.25, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.text(tau_opt * 60 * 0.5, 19.2, 'writes\ndominate', ha='center', va='top', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['BlueLine'])
ax.text(
    tau_opt * 60 + (x_max - tau_opt * 60) / 2,
    19.2,
    'rework dominates',
    ha='center',
    va='top',
    fontsize=10,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
)

ax.plot(x_min, over_ckpt * 100, color=COLORS['BlueLine'], linestyle='--', linewidth=1.6)
ax.plot(x_min, over_rework * 100, color=COLORS['RedLine'], linestyle='--', linewidth=1.6)
ax.plot(x_min, total_waste * 100, color=COLORS['primary'], linewidth=2.5)

# Direct labels at the right end of each curve
x_lab = x_max * 0.97

def _at(arr):
    return float(np.interp(x_lab, x_min, arr * 100))

ax.text(x_lab, _at(total_waste) + 0.6, 'total wasted time', ha='right', va='bottom', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'])
x_rw = tau_opt * 60 * 2.3
ax.text(
    x_rw,
    float(np.interp(x_rw, x_min, over_rework * 100)) - 1.3,
    'expected rework\n$T_{\\mathrm{ckpt}}/(2\\,\\mathrm{MTBF}_{\\mathrm{system}})$',
    ha='left',
    va='top',
    fontsize=10,
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
)
ax.text(
    x_lab,
    _at(over_ckpt) + 0.6,
    'save overhead  $T_{\\mathrm{write}}/T_{\\mathrm{ckpt}}$',
    ha='right',
    va='bottom',
    fontsize=10,
    color=COLORS['BlueLine'],
)

# Young-Daly optimum: green dot with a dropline; the two dashed terms cross on the dropline
ax.plot([tau_opt * 60, tau_opt * 60], [0, waste_opt * 100], color=COLORS['GreenLine'], linestyle=':', linewidth=1.0, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([tau_opt * 60], [waste_opt * 100 / 2], facecolor='white', edgecolor=COLORS['primary'], linewidth=1.0, s=28, zorder=5)
ax.text(tau_opt * 60 + 0.5, 1.45, 'terms equal', ha='left', va='center', fontsize=10, color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.scatter([tau_opt * 60], [waste_opt * 100], color=COLORS['GreenLine'], edgecolor='white', linewidth=1.0, s=55, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f'$T^*_{{\\mathrm{{ckpt}}}} \\approx {tau_opt * 60:.0f}$ min\n{waste_opt * 100:.1f}% wasted',
    xy=(tau_opt * 60, waste_opt * 100),
    xytext=(0, 12),
    textcoords='offset points',
    ha='center',
    va='bottom',
    fontsize=10.5,
    color=COLORS['GreenLine'],
)

ax.set_xlabel('Checkpoint interval $T_{\\mathrm{ckpt}}$ (minutes)')
ax.set_ylabel('Share of wall time wasted (%)')
ax.set_xlim(0, x_max)
ax.set_yticks([0, 5, 10, 15, 20])
ax.set_ylim(0, 20)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-young-daly-formula-assumptions .callout-perspective title="Young-Daly formula assumptions"}

The first-order Young-Daly formula provides valuable intuition but rests on assumptions that may not hold when write times are non-negligible relative to MTBF; the renewal model derived in @sec-appdx-reliability-daly-2nd-order shows how finite checkpoint time changes the optimum. The assumptions are:

- Exponentially distributed failures\index{Young-Daly formula!exponential failure assumption}: Assumes a constant failure rate. Real hardware follows the bathtub curve, with higher rates during burn-in and wear-out phases.
- Deterministic checkpoint time\index{Young-Daly formula!constant write time assumption}: Assumes $\CheckpointWriteTime$ is constant. In practice, checkpoint time varies from save to save with storage contention, network congestion, and memory pressure.
- Recovery cost is independent of the chosen interval\index{Young-Daly formula!recovery time assumption}: A fixed per-failure recovery cost does not change the first-order minimizing interval. Recovery can take longer than checkpoint writing because it also includes job scheduling delays, topology reconstruction, and warmup; it still belongs in the total-waste budget.
- Aggregate interruption process\index{Young-Daly formula!single failure assumption}: Independent constant-rate failure sources can contribute to one job-interruption rate. Shared power, cooling, or switch failures require a model of incident frequency and recovery cost; adding per-device rates alone misses those common causes.
- Infinite timeline\index{Young-Daly formula!infinite horizon assumption}: Optimizes for long training runs. Short runs, where total time is comparable to MTBF, require different analysis.

When assumptions are violated, the optimal interval may shift significantly, but restart overhead should not be treated as if it were paid at every checkpoint. In the first-order lost-time model, restart time adds a per-failure recovery term to total expected waste; it does not replace $\CheckpointWriteTime$ inside @eq-ft-young-daly-interval unless a recovery-aware Daly-style model is explicitly derived and calibrated.

:::

Along an execution timeline, a training run alternates productive compute intervals ($\CheckpointInterval$) with synchronous save barriers ($\CheckpointWriteTime$), and a failure charges two distinct penalties (@fig-checkpoint-recovery-timeline). Uncheckpointed progress is discarded as lost rework, and the restart latency ($\FailureRecoveryTime$) of job scheduling\index{Recovery procedure!job scheduling delay}, checkpoint loading, and pipeline warmup\index{Warmup!recovery overhead} follows before useful work resumes. Recovery latency therefore matters as much as write duration. Restart adds scheduling and warmup to reading the saved state back, so total restart time can exceed the checkpoint write time. It belongs in the total-waste and service-level objective (SLO) budgets as a per-failure term (perspective \ref{psp-fault-tolerance-young-daly-formula-assumptions}) rather than inside the per-checkpoint write term.

::: {#fig-checkpoint-recovery-timeline data-explore="mechanism-scene" data-explore-key="vol2:fig-checkpoint-recovery-timeline" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Checkpoint-Recovery Timeline**: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint." fig-alt="Top, a horizontal timeline: blue compute, green save, blue compute, green save, a red-hatched block labeled lost that ends at a red vertical line, a red recover block, and a final blue compute block. A bracket above the lost and recover blocks reads cost of one failure; brackets below label T ckpt, T write, rework, and T recovery. Bottom, a progress line on the same time axis rises during compute and stays flat during each save, with green dots marking durable progress at the end of each save. During the lost block the line rises in red, then at the failure a red dashed arrow drops it back to the last durable level, it stays flat through recovery, and it climbs again."}
![](images/svg/checkpoint-recovery-timeline.svg)

:::

### Checkpoint overhead analysis {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-overhead-analysis-f5df}

The interval calculation chooses *when* the system preserves state; the write path decides what each save costs while training waits. @Eq-checkpoint-overhead generalizes the save-side term of @eq-ft-checkpoint-waste to include any pause beyond the write itself:

$$ \CheckpointOverheadFraction= \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointExtraPauseTime}{\CheckpointInterval} $$ {#eq-checkpoint-overhead}

Here, $\CheckpointOverheadFraction$ is the dimensionless fraction of time lost to checkpointing, $\CheckpointWriteTime$ is checkpoint write time, $\CheckpointInterval$ is the checkpoint interval, and $\CheckpointExtraPauseTime$ is any training pause beyond the checkpoint write itself. This includes memory allocation, coordination, and serialization. Total first-order waste is then $\CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \CheckpointOverheadFraction+ \CheckpointInterval/(2 \cdot \SystemMtbf)$, so checkpoint overhead in this section means the save side alone, with expected rework counted separately. How large $\CheckpointOverheadFraction$ becomes depends first on whether training waits for durable storage.

#### Synchronous vs. asynchronous checkpointing {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-synchronous-vs-asynchronous-checkpointing-ecc1}

Synchronous checkpointing\index{Checkpointing!synchronous} resumes training only after every worker's portion reaches durable storage. Asynchronous checkpointing\index{Checkpointing!asynchronous}\index{Asynchronous checkpointing|see{Checkpointing}} instead pauses the accelerators only long enough to copy the weights and optimizer tensors from GPU memory into host memory\index{Checkpointing!in-memory staging} or local staging, then flushes that staged copy to remote storage in the background while training continues. The brief device-to-host copy is necessary because the next optimizer step updates the live GPU tensors in place, which would otherwise overwrite state that is still being serialized. @Sec-storage-distributed-checkpoint develops the write path behind both approaches. For recovery, blocking alone does not establish consistency, so the protocol must ensure that every shard belongs to the same recoverable training state. Recovery can use an asynchronous generation only after all required shards reach the storage tier that survives the modeled failure and the coordinator publishes completion. If a failure strikes while the background flush is still in flight, recovery must fall back to the previous committed generation.

A synchronous save pauses every accelerator in the job for the full remote write, and @sec-storage-checkpointing prices that exposed pause on a slow shared tier. Asynchronous capture shrinks the exposed pause to the local staging copy and moves the remote flush off the critical path, which is why production systems stage checkpoints rather than block on shared storage. Write time also varies widely across model types, because larger models require longer writes but also earn longer optimal intervals (@tbl-checkpoint-overhead-by-model).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: checkpoint-overhead-by-model-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHECKPOINT OVERHEAD BY MODEL TYPE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-checkpoint-overhead-by-model immediately below this cell.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute write time, optimal checkpoint interval, and save overhead
# │       for six model archetypes using the Young-Daly square-root formula.
# │ Show: All numeric cells in the checkpoint overhead comparison table.
# │ How: Load named model sizes, reusable checkpoint archetype sizes, reliability
# │      bandwidth/MTBF anchors; then compute write_time, tau_opt, and overhead.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim.physics import calc_young_daly_interval

class CheckpointOverheadCalc:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Checkpoint sizes for each model archetype.
    checkpoint_archetypes = ReferenceStats.CheckpointArchetypes
    # Archetype A: 14 B/param resumable checkpoint (calc_checkpoint_size default),
    # the same 2.45 TB contract used throughout the chapter.
    ckpt_bpp = ReferenceStats.MixedPrecisionAdam.CheckpointBytesPerParameter
    archA_size = calc_checkpoint_size(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters)
    check(2.3 * TB < archA_size < 2.6 * TB, "Archetype A checkpoint must be about 2.45 TB")
    check(
        abs((archA_size / (Models.Language.GPT3.parameters * ckpt_bpp)).to("").magnitude - 1) < 1e-9,
        "calc_checkpoint_size must match the registry bytes/param anchor",
    )
    dense20b_size = checkpoint_archetypes.Dense20BTransformerCheckpointSize
    bert_size = Models.Language.BERT_Large.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    archB_size = checkpoint_archetypes.EmbeddingHeavyRecommenderCheckpointSize
    resnet_size = Models.Vision.ResNet50.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    vision_transformer_size = checkpoint_archetypes.MediumVisionTransformerCheckpointSize

    write_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    mtbf = (float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours) / Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators) * hour

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Write time = checkpoint_size / write_bandwidth
    archA_write = (archA_size / write_bw).to(second)
    dense20b_write = (dense20b_size / write_bw).to(second)
    bert_write = (bert_size / write_bw).to(second)
    archB_write = (archB_size / write_bw).to(second)
    resnet_write = (resnet_size / write_bw).to(second)
    vision_transformer_write = (vision_transformer_size / write_bw).to(second)

    # Optimal interval = sqrt(2 * write_time * MTBF) [Young-Daly formula]
    # Bind the class-level MTBF at call time to avoid any upstream namespace collision
    # with later tutorial cells that define bare `mtbf` scalars.
    archA_interval = calc_young_daly_interval(archA_write, mtbf)
    dense20b_interval = calc_young_daly_interval(dense20b_write, mtbf)
    bert_interval = calc_young_daly_interval(bert_write, mtbf)
    archB_interval = calc_young_daly_interval(archB_write, mtbf)
    resnet_interval = calc_young_daly_interval(resnet_write, mtbf)
    vision_transformer_interval = calc_young_daly_interval(vision_transformer_write, mtbf)

    # Save overhead = write_time / optimal_interval * 100
    archA_overhead_ratio = (archA_write / archA_interval).to_base_units().magnitude
    dense20b_overhead_ratio = (dense20b_write / dense20b_interval).to_base_units().magnitude
    bert_overhead_ratio = (bert_write / bert_interval).to_base_units().magnitude
    archB_overhead_ratio = (archB_write / archB_interval).to_base_units().magnitude
    resnet_overhead_ratio = (resnet_write / resnet_interval).to_base_units().magnitude
    vision_transformer_overhead_ratio = (vision_transformer_write / vision_transformer_interval).to_base_units().magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(920 * second < archA_interval < 960 * second, "Archetype A interval should be ~15.7 minutes")
    check(280 * second < dense20b_interval < 310 * second, "20B dense transformer interval should be ~4.9 minutes")
    check(20 * second < bert_interval < 25 * second, "BERT interval should be ~22 seconds")
    check(1190 * second < archB_interval < 1210 * second, "Archetype B interval should be 20 minutes")
    check(5 * second < resnet_interval < 8 * second, "ResNet-50 interval should be ~6 seconds")
    check(18 * second < vision_transformer_interval < 23 * second, "Vision transformer interval should be ~21 seconds")
    check(archA_overhead_ratio < 0.10, "Archetype A overhead must be < 10%")
    check(dense20b_overhead_ratio < 0.10, "20B dense transformer overhead must be < 10%")
    check(bert_overhead_ratio < 0.10, "BERT overhead must be < 10%")
    check(archB_overhead_ratio < 0.10, "Archetype B overhead must be < 10%")
    check(resnet_overhead_ratio < 0.10, "ResNet-50 overhead must be < 10%")
    check(vision_transformer_overhead_ratio < 0.10, "Vision transformer overhead must be < 10%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    # -- Checkpoint sizes
    ckpt_bpp_str = fmt(ckpt_bpp.magnitude, precision=0)
    archA_ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(archA_size, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
    dense20b_ckpt_gb_str = fmt_memory(dense20b_size, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    bert_ckpt_gb_str = fmt_memory(bert_size, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    archB_ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(archB_size, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    resnet_ckpt_mb_str = fmt_memory(resnet_size, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    vision_transformer_ckpt_gb_str = fmt_memory(vision_transformer_size, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)

    write_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(write_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    mtbf_hr_str = fmt_time(mtbf, unit=hour, precision=0, commas=False)

    # -- Write times
    archA_write_s_str = fmt_time(archA_write, unit=second, precision=1, commas=False)
    dense20b_write_s_str = fmt_time(dense20b_write, unit=second, precision=1, commas=False)
    bert_write_s_str = fmt_time(bert_write, unit=second, precision=3, commas=False)
    archB_write_s_str = fmt_time(archB_write, unit=second, precision=0, commas=False)
    resnet_write_s_str = fmt_time(resnet_write, unit=second, precision=3, commas=False)
    vision_transformer_write_s_str = fmt_time(vision_transformer_write, unit=second, precision=3, commas=False)

    # -- Optimal intervals (min for >= 60s, s for < 60s)
    archA_interval_min_str = fmt_time(archA_interval, unit=minute, precision=1, commas=False)
    dense20b_interval_min_str = fmt_time(dense20b_interval, unit=minute, precision=1, commas=False)
    bert_interval_s_str = fmt_time(round(bert_interval.to(second).magnitude), unit=second, precision=0, commas=False)
    archB_interval_min_str = fmt_time(archB_interval, unit=minute, precision=0, commas=False)
    resnet_interval_s_str = fmt_time(round(resnet_interval.to(second).magnitude), unit=second, precision=0, commas=False)
    vision_transformer_interval_s_str = fmt_time(round(vision_transformer_interval.to(second).magnitude), unit=second, precision=0, commas=False)

    # -- Save overhead percentages
    archA_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(archA_overhead_ratio, precision=1, commas=False, style='symbol')
    dense20b_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(dense20b_overhead_ratio, precision=1, commas=False, style='symbol')
    bert_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(bert_overhead_ratio, precision=2, commas=False, style='symbol')
    archB_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(archB_overhead_ratio, precision=1, commas=False, style='symbol')
    resnet_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(resnet_overhead_ratio, precision=2, commas=False, style='symbol')
    vision_transformer_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(vision_transformer_overhead_ratio, precision=2, commas=False, style='symbol')
```

The Archetype A row in @tbl-checkpoint-overhead-by-model uses the same `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.ckpt_bpp_str`-byte-per-parameter resumable checkpoint (`{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archA_ckpt_tb_str`) as the rest of the chapter. Its interval calculation uses the GPU-only cluster MTBF rather than the shorter full-system MTBF of the worked cascade, so the square-root rule gives a longer interval than the Young-Daly notebook. The table keeps the GPU-only basis because its purpose is comparison across model types. Switching every row to the full-system MTBF would shorten each interval, and raise each overhead, by the same square-root factor, leaving the ranking across rows unchanged. The ResNet-50 and BERT-Large rows count only FP32 weights, so their write times and resulting intervals are lower bounds for a resumable checkpoint. Their intervals of seconds describe the balance for that smaller payload; selecting a recovery cadence requires including optimizer, schedule, and input-stream state. Small-state jobs rarely run on a cluster this large, and their actual storage bandwidth and complete recovery state determine whether saves every few minutes or every epoch have negligible overhead. The large-state rows show why interval selection becomes consequential when each save moves hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes.

|:--------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------:|:------------------------------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------------------:|
| **Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3)** |       `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archA_ckpt_tb_str`        |           `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archA_write_s_str`            |              `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archA_interval_min_str`              |        `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archA_overhead_pct_str`       |

| **BERT-Large**                  |        `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.bert_ckpt_gb_str`        |            `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.bert_write_s_str`            |               `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.bert_interval_s_str`                |        `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.bert_overhead_pct_str`        |
| **Embedding-heavy recommender** |       `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archB_ckpt_tb_str`        |           `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archB_write_s_str`            |              `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archB_interval_min_str`              |        `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archB_overhead_pct_str`       |
| **ResNet-50**                   |       `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.resnet_ckpt_mb_str`       |           `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.resnet_write_s_str`           |              `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.resnet_interval_s_str`               |       `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.resnet_overhead_pct_str`       |
| **Vision transformer class**    | `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.vision_transformer_ckpt_gb_str` |     `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.vision_transformer_write_s_str`     |        `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.vision_transformer_interval_s_str`         | `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.vision_transformer_overhead_pct_str` |

: **Checkpoint Overhead by Model Type**: The Archetype A row is the 175B running example at `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter (weights, FP32 master weights, and Adam moments); the 20B, recommender, and vision transformer rows are representative scenario sizes, and the `{python} CheckpointOverheadCalc.archB_ckpt_tb_str` embedding-heavy recommender is a smaller scenario than the `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.recsys_table_str` embedding tables of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) in @tbl-failure-impact-by-model; the BERT-Large and ResNet-50 rows count FP32 weights only and omit optimizer state, so their write times understate a full resumable checkpoint. Larger models require longer save times but also benefit from longer optimal checkpoint intervals. The percentage column reports the save-side overhead $\CheckpointOverheadFraction$ of @eq-checkpoint-overhead with no extra pause, not total Young-Daly waste; at the optimum, expected rework adds a comparable term. {#tbl-checkpoint-overhead-by-model}

These per-model overheads assume the write path is uncontended. When thousands of workers save at the same step, their combined burst becomes the checkpoint storm that @sec-storage-checkpointing defines and sizes; for recovery, the burst matters because a stalled write delays the generation that a failure would fall back on. Staging hides the write from training, yet a snapshot held only on local staging does not survive loss of its node, so where each copy lives decides which failures the saved state outlasts and how quickly it returns.

### Checkpoint storage and recovery {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-storage-recovery-6634}

Writing a checkpoint to node-local NVMe makes the save fast, but if the node itself fails, that local snapshot vanishes along with the hardware it was meant to recover. Writing only to a durable remote filesystem or object store survives the node failure, but pulling multi-terabyte state back across shared storage links slows every recovery. Recovery mechanisms therefore pair tiers from the storage hierarchy. Local NVMe provides fast staging and survivor reads, distributed filesystems provide durability across node failures, and object storage provides long-term retention. Together, the tiers let the saved state both outlast the fault and reload within the recovery budget.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tiered checkpoint storage designs and asynchronous write pipelines are established in @sec-storage-checkpointing.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: checkpoint-placement-restore
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHECKPOINT PLACEMENT AND RESTORE PATH (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: §Checkpoint storage and recovery paragraph below; reused by the
# │          recovery-time-budget notebook's T_load bullet.
# │
# │ Goal: Contrast a node-local restore with a shared-storage restore for the
# │       175B running example on the 1,024-GPU Archetype A reference cluster.
# │ Show: ~19.1 GB per node from local NVMe at 5 GB/s (~3.8 s, all nodes in
# │       parallel) vs. the full ~2.45 TB checkpoint at 100 GB/s aggregate (~24.5 s).
# │ How:  node share = checkpoint / nodes; t = bytes / bandwidth. Bandwidths from
# │       Systems.Storage.LocalNvmeTrainingTypical and Systems.Reliability.Recovery.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory, fmt_time

class CheckpointPlacementRestore:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters)  # 14 B/param resumable checkpoint
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    gpus_per_node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node
    nvme_bw = Systems.Storage.LocalNvmeTrainingTypical.bandwidth
    shared_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    n_nodes = n_gpus // gpus_per_node
    node_share = ckpt_bytes / n_nodes
    t_local = (node_share / nvme_bw).to(second)
    t_shared = (ckpt_bytes / shared_bw).to(second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(n_nodes * gpus_per_node == n_gpus, "reference cluster must be a whole number of nodes")
    check(t_local < t_shared, "parallel local reads must beat one shared aggregate read")
    check(3 < t_local.to(second).magnitude < 5, "per-node local restore should take about 4 s")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    n_nodes_str = fmt(n_nodes, precision=0)
    node_share_gb_str = fmt_memory(node_share, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    nvme_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvme_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    shared_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(shared_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    t_local_str = fmt_time(t_local, second, precision=1, commas=False)
    t_shared_str = fmt_time(t_shared, second, precision=1, commas=False)
    ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(ckpt_bytes, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
```

For fault tolerance, checkpoint placement determines which failures the saved state survives, while the restore path determines how quickly that surviving state becomes useful. On the `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.n_nodes_str`-node Archetype A reference cluster, each node holds about `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.node_share_gb_str` of the `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.ckpt_tb_str` checkpoint for the 175B running example. Reading that share from local NVMe at `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.nvme_bw_str` takes about `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.t_local_str`, with every node reading in parallel, while pulling the full checkpoint back through shared storage at `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.shared_bw_str` aggregate takes about `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.t_shared_str`. The local path is faster because it multiplies drive bandwidth by node count, but a sole copy on a lost node cannot restore that node's shard. The replacement node must read its share from a copy outside the failed domain, such as a distributed filesystem or object store, whose recovery time is set by sustained aggregate reads, network capacity, and deserialization. A sound placement therefore keeps a fast local copy for the survivors and a durable remote copy for whatever the failure took away, and these rates must still be measured under the job's own load.

### Checkpoint coordination patterns {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-checkpoint-coordination-patterns-f670}

If workers in a sharded training job save their local shards at different steps without coordinating, rolling one failed worker back to its last save invalidates every peer that already consumed gradients or activations from its later steps. Rollbacks then cascade backward through the run in the classic domino effect [@elnozahy2002survey]. Avoiding that cascade requires choosing how workers coordinate across two orthogonal dimensions. Workers can vary in whether they synchronize to capture a consistent cut (**coordinated** versus **uncoordinated checkpointing**\index{Checkpointing!uncoordinated}\index{Uncoordinated checkpointing|see{Checkpointing}}). They can also vary in whether they funnel state through one writer or persist shards in parallel (centralized versus distributed checkpointing). Because distributed ML workers exchange state at every step, production training relies on **coordinated checkpointing**\index{Checkpointing!coordinated}\index{Coordinated checkpointing|see{Checkpointing}}. In this scheme, workers synchronize at step boundaries or through an explicit two-phase commit protocol, so that all saved shards belong to a single globally consistent recovery line. Once coordination guarantees consistency, the remaining architectural decision is how those shards reach persistent storage: whether workers funnel their state through a single coordinator or write their partitions directly in parallel.

#### Centralized checkpointing {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-centralized-checkpointing-83a7}

In centralized checkpointing, workers send their state to a coordinator process that assembles and writes the complete checkpoint. This approach simplifies checkpoint management and can produce self-contained checkpoint files, but all state crosses the coordinator's network links, and coordinator failure interrupts the save. A streaming writer can avoid buffering the entire checkpoint, although it cannot remove the ingress bottleneck. That bottleneck is structural. The coordinator receives through one node's network links, so its write time grows with total state volume, whereas independent writers each move only their own share of the state through their own links. The gap between the two patterns therefore widens in proportion to the number of writers. For the 175B running example, the `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.n_nodes_str` nodes of the reference cluster would funnel `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.ckpt_tb_str` through one node's links instead of `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.node_share_gb_str` through each. The pattern is viable while that one path meets the checkpoint budget; state volume and sustained bandwidth determine the limit more directly than a fixed worker count. Centralized checkpointing is therefore attractive when operational simplicity matters more than aggregate bandwidth, whereas distributed and sharded approaches become necessary once the checkpoint itself is a fleet-scale object.

#### Distributed checkpointing {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-checkpointing-5dcc}

Distributed checkpointing eliminates this coordinator funnel by having each worker persist its own shard directly. @Fig-distributed-checkpoint-architecture contrasts the dataflow topologies: the centralized pattern concentrates traffic at the coordinator's ingress, while the distributed pattern writes in parallel to local NVMe and drains the shards to remote object storage in the background. With fixed per-worker shard sizes and sufficient independent staging bandwidth, adding workers need not lengthen the local write pause. Shared drain capacity and completion coordination can still limit scaling. A coordinator signals when to checkpoint and confirms completion, but state flows directly from workers to storage without aggregation.

::: {#fig-distributed-checkpoint-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Distributed Checkpoint Architecture**: Centralized vs. sharded checkpoint writes. In the centralized pattern (left), every worker funnels its shard through one coordinator, whose ingress bandwidth and buffering constrain the write path and whose failure halts the save. In the distributed pattern (right), each worker writes its own shard to local NVMe in parallel and a background process drains the shards to remote object storage, so the local blocking write time can remain roughly constant with fixed shard sizes and sufficient staging bandwidth; shared drain capacity still limits completion." fig-alt="Two panels divided by a dashed line. Left, centralized: four workers send red arrows that merge into one coordinator box labeled ingress limit, which writes to shared storage; beneath, a timing strip shows the four workers' green shard writes in a staircase, one after another, with a red bracket reading blocking write grows with workers. Right, distributed: each of four workers writes with a green arrow to its own NVMe drive, and dashed arrows drain the drives to an object store labeled background; beneath, the four green shard writes start together and end together under a green bracket labeled blocking, followed by dashed gray bars under a bracket labeled drain in background."}
![](images/svg/distributed-checkpoint-architecture.svg)

:::

A synchronous version of the coordination protocol proceeds in six steps:

1. Coordinator broadcasts checkpoint request with checkpoint ID
2. Each worker reaches a consistent state (barrier synchronization)
3. Each worker writes an immutable shard to a generation-specific staging prefix and records its byte length and cryptographic digest
4. Each worker confirms durable write completion to the coordinator
5. The coordinator writes an immutable manifest after all confirmations; the manifest names the training step, topology, model and optimizer formats, data-loader position, random state, and the length and digest of every shard, then publishes a commit marker or atomic pointer to that manifest
6. Coordinator broadcasts checkpoint complete, training resumes

The idealized protocol assumes step 2 completes quickly. The barrier, however, waits for the slowest of thousands of arrivals, so a single slow worker can make it dominate the checkpoint pause even when the storage path has ample bandwidth. Measuring arrival skew separately from copying and writing reveals whether coordination or data movement limits the save.

The manifest, not the presence of a directory or a plausible set of shard names, defines a committed checkpoint generation. Restore accepts only a published manifest whose shards all match their recorded lengths and digests; staged shards without that final publication remain unreachable and can be garbage collected. This rule prevents a partially overwritten `latest` directory from masquerading as recoverable state and makes generation rollback explicit. PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint\index{Distributed Checkpoint!manifest publication} follows this ordering, with storage writers persisting each rank's data before the coordinator's `finish()` operation writes the metadata and marks the checkpoint successful, while the storage backend supplies the publication semantics [@pytorchDistributedCheckpointDocs]. The set of per-worker states a manifest names is a cut\index{Checkpointing!consistency cut}, and the cut is consistent when all of those states could have existed together at one moment of a valid execution. In a consistent cut, no shard reflects an update another shard has not yet seen. That consistency cut determines whether the system can claim strict, bounded-asynchronous, or eventual consistency.

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-checkpoint-consistency-models .callout-perspective title="Checkpoint consistency models"}

Strict synchronous\index{Checkpointing!strict synchronous}: All workers checkpoint at exactly the same training step. Provides strongest consistency but highest overhead from barrier synchronization.

Bounded asynchronous\index{Checkpointing!bounded asynchronous}: Workers may progress at different rates while the checkpoint manager tracks which snapshots can form a consistent recovery cut. Bounding step skew alone is insufficient, because the system must retain compatible shard versions or enough replay information to reconstruct that cut. Asynchronous flushing can also preserve a single synchronized snapshot while its writes complete in the background, avoiding training stalls without relaxing recovery consistency.
