Eventual consistency\index{Checkpointing!eventual consistency}: Workers save independently and recovery attempts to reconcile their versions. A usable design must retain enough compatible versions or replay information to reconstruct a valid state; arbitrary recent shards do not necessarily form a recoverable generation. Reduced coordination at save time therefore transfers work and storage requirements to recovery.

:::

Steps 3 through 5 are two-phase commit,[^fn-twophase-checkpoint-protocol] the classic distributed-systems protocol for making one decision atomic across many participants [@gray1978], applied to a checkpoint. Steps 3 and 4 form its prepare phase, in which each worker stages its shard and reports success, and step 5 is its commit phase, in which the coordinator durably records the decision by publishing the manifest. The manifest publication rule inherits the protocol's guarantee and its known weakness. If the coordinator crashes after workers prepare but before it records a decision, the system must not expose those shards as a valid checkpoint, and the prepared participants remain blocked until the original or a replacement coordinator recovers the durable decision. Uncommitted staged shards can be garbage collected only after recovery establishes that no commit decision exists. Atomic publication also does not by itself make the published shards consistent: synchronous gradient updates naturally create step boundaries where all workers have applied the same updates, whereas asynchronous training and pipeline parallelism require explicit coordination to define a consistent cut.

[^fn-twophase-checkpoint-protocol]: **Two-phase commit (2PC)**\index{Two-phase commit!checkpoint atomicity}: Formalized by @gray1978, 2PC ensures all participants either commit or abort atomically. A timeout can trigger coordinator recovery, but it cannot by itself authorize unilateral rollback.

#### Sharded checkpointing {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-sharded-checkpointing-58d0}

Modern distributed training frameworks partition model state across workers using techniques like ZeRO and FSDP, which shard parameters, gradients, and optimizer state instead of replicating them on every data-parallel worker. In these configurations, no single worker holds complete model state. Each worker holds only its assigned parameter shard plus corresponding optimizer state.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ How ZeRO and FSDP partition training state across data-parallel workers is established in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-memoryefficient-data-parallelism-zero-fsdp-0e69.
:::

Sharded checkpointing\index{Checkpointing!sharded}[^fn-sharded-checkpoint-state] [@rajbhandari2020] uses this distribution. Each worker writes only its shard, which divides the per-worker write volume by the number of shards. Recovery loads shards and redistributes state to workers based on the recovery configuration.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Sharded checkpointing prose and footnote below.
# │ Note: 14 B/param resumable checkpoint (no gradients or activations).
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_memory

class FaultToleranceShardRecap:
    m = Models.Language.GPT3
    gpt3_ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(m.parameters)  # 14 B/param default
    n_workers = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    from mlsysim.fmt import fmt

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_params_b_str = fmt_params(m.parameters, scale="B", precision=0, commas=False)
    gpt3_ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_ckpt_bytes, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
    gpt3_shard_gb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_ckpt_bytes / n_workers, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    n_workers_str = fmt(n_workers, precision=0, commas=True)
```

[^fn-sharded-checkpoint-state]: **Sharded checkpointing**\index{Checkpointing!sharded I/O parallelism}: Each worker saves only its local partition rather than gathering state to a single writer, parallelizing I/O across all nodes. The trade-off is that recovery requires every shard to be available and consistent, making the checkpoint protocol more complex. Losing one storage device invalidates the generation only if a required shard cannot be recovered from another copy or sufficient storage redundancy.

Dividing state across the fleet keeps per-worker saves small even for multi-terabyte models. A `{python} FaultToleranceShardRecap.gpt3_params_b_str` parameter model with a `{python} FaultToleranceShardRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` checkpoint distributed across `{python} FaultToleranceShardRecap.n_workers_str` workers requires each worker to write only `{python} FaultToleranceShardRecap.gpt3_shard_gb_str`, achievable in seconds with local NVMe storage. When elastic scaling or hardware replacement changes the worker count between save and restore, shard redistribution must remap the saved partitions to the new worker configuration, which is why frameworks need flexible resharding support to recover across topology changes. Yet possessing a valid checkpoint is only half the recovery path. Sharding distributes the write work and staging controls the shared I/O burst, but the system must still detect the failure, trigger restoration, and coordinate the distributed shards before training can resume. The speed of detection and recovery therefore governs the cost of the interruption.

::: {#chk-fault-tolerance-checkpoint-cost .callout-checkpoint title="Reasoning about checkpoint overhead"}

Verify your understanding of how failure rate and checkpoint cost set the optimal checkpoint interval:

- [ ] **Young-Daly shift**: use the Young-Daly formula to estimate how the optimal interval $\OptimalCheckpointInterval$ shifts when a cluster doubles in size and its system MTBF halves, with $\CheckpointWriteTime$ held fixed. State whether the interval lengthens or shortens and by about what factor.
- [ ] **Two-sided overhead**: explain why writing checkpoints too frequently and writing them too rarely both raise checkpoint overhead, including the two costs $\OptimalCheckpointInterval$ balances.
- [ ] **Faster writes**: determine how an order-of-magnitude reduction in $\CheckpointWriteTime$ from sharded checkpointing changes the optimal interval and expected lost work per failure.
- [ ] **Square-root scaling**: explain why the Young-Daly interval depends on the square root of MTBF rather than scaling linearly with it.

:::

## Failure Detection and Recovery {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-recovery-0f54}

A GPU silently hangs, dropping its utilization to zero while its peer GPUs wait indefinitely at an AllReduce barrier. On the chapter's `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.gpus_example_str`-GPU cluster, every minute the system takes to notice this hung rank and reboot the node costs about `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.idle_cost_per_min_str` in idle compute. Checkpoints preserve state, but the recovery process itself determines how much compute a failure wastes. In the accounting of the Fleet Law (@eq-fleet-law), that waiting belongs to the synchronization term $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$. Every surviving rank idles at the barrier until the group is whole again, so detection, restart, and reload add directly to step time averaged over the run. The goodput accounting of @sec-performance-engineering-goodput-boundaries charges the same time to runtime goodput.

@Eq-recovery-time decomposes recovery time into four primary components:

$$ \FailureRecoveryTime= \FailureDetectionTime+ \JobRestartTime+ \CheckpointLoadTime+ \RecoveryWarmupTime$$ {#eq-recovery-time}

where $\FailureDetectionTime$ is the time between the physical hardware fault and system classification as a failure. The term $\JobRestartTime$ is the latency required for the job scheduler to allocate resources and launch replacement processes. The term $\CheckpointLoadTime$ is the I/O duration to read checkpoint state from distributed storage into GPU memory. The term $\RecoveryWarmupTime$ is the interval needed to refill data pipelines, compile just-in-time (JIT) kernels, and stabilize training throughput. Each component presents distinct optimization opportunities, and the dominant term varies by cluster configuration. Understanding this decomposition enables targeted investment in the bottleneck rather than uniform improvement across all components.

### Failure detection mechanisms {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-mechanisms-efed}

::: {.column-margin}
```{=latex}
\vspace*{-5mm}
```
![](images/svg/fault_tolerance_detection_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A ladder of bars for detection latency on a log scale, ordered by how hard a failure is to see: a process crash within 30 seconds, a GPU hang within 120 seconds, a network partition within 180 seconds, and silent data corruption as the longest bar, labeled hours, whose end continues as a dotted open extension."}

*Detection latency climbs from seconds (crash) to hours (silent corruption).*
:::

To the rest of the cluster, a dead rank and a rank busy flushing a multi-gigabyte checkpoint shard both look silent. Every failure detector must therefore balance two expensive mistakes: setting timeouts too short kills healthy workers during transient network or storage stalls, while setting them too long leaves thousands of peer GPUs idling at a collective barrier. Heartbeat monitoring\index{Heartbeat protocol!liveness signal}\index{Heartbeat protocol!failure detection}\index{Failure detection!heartbeat protocol} is the first detection layer and usually sets the floor on $\FailureDetectionTime$. Each GPU rank periodically signals liveness to a coordinator, and if no heartbeat arrives within the timeout period $\HandoverTimeout$, the coordinator declares the worker failed.

For a heartbeat interval of $\HeartbeatInterval$ seconds and network-delay standard deviation $\NetworkDelayStandardDeviation$ in seconds, @eq-timeout-calculation defines the timeout heuristic:

$$ \HandoverTimeout = \HeartbeatInterval+ \TimeoutSafetyMultiplier\NetworkDelayStandardDeviation$$ {#eq-timeout-calculation}

Here, $\TimeoutSafetyMultiplier$ is a dimensionless safety multiplier; values from three to five illustrate a tuning range rather than a guaranteed false positive rate. The heuristic treats the normal heartbeat delivery delay as small relative to the heartbeat interval. A deployment with substantial baseline delay or a heavy delay tail must account for those measurements as well as $\NetworkDelayStandardDeviation$. Tuning $\HandoverTimeout$ too tightly causes legitimate checkpoint writes or long collectives to trigger false failure declarations; tuning it too loosely extends the window during which other ranks wait for the missing contribution.

Collective communication timeouts provide a second detection layer. During synchronous training, a collective required by the next step remains an incomplete critical-path dependency if a required rank disappears. AllReduce needs every rank's contribution before it can produce the reduced result; the progress and failure behavior of other collectives depends on the operation and runtime. Transport and process-group timeouts bound how long the job waits before declaring the operation failed and entering recovery. NCCL[^fn-nccl-collective-timeout] provides configurable transport and reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) timeout parameters for this purpose, while higher-level frameworks may impose process-group operation timeouts. These settings are often set conservatively to avoid crashing jobs during legitimate periods of slow communication, which unfortunately extends $\FailureDetectionTime$.

[^fn-nccl-collective-timeout]: **NCCL timeout**\index{NCCL!timeout}\index{NCCL!timeout trade-off}: NVIDIA's collective communication library exposes transport and RAS timeout controls such as `NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT` and `NCCL_RAS_TIMEOUT_FACTOR` [@nvidiaNcclUserGuide]. Higher-level launch and distributed-training frameworks can add their own restart and operation-timeout behavior [@pytorchElasticDocs]. Aggressive timeout settings accelerate failure detection but risk false positives during legitimate long collective operations on large models, forcing a trade-off between detection latency and training stability that has no universal optimum.

Container orchestration health checks\index{Health check!orchestration layer} provide a third layer. Kubernetes, the container orchestration system, offers liveness probes\index{Liveness probe!container orchestration} (verifying that a process still responds and makes progress) and readiness probes\index{Readiness probe!container orchestration} (verifying that a process is ready to handle requests). Slurm, the batch scheduler common on HPC-style training clusters, instead runs a periodic node health-check program that can drain a node whose GPUs, links, or file systems fail their tests. Both operate independently of the training framework, catching failures that application-level heartbeats might miss; a liveness probe that tests forward progress rather than mere process existence can catch a process that is alive but deadlocked.

Loss spike\index{Loss spike!failure anomaly} detection exposes an anomaly, not its cause. @Fig-training-failure-signatures contrasts an idealized healthy loss trend with gradient explosion, a premature plateau, and NaN divergence. Real stochastic training need not decrease monotonically, so a transient rise alone does not establish failure, and nonfinite values need not crash the process. Silent hardware corruption can produce an abrupt loss or gradient-norm spike, but so can a bad batch, an optimizer instability, a data-ordering defect, or a distributed-state mismatch. Robust systems therefore pause before the suspect update commits, preserve the input and worker evidence, and replay the step on known-good hardware. The system drains hardware only after that evidence implicates the device; otherwise, it repairs the data, optimizer, or synchronization path that produced the same symptom.

::: {#fig-training-failure-signatures fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Training Failure Signatures**: Common patterns of model loss over time that indicate underlying system or algorithmic failures. (A) Normal training. (B) Gradient explosion. (C) Loss plateau. (D) NaN divergence, ending where a nonfinite-value check halts the run; without such a check the process can keep running on NaN values rather than crash. Identifying these signatures automatically is essential for rapid recovery in autonomous training pipelines. The curves are synthetic illustrations of each pattern, not logs from a training run." fig-alt="Four loss-versus-steps panels in a two-by-two grid on a shared loss axis. (A) Normal training: a green curve descending smoothly. Panels B to D repeat that healthy curve as a faint green reference line behind each pathology. (B) Gradient explosion: a descending curve with a red spike segment midway that then rejoins the healthy reference, labeled healthy. (C) Loss plateau: a curve that flattens early, with the gap between it and the healthy reference shaded red and labeled gap to healthy. (D) NaN divergence: a curve that pulls away above the healthy reference, oscillating with growing amplitude, then climbs steeply to a red X labeled NaN check halts run."}
```{python}
#| echo: false
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style
import numpy as np

book_style.set_book_style()
COLORS = book_style.COLORS

# Four small multiples on one shared loss axis; the healthy curve is green, the
# pathological curves are neutral with only the failure itself marked in red.
# Laid out 2x2 at book width so every label prints at or above the floor.
fig, axes2d = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.2, 4.5), sharey=True, sharex=True)
axes = axes2d.ravel()

steps = np.linspace(0, 100, 200)
np.random.seed(42)

# PANEL A: Normal Training
noise = np.random.normal(0, 0.02, len(steps))
loss_a = 2.4 * np.exp(-0.035 * steps) + 0.35 + noise

# PANEL B: Gradient Explosion
loss_b = 2.4 * np.exp(-0.035 * steps) + 0.35 + np.random.normal(0, 0.02, len(steps))
spike_idx = 90
loss_b[spike_idx : spike_idx + 15] += np.linspace(0, 1.7, 15)
# Recovery: the excess decays smoothly back onto the healthy baseline and carries
# the same measurement noise as the rest of the trace.
decay_k = np.arange(1, 21)
loss_b[spike_idx + 15 : spike_idx + 35] += 1.7 * np.exp(-decay_k / 4.5)

# PANEL C: Loss Plateau
loss_c = np.copy(loss_a)
plateau_idx = 40
loss_c[plateau_idx:] = loss_c[plateau_idx] + np.random.normal(0, 0.015, len(steps) - plateau_idx)

# PANEL D: NaN Divergence
nan_steps = steps[:140]
# The run tracks healthy training at first, then its baseline drifts upward and a
# one-sided oscillation of growing amplitude rides on top, so even its troughs sit
# above the healthy curve. The last few steps climb steeply before the halt.
healthy_d = 2.4 * np.exp(-0.035 * nan_steps) + 0.35
drift = 1.25 * (nan_steps / nan_steps[-1]) ** 1.6
amp = 0.06 * np.exp(0.034 * nan_steps)
osc = amp * (0.5 + 0.5 * np.sin(nan_steps * 0.4))
loss_d = healthy_d + drift + osc + np.random.normal(0, 0.012, len(nan_steps)).clip(0)
n_ramp = 12
loss_d[-n_ramp:] += np.linspace(0, 1, n_ramp) ** 2.2 * (2.85 - loss_d[-1])

ax_a, ax_b, ax_c, ax_d = axes
lw = 1.8

ax_a.plot(steps, loss_a, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], linewidth=lw)

# Healthy reference: the panel-A curve, drawn faintly behind each pathology so
# the deviation itself is what the eye reads.
for ax_ref in (ax_b, ax_c, ax_d):
    ax_ref.plot(steps, loss_a, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.45, zorder=1)
ax_b.text(54, 0.55, 'healthy', fontsize=10, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], ha='center', va='top')

ax_b.plot(steps, loss_b, color=COLORS['primary'], linewidth=lw)
seg = slice(spike_idx - 1, spike_idx + 35)
ax_b.plot(steps[seg], loss_b[seg], color=COLORS['RedLine'], linewidth=lw + 0.4)
peak = spike_idx + 14
ax_b.text(steps[peak] + 4, loss_b[peak] + 0.05, 'spike', fontsize=10.5, color=COLORS['RedLine'], ha='left', va='bottom')

ax_c.fill_between(steps[plateau_idx:], loss_a[plateau_idx:], loss_c[plateau_idx:], color=COLORS['RedL'], alpha=0.8, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax_c.plot(steps, loss_c, color=COLORS['primary'], linewidth=lw)
ax_c.text(70, loss_c[plateau_idx] + 0.3, 'plateau', fontsize=10.5, color=COLORS['RedLine'], ha='center', va='bottom')
ax_c.text(70, 0.98, 'gap to healthy', fontsize=10.5, color=COLORS['RedLine'], ha='center', va='center')

ax_d.plot(nan_steps, loss_d, color=COLORS['primary'], linewidth=lw)
ax_d.scatter([nan_steps[-1]], [loss_d[-1]], marker='X', color=COLORS['RedLine'], edgecolor='white', linewidth=0.8, s=70, zorder=6)
ax_d.text(
    nan_steps[-1] - 5, loss_d[-1] - 0.4, 'NaN check\nhalts run', fontsize=10.5, linespacing=1.1, color=COLORS['RedLine'], ha='right', va='center'
)

titles = ['(A) Normal training', '(B) Gradient explosion', '(C) Loss plateau', '(D) NaN divergence']
for ax, title in zip(axes, titles):
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11.5, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['primary'], loc='left', pad=6)
    ax.set_xlim(-2, 102)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 3.1)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 50, 100])
    ax.set_yticks([0, 1, 2, 3])
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
    ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', color=COLORS['grid'], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.6)
for ax in (ax_c, ax_d):
    ax.set_xlabel('Steps', fontsize=11)
for ax in (ax_a, ax_c):
    ax.set_ylabel('Loss', fontsize=11)

plt.tight_layout()
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.08, hspace=0.32)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```
:::

@Tbl-training-failure-response-map pairs each signature, plus the silent hang that a loss curve cannot show, with a candidate cause and a first response. The pairing guides investigation without treating the curve as a unique diagnosis, and the operational question that follows is how long detection actually takes once these monitoring layers interact.

| **Signature**              | **Likely interpretation**                                                         | **Recovery response**                                                                                |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Spike followed by recovery | Transient input or numerical anomaly; the curve alone does not identify the cause | Preserve the suspect batch and step evidence, then replay before deciding whether to continue.       |
| Spike followed by plateau  | Optimizer instability, corrupted state, or a persistent data-path defect          | Pause, replay from a known-good checkpoint, and compare input, optimizer, and worker evidence.       |
| Gradual divergence         | Data drift, numerical instability, corrupted state, or worker desynchronization   | Compare per-rank telemetry and evaluation evidence; isolate hardware only when replay implicates it. |
| Hang without an error      | Collective deadlock or crashed worker blocking synchronization                    | Use timeout detection and restart or reconstruct the worker group.                                   |

: **Training Failure Response Map**: Training-loss curves are operational evidence only when they lead to different recovery actions. The response map ties each signature to the failure class most likely to explain it and to the first action operators should take. {#tbl-training-failure-response-map}

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-realistic-detection-latencies .callout-perspective title="Realistic failure detection latencies"}

Failure detection includes more than the configured heartbeat timeout when the policy requires verification before recovery. The ranges in @tbl-fault-tolerance-detection-latencies illustrate planning scenarios, not universal detection guarantees. Aggressive timeouts risk false positives (killing healthy-but-slow workers), while conservative timeouts delay real failure detection. A multi-stage policy can use an initial timeout to trigger investigation and a later threshold to trigger recovery. Its actual latency must be measured under the workload and failure conditions it is intended to handle.

| **Failure type**           | **Planning range** | **Why**                                        |
|:---------------------------|:------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------|
| **Process crash**          |   5--30 seconds    | Heartbeat timeout + verification retries       |
| **GPU hang**               |  30--120 seconds   | Must distinguish from legitimately slow kernel |
| **Network partition**      |  60--180 seconds   | Must distinguish from temporary congestion     |
| **Silent data corruption** |  Minutes to hours  | Requires statistical anomaly detection         |

: **Illustrative Failure Detection Latencies**: Planning ranges for detecting process crashes, GPU hangs, network partitions, and silent data corruption, with the dominant cause of latency for each category, showing why static heartbeat timeouts alone are insufficient. The ranges are illustrative assumptions, not measurements; a deployment must measure its own. {#tbl-fault-tolerance-detection-latencies}

:::

### Recovery procedures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-recovery-procedures-002d}

Once a failure is classified, a cold-restart recovery path executes a coordinated sequence to restore consistency. The warm-restart alternative developed next preserves surviving processes when their state can be trusted.

1. Job termination\index{Recovery procedure!job termination}: A `SIGTERM` is broadcast to all surviving workers. This cold-restart path tears down the affected training group so that no survivor continues using the old membership or partially completed collective state.
2. Resource reclamation\index{Recovery procedure!resource reclamation}: The scheduler marks the failed node as "draining" to prevent immediate rescheduling and requests a replacement from the spare pool.
3. Job restart\index{Recovery procedure!job restart}: New containers are launched (from cache if available), and the training binary is re-initialized on all nodes.
4. Checkpoint loading: Each worker reads the state assigned to it from the distributed filesystem. When membership or parallelism changes, recovery remaps the saved shards to the new partitions.
5. State synchronization\index{Recovery procedure!state synchronization}: Ranks handshake to establish a new communicator (for example, `ncclCommInitRank`), and workers verify they are all at the same training step.
6. Training resumption\index{Recovery procedure!training resumption}: The data loader restores its recorded position and sampling state, and the training loop resumes from the checkpoint step. A batch index alone suffices only when it reconstructs the same logical input stream.

Automatic recovery systems perform these steps without human intervention. Modern training frameworks integrate with cluster managers to automate parts of the sequence. DeepSpeed documents save/load routines for model and ZeRO optimizer checkpoints, which provide the durable state needed after failure [@deepspeedCheckpointingDocs]. PyTorch's `torchrun` elastic launch documents failure and membership-change behavior through its rendezvous mechanism,[^fn-rendezvous-elastic-barrier] the coordinator-backed protocol by which surviving workers agree on membership and ranks after a restart [@pytorchElasticDocs; @pytorchRendezvousDocs].

[^fn-rendezvous-elastic-barrier]: **Rendezvous**\index{Rendezvous!elastic training}: From French "rendez-vous" (present yourselves), this coordination protocol lets restarted workers discover one another and establish a new group before training resumes. Recovery waits for the membership policy to be satisfied, so slow startup, delayed communication, and missing workers can extend this phase. Heterogeneity affects those delays but does not by itself imply a proportional latency law.

Recovery validation tests whether the restored job behaves consistently with its recorded state. Parameter shapes, dtypes, and shard identities must match the manifest. A short replay or validation workload then checks loss and gradient statistics under the expected numerical tolerance; different batches need not reproduce the last prefailure loss. Immediate divergence is evidence to investigate the checkpoint, data state, and execution configuration, not proof that the snapshot is corrupt. Falling back to an earlier validated generation is appropriate when the newest state cannot be trusted.

Recovery must also prevent the failed ownership epoch from returning. A coordinator grants each worker-group incarnation a monotonically increasing epoch (a membership counter, unrelated to a training epoch over the dataset) and associates membership with a renewable lease. Every state-changing write carries that epoch as a fencing token. Before replacement writes proceed, the recovery protocol advances the enforced epoch at each protected resource, which rejects writes carrying an older token (@fig-epoch-fencing). The old worker then cannot publish a checkpoint or update job progress, even if it resumes after a long pause; rendezvous likewise admits only the current membership. A lease alone is insufficient because expiration changes the coordinator's ownership decision, not the old worker's ability to reach storage. Fencing enforces that decision at the resource boundary [@kleppmann2017designing].

::: {#fig-epoch-fencing fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Epoch Fencing during Recovery**: When the old worker's lease expires, the coordinator starts epoch 8 and advances the epoch the checkpoint store enforces before the replacement begins writing. The replacement's writes carry token 8 and are accepted; when the old worker resumes from its pause or partition, its write still carries token 7 and the store rejects it. The lease decides ownership, and the fence at the store enforces that decision even against a worker that never learned it lost ownership." fig-alt="Swim-lane timeline with four lanes: coordinator, replacement, old worker, and checkpoint store, with time running left to right. The coordinator lane shows epoch 7 then epoch 8, split at a mark labeled lease expires. A dashed violet arrow labeled advance fence runs from the epoch boundary down to the store, whose bar changes from accepts epoch at least 7 to accepts epoch at least 8. The replacement lane begins after the boundary with a bar labeled token 8, and a green arrow from it to the store is labeled write, token 8: accepted. The old worker lane shows a token 7 bar, a dashed gray line labeled paused or partitioned, and a bar labeled resumes, from which a red arrow ends at a red X labeled write, token 7: rejected."}
![](images/svg/epoch-fencing.svg)

:::

Retries complete the recovery contract. An operation may be retried automatically only when it is idempotent or carries a stable operation identifier that lets the receiver deduplicate repeated effects. Each attempt inherits the caller's absolute deadline rather than receiving a fresh timeout, and the system caps attempts with a retry budget shared across the request or recovery tree. Exponential backoff and jitter spread attempts in time, but they do not prevent overload if every layer retries independently. The budget therefore belongs at one retry-owning layer; exhausted budget returns a failure or invokes degradation instead of amplifying the original incident [@beyer2016sre; @nygard2007releaseit].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-recovery-budget
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics import calc_mtbf_cluster, calc_checkpoint_size

class RecoveryBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters)  # 14 B/param resumable checkpoint
    recovery = Systems.Reliability.Recovery
    t_detect = float(recovery.detection_time_s) * second
    t_restart = float(recovery.restart_time_s) * second
    aggregate_ckpt_bw = float(recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    t_load = (ckpt_bytes / aggregate_ckpt_bw).to(second)
    t_warmup = float(recovery.warmup_time_s) * second
    shard_read_bw = Systems.Storage.LocalNvmeTrainingTypical.bandwidth
    n_gpus_1k = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    n_gpus_10k = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    mtbf_1k = calc_mtbf_cluster(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours, n_gpus_1k)
    mtbf_10k = calc_mtbf_cluster(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours, n_gpus_10k)
    failures_per_day_1k = (24 * hour / mtbf_1k).to("").magnitude
    failures_per_day_10k = (24 * hour / mtbf_10k).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    # One source for the four-term budget: the preemption overhead in fleet
    # orchestration and the runtime-goodput composition call the same helper.
    t_total = recovery.cold_restart_time(ckpt_bytes)
    daily_loss_1k = failures_per_day_1k * t_total
    daily_loss_10k = failures_per_day_10k * t_total
    overhead_pct_1k = (daily_loss_1k / (24 * hour)).to("").magnitude * 100
    overhead_pct_10k = (daily_loss_10k / (24 * hour)).to("").magnitude * 100
    waste_gpu_hours_10k = daily_loss_10k.to(hour).magnitude * n_gpus_10k

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_total.to(minute).magnitude - 6.6) < 1.0, f"Expected ~6.6 min total recovery time, got {t_total.to(minute).magnitude:.1f}")
    check(t_total < 30 * minute, "Recovery time should be under 30 min")
    check(
        abs((t_detect + t_restart + t_load + t_warmup - t_total).to(second).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "Notebook terms must sum to the registry's cold_restart_time",
    )
    check(abs(daily_loss_1k.to(minute).magnitude - 3.0) < 0.5, f"1k daily loss ({daily_loss_1k.to(minute).magnitude:.1f} min)")
    check(22 < t_load.to(second).magnitude < 27, f"Aggregate checkpoint load should be ~24.5 s, got {t_load.to(second).magnitude:.1f}")
    check(abs(daily_loss_10k.to(minute).magnitude - 31.0) < 2.0, f"10k daily loss ({daily_loss_10k.to(minute).magnitude:.1f} min)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_total_min_str = fmt_time(t_total, unit=minute, precision=1, commas=False)
    t_detect_s_str = fmt_time(t_detect, second, precision=0, commas=False)
    t_restart_min_str = fmt_time(t_restart, minute, precision=0, commas=False)
    t_load_s_str = fmt_time(t_load, second, precision=None, commas=False)
    t_warmup_min_str = fmt_time(t_warmup, minute, precision=0, commas=False)
    aggregate_read_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(aggregate_ckpt_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    shard_read_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(shard_read_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_gpus_1k_str = fmt(n_gpus_1k, precision=0, commas=True)
    n_gpus_10k_str = fmt(n_gpus_10k, precision=0, commas=True)
    mtbf_1k_hrs_str = fmt_time(round(mtbf_1k.to(hour).magnitude), hour, precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    mtbf_10k_hrs_str = fmt_time(round(mtbf_10k.to(hour).magnitude), hour, precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    failures_per_day_1k_str = fmt_rate(failures_per_day_1k, "failures/day", precision=2, commas=False)
    failures_per_day_10k_str = fmt_rate(failures_per_day_10k, "failures/day", precision=1, commas=False)
    daily_loss_min_1k_str = fmt_time(round(daily_loss_1k.to(minute).magnitude), minute, precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    daily_loss_min_10k_str = fmt_time(round(daily_loss_10k.to(minute).magnitude), minute, precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    overhead_pct_1k_str = fmt_percent(overhead_pct_1k / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    overhead_pct_10k_str = fmt_percent(overhead_pct_10k / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    waste_gpu_hours_10k_str = fmt_count(round(waste_gpu_hours_10k), label="GPU-hour", plural_label="GPU-hours")
```

::: {#nbk-fault-tolerance-recovery-time-budget .callout-notebook title="The recovery time budget"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Recovery time budget notebook below.
# │ Note: 14 B/param resumable checkpoint (no gradients or activations).
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim import *

class FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap:
    m = Models.Language.GPT3
    gpt3_ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(m.parameters)  # 14 B/param default
    n_workers = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    params_b_str = fmt_params(m.parameters, scale="B", precision=0, commas=False)
    gpt3_ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_ckpt_bytes, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
    gpt3_shard_gb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_ckpt_bytes / n_workers, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    n_workers_str = fmt_count(n_workers, commas=True, label="GPU")
```

**Problem**: Consider a `{python} FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap.params_b_str` parameter model training on `{python} FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap.n_workers_str`. The checkpoint size is approximately `{python} FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` (BF16 weights, FP32 master weights, and Adam moments at `{python} YoungDalyCheckpointState.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter). Estimate the cost of a single failure event.

**Setup**: The recovery budget $\FailureRecoveryTime$ has four terms.

- **$\FailureDetectionTime$**: `{python} RecoveryBudget.t_detect_s_str` (conservative heartbeat timeout with verification retries).
- **$\JobRestartTime$**: `{python} RecoveryBudget.t_restart_min_str` (scheduler queue time + container launch + Python import overhead + NCCL initialization).
- **$\CheckpointLoadTime$**: `{python} RecoveryBudget.t_load_s_str` (this is the aggregate-shared-storage read of the full `{python} FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` checkpoint at `{python} RecoveryBudget.aggregate_read_gb_per_s_str` aggregate). With sharded local-NVMe reads at `{python} RecoveryBudget.shard_read_gb_per_s_str`, one GPU's `{python} FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap.gpt3_shard_gb_str` shard alone would load in under a second. The GPUs of a node share its drive, however, so the node's `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.node_share_gb_str` share takes about `{python} CheckpointPlacementRestore.t_local_str`, and only on nodes that survived with their local copy).
- **$\RecoveryWarmupTime$**: `{python} RecoveryBudget.t_warmup_min_str` (JIT kernel compilation, data pipeline buffer fill, TCP connection re-establishment).

**Total**: $\FailureRecoveryTime= \FailureDetectionTime+ \JobRestartTime+ \CheckpointLoadTime+ \RecoveryWarmupTime\approx$ `{python} RecoveryBudget.t_total_min_str` per failure event.

**Impact**: For this recovery path, $\FailureRecoveryTime$ is the operational MTTR\index{MTTR!recovery time budget} term in the steady-state availability relation (perspective \ref{psp-fault-tolerance-scale-transforms-failure}). It is not the whole cost of a failure. Every failure also discards the work done since the last completed checkpoint, on average half the checkpoint interval (@fig-checkpoint-recovery-timeline), and the Young-Daly waste of @eq-ft-checkpoint-waste already counts that rework, so the figures below price only the recovery term. Recovery time optimization matters more as clusters grow. The GPU-only baseline from @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling compares the two sizes on a common basis and understates both failure counts. On that basis, a `{python} RecoveryBudget.n_gpus_1k_str`-GPU cluster has MTBF of `{python} RecoveryBudget.mtbf_1k_hrs_str` and experiences about `{python} RecoveryBudget.failures_per_day_1k_str`, losing about `{python} RecoveryBudget.daily_loss_min_1k_str` daily, a modest `{python} RecoveryBudget.overhead_pct_1k_str` overhead. However, a `{python} RecoveryBudget.n_gpus_10k_str`-GPU cluster has GPU-only MTBF of `{python} RecoveryBudget.mtbf_10k_hrs_str` and experiences about `{python} RecoveryBudget.failures_per_day_10k_str`, losing about `{python} RecoveryBudget.daily_loss_min_10k_str` daily (`{python} RecoveryBudget.overhead_pct_10k_str` overhead). That is equivalent to wasting roughly `{python} RecoveryBudget.waste_gpu_hours_10k_str` every day (the daily lost minutes multiplied across all `{python} RecoveryBudget.n_gpus_10k_str` GPUs).

:::

### Warm restart vs. cold restart {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-warm-vs-cold-restart}

The recovery procedure described in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-recovery-procedures-002d is a cold restart\index{Cold restart!recovery trade-offs}: every process in the affected job group exits, and the group reloads state from a valid checkpoint. This simplifies recovery by avoiding dependence on surviving in-memory state, but it can discard useful state. After one GPU fails in the `{python} FaultToleranceShardRecap.n_workers_str`-GPU reference job, every surviving worker may retain reusable values; an interrupted update or silent corruption, however, can make some of those values unsafe to keep.

A warm restart\index{Warm restart!survivor preservation} preserves the state of surviving workers. When a rank fails, surviving ranks detect the failure but do not exit. They enter a waiting state, preserving loaded model weights and optimizer states in GPU memory. The scheduler replaces only the failed node. The new node joins, loads its partition of the state from disk (or receives it via broadcast from a peer), and the communicator is rebuilt. The replacement and survivors must agree on the same committed training step before resuming. A shard restored from an older checkpoint cannot be combined with survivor shards that have advanced beyond it; the runtime must reconstruct the missing current state or roll the group back to a common recovery point. Training resumes only after that consistency check.

When the missing state can be reconstructed at the survivors' current step, warm restart avoids a full-cluster reload and repeated warmup. For the `{python} FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap.n_workers_str` example, that fast path avoids rereading the full `{python} FaultToleranceRecoveryRecap.gpt3_ckpt_tb_str` checkpoint through shared storage, whose cold-path $\CheckpointLoadTime$ is `{python} RecoveryBudget.t_load_s_str`. The replacement still needs state transfer and initialization, and all ranks wait until it is ready. If consistency instead requires a rollback, the recovery budget must include the corresponding survivor-state restoration and lost work.

The trade-off is software complexity. Survivor-preserving warm restarts require specialized application and runtime support for dynamic membership changes without leaking CUDA memory, corrupting shared state, or deadlocking during communicator reconstruction. Common training frameworks restart the worker group or reload a checkpoint rather than preserve survivors (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-framework-support-elastic-training-8b75). A deployment that implements a warm-restart fast path still needs cold restart as a safety net. The cold-restart range in @tbl-cold-vs-warm-restart brackets the `{python} RecoveryBudget.t_total_min_str` budget computed above. The warm-restart range is a planning range for the fast path, which avoids the full-cluster reload and warmup; its actual duration depends on how quickly the replacement receives its state and the communicator is rebuilt.

| **Aspect**                  | **Cold restart**                 | **Warm restart**                       |
|:----------------------------|:---------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
| **Recovery time**           | 4--10 minutes (full reload)      | 30--90 seconds (single node reload)    |
| **State guarantee**         | Clean: all state from checkpoint | Assumes surviving state is valid       |
| **Implementation**          | Simple: kill all, reload all     | Complex: dynamic membership management |
| **Failure during recovery** | Retry cold restart               | Fall back to cold restart              |
| **Best for**                | Correlated failures, SDC events  | Single-node failures, GPU errors       |

: **Cold vs. Warm Restart Trade-Offs**: Cold restart kills every process and reloads from disk; warm restart preserves surviving workers and replaces only the failed node. Warm restart cuts recovery from minutes to tens of seconds for the typical single-node failure but introduces software complexity around dynamic membership management. Mature deployments can run warm restart as the fast path and cold restart as the safety net. Recovery times are illustrative planning ranges, not measurements. {#tbl-cold-vs-warm-restart}

### Recovery automation pipeline {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-recovery-automation-pipeline}

At the scale of 10,000+ GPUs, failures occur multiple times per day, so human operators cannot intervene manually on each incident. Recovery must be an autonomous control loop managed by the cluster control plane. Published reports from large training fleets describe multi-stage automation that classifies failures and selects the minimum viable remediation [@dubey2024llama; @kokolis2025; @zu2024tpuv4].

The pipeline operates in four ordered stages:

1.  Health monitoring daemon\index{Recovery automation!health monitoring daemon}: Continuously scrapes GPU telemetry (ECC error counters, temperature, fan speed, NVLink status) alongside application metrics like training loss and step throughput, often from a sidecar container.
2.  Failure classifier\index{Recovery automation!failure classifier}: Determines whether a signal indicates a fatal error (for example, NVIDIA Xid error 48: double-bit ECC error\index{ECC error!uncorrectable}), a transient stall (for example, temporary network congestion), or a performance degradation (for example, thermal throttling).
3.  Action selector\index{Recovery automation!action selector}: Chooses the cheapest response consistent with the affected state and communication group. A process hang on one rank usually requires restarting the whole communication group rather than one container, because every surviving rank still holds a communicator that includes the hung rank. A confirmed hardware fault requires draining the node and drawing a replacement from the spare pool, which is slower and consumes standby capacity. A network partition can justify a bounded wait that preserves in-memory state, but if the wait expires, replacement must fence the old ownership before accepting new writes.
4.  Validation stage\index{Recovery automation!validation stage}: Runs a recorded "canary batch" or validation workload under the expected numerical tolerance. Unexpected loss or gradient behavior triggers investigation of restored state and execution configuration, with fallback to an earlier validated snapshot when the new state cannot be trusted.

This automation removes the human page-diagnose-repair cycle from the recovery path for the common failure types, which shortens mean time to recovery. The classification stage matters most. Treating every failure as a cold restart wastes compute on transient issues, while treating a hardware failure as transient allows corrupted computation to continue. The Llama 3 pretraining run shows what such a pipeline buys at fleet scale.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: llama3-recovery-record
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LLAMA 3 RECOVERY RECORD (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: war story ws-fault-tolerance-llama3-failure-cadence.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin Meta's reported effective training time and manual-intervention
# │       count for the Llama 3 405B pretraining snapshot to MLSysIM.
# │ Show: >90 percent effective training time; three manual interventions.
# │ How: Literature.TrainingRuns (Dubey 2024).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent

class Llama3RecoveryRecord:
    """Recovery outcome of the Llama 3 405B pretraining snapshot (Dubey et al. 2024)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    effective_time_fraction = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_EffectiveTrainingTimeFraction)
    manual_interventions = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_ManualInterventions)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    # (no derived values; both figures are quoted directly)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(manual_interventions == 3, "Prose spells out 'only three times'")
    check(effective_time_fraction >= 0.9, f"Prose says more than 90 percent effective time, got {effective_time_fraction}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    effective_time_pct_str = fmt_percent(effective_time_fraction, precision=0, style='prose')
```

::: {#ws-fault-tolerance-llama3-failure-cadence .callout-war-story title="The training run that failed every few hours (2024)"}

**Context**: Meta reports training Llama 3\index{Llama-3!training failure cadence} 405B on `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpus_str` H100 GPUs during a `{python} InterruptionCauses.days_str`-day snapshot of pretraining [@dubey2024llama].

**Mechanism**: The snapshot recorded `{python} InterruptionCauses.total_str` unexpected interruptions, about one every `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_str`, with the root causes shown in @fig-llama3-interruptions.

**Impact**: Meta nevertheless reported more than `{python} Llama3RecoveryRecord.effective_time_pct_str` effective training time, measured as useful training time divided by elapsed time. Significant manual intervention was required only three times.

**Fix**: Meta reduced job startup and checkpointing\index{Checkpointing!automated recovery} time and developed automated diagnosis and recovery tools. Communication traces helped locate stalled collectives and slow workers before restarting useful work.

**Systems lesson**: At fleet scale, reliability is a property of the recovery system rather than of the hardware. Effective training time stayed high because automation, not operators, handled nearly every interruption.

:::

### Stragglers versus fail-stop failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distinguishing-stragglers-failures-285d}

Not every recovery decision starts from a crashed process. When one GPU in a synchronous job slows down without dying, every healthy peer still waits at the AllReduce barrier, forcing the recovery pipeline to decide whether the slow rank is a temporary straggler or an incipient failure (perspective \ref{psp-fault-tolerance-straggler-or-failure}).

::: {#psp-fault-tolerance-straggler-or-failure .callout-perspective title="Straggler or failure"}

A straggler, the slow rank of a synchronous step (@sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-synchronization-models-396f), bounds the throughput of every peer that waits on it, so one node running 10 percent slow can cost thousands of nodes 10 percent of their capacity. Fault tolerance must decide what that slowness means. A straggler can still produce correct results, so slowness alone establishes neither incorrect values nor a failed process, and its cause is often system jitter\index{Straggler!system jitter cause} from background OS processes, network congestion, or thermal throttling rather than bad hardware. The decision is between mitigation, which keeps the job running and removes the slowdown, and recovery, which treats the rank as failed and pays for a restart.

:::

Under the simplified no-overlap straggler model, the slowest rank sets the step time of the entire cluster because AllReduce cannot complete until every participant has submitted its gradients:
$$ \StragglerStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \max(\FirstRankComputeTime, \SecondRankComputeTime, \dots, \LastRankComputeTime) + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) $$

Many stragglers are gray failures\index{Gray failure!silent degradation}\index{Gray failure!straggler cause}\index{Straggler!gray failure cause}, the silent degradations named in the failure taxonomy, seen from inside a synchronous job, and none of their common causes raises an explicit error. Thermal throttling reduces clock speed, degrading interconnect cables increase communication latency, OS background processes (memory scrubbing, log rotation) consume CPU cycles, and data loading from a congested network filesystem introduces variable I/O delays. A slow worker can continue meeting a liveness timeout while reducing training throughput, or become slow enough to trigger the same timeout as a failed worker. Progress measurements are therefore needed alongside liveness checks.

Timeout policy governs where the system draws the line between *mitigation* (redistributing work or replacing the slow node) and *recovery* (checkpoint-restart). Aggressive timeouts treat transient stragglers as fail-stop crashes, causing unnecessary job restarts that waste more compute than the slowdown itself, whereas conservative timeouts leave thousands of healthy GPUs waiting on a degraded node that will never speed up. The two responses also land in different places in the goodput accounting of @sec-performance-engineering-goodput-boundaries. A slow rank that stays in the job lowers program goodput, while replacing it spends runtime goodput on the restart. The replacement decision therefore weighs one loss against the other.

Straggler mitigation strategies\index{Straggler!mitigation strategies}\index{Straggler mitigation|see{Straggler}} change either the work assignment or the execution resources. Dynamic load balancing\index{Straggler!dynamic load balancing} moves work away from slow workers while preserving the intended update, whereas bounded staleness\index{Straggler!bounded staleness} allows delayed gradients under an algorithm that tolerates them; its convergence cost depends on the workload and delay bound. Backup workers\index{Straggler!backup worker} replicate selected tasks and accept one result per logical contribution, trading extra GPU cycles for a shorter wait without double-counting gradients. At the infrastructure boundary, proactive replacement\index{Straggler!proactive replacement} uses hardware telemetry, such as rising operating temperatures or growing correctable-ECC error counts, to identify suspect components and replace them when the expected benefit exceeds migration and recovery costs. A simple cost calculation shows why a severe straggler is often cheaper to replace than to tolerate.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-straggler-tax
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class StragglerTax:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    normal_step_s = 1.0
    throttle_factor = 0.50  # straggler runs at 50% speed
    gpu_cost_per_hour = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    straggler_step_s = normal_step_s / throttle_factor
    healthy_gpus = n_gpus - 1
    effective_speed = 1 / straggler_step_s
    straggler_frac_pct = 1 / n_gpus * 100
    throughput_loss_pct = (1 - normal_step_s / straggler_step_s) * 100
    wasted_cost_per_hour = n_gpus * gpu_cost_per_hour * (1 - normal_step_s / straggler_step_s)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(straggler_step_s > normal_step_s, "Straggler must be slower")
    check(abs(throughput_loss_pct - 50.0) < 0.01, f"Expected 50% throughput loss, got {throughput_loss_pct}")
    check(abs(wasted_cost_per_hour - 1024.0) < 0.1, f"Expected $1024/hr wasted cost, got {wasted_cost_per_hour}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0)
    normal_step_str = fmt(normal_step_s, precision=0, commas=False)
    throttle_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(throttle_factor * 100) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    straggler_step_str = fmt(straggler_step_s, precision=0, commas=False)
    healthy_gpus_str = fmt(healthy_gpus, precision=0)
    effective_speed_str = fmt(effective_speed, precision=1, commas=False)
    straggler_frac_str = fmt_percent(straggler_frac_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    throughput_loss_str = fmt_int(throughput_loss_pct, commas=False)
    gpu_cost_str = fmt_usd(gpu_cost_per_hour, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    wasted_cost_str = fmt_usd(wasted_cost_per_hour, precision=0, per="hour")
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_fault_tolerance_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A red square source node with five arrows fanning out to five hollow gray nodes."}

*One straggler stalls every healthy peer at the barrier.*
:::

:::: {#nbk-fault-tolerance-straggler-tax .callout-notebook title="The cost of a straggler"}

Consider a `{python} StragglerTax.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster where a normal training iteration takes `{python} StragglerTax.normal_step_str` second. A single GPU enters a thermally throttled state, clocking down to `{python} StragglerTax.throttle_pct_str` speed, and now takes `{python} StragglerTax.straggler_step_str` seconds to complete its computation.

Because AllReduce cannot complete until every rank has submitted its gradients, the other `{python} StragglerTax.healthy_gpus_str` healthy GPUs sit idle waiting for the straggler.

```{=latex}
\tcbbreak
```

**Impact**:

- Normal step time: `{python} StragglerTax.normal_step_str` second
- Straggler step time: `{python} StragglerTax.straggler_step_str` seconds
- Effective cluster speed: 1 step/`{python} StragglerTax.straggler_step_str`s = `{python} StragglerTax.effective_speed_str` steps/sec

A single failing device (`{python} StragglerTax.straggler_frac_str` of the hardware) has reduced the throughput of the entire cluster by `{python} StragglerTax.throughput_loss_str` percent. At `{python} StragglerTax.gpu_cost_str`, this straggler wastes `{python} StragglerTax.wasted_cost_str` in idle compute.

**Systems insight**: Replacement is worthwhile only when the expected time saved exceeds recovery and replay costs. Suppose the slowdown is expected to persist for the next $\SlowdownPersistenceUpdateCount$ useful updates, whose step times are $\DegradedStepTime$ on the degraded allocation and $\HealthyStepTime$ after replacement. The simplified break-even condition is then $\SlowdownPersistenceUpdateCount(\DegradedStepTime-\HealthyStepTime) > \JobRestartTime+ \LostWorkReplayTime$. The right side includes waiting for capacity and restoring state. A short-lived slowdown may clear before replacement pays off; false-positive detection and uncertain persistence also affect the decision. MTBF describes failure recurrence, not how long this slowdown will last.

::::

Replacing a slow node while maintaining the original GPU count requires available capacity. An $\DeviceCount+1$ redundancy model reserves a hot spare for the isolation and promotion stages of @fig-sdc-controller, reducing allocation delay. Promotion still requires compatible resources, valid state, and communication-group reconstruction; an idle device alone does not guarantee recovery within seconds. A cold spare adds startup work, while a job without a reserved spare depends on the scheduler finding capacity or on repair. The hot spare buys shorter waiting time with devices that sit idle while the fleet is healthy. Fixed-size checkpoint-restart recovery restores the original resource count. Elastic recovery relaxes that requirement by allowing the job to continue with fewer workers when the remaining allocation can support it.

::: {#chk-fault-tolerance-detection-vs-recovery .callout-checkpoint title="Tuning detection and recovery"}

Verify your understanding of how detection latency and recovery strategy trade against one another:

- [ ] **Timeout tuning**: given the heartbeat timeout rule $\HandoverTimeout = \HeartbeatInterval+ \TimeoutSafetyMultiplier\NetworkDelayStandardDeviation$, explain what failure mode is traded away when $\TimeoutSafetyMultiplier$ is lowered from 5 to 3, and which failure mode worsens.
- [ ] **Warm vs. cold restart**: choose a warm restart or a cold restart for a single GPU failure in a 1,000-GPU job with surviving state intact, and identify two conditions that push recovery back toward the cold path.
- [ ] **Hot spare cost**: explain why a hot spare cuts recovery latency relative to detect-then-restart, including the standing cost the cluster pays to keep that spare available.
- [ ] **Straggler decision**: determine what governs whether to wait out a slowed node or kill it and recover onto healthy hardware.

:::

## Elastic Recovery {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-elastic-training-4f87}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: elastic-recovery-node-loss
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ELASTIC RECOVERY NODE LOSS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-elastic-training-4f87 opener.
# │
# │ Goal: Size the survivors when the Archetype A reference job loses one node.
# │ Show: 1,024-GPU job, 8-GPU node, 1,016 surviving GPUs.
# │ How:  Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference system: total minus one node.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent

class ElasticNodeLoss:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    job_gpus = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference.system.total_accelerators
    gpus_per_node = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference.system.node.accelerators_per_node

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    survivors = job_gpus - gpus_per_node

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(survivors == 1016, "prose quotes 1,016 surviving GPUs")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    job_gpus_str = fmt(job_gpus, precision=0)
    gpus_per_node_str = fmt(gpus_per_node, precision=0)
    survivors_str = fmt(survivors, precision=0)
    retained_pct_str = fmt_percent(survivors / job_gpus, precision=1, style="prose")
```

Suppose a `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.job_gpus_str`-GPU training job loses an `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.gpus_per_node_str`-GPU node to a hardware fault, but the cluster has no spare nodes available. A fixed-size recovery policy leaves the remaining `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.survivors_str` GPUs waiting until replacement capacity becomes available or the allocation is released. Elastic recovery allows the job to resize and continue with less compute, provided its state and parallel decomposition fit the smaller allocation.

::: {#dfn-fault-tolerance-elastic-training .callout-definition title="Elastic training"}

***Elastic training***\index{Elastic training!definition}\index{Training!elastic} is the capability of a distributed training job to adjust its worker count across membership changes, potentially through a coordinated worker-group restart.

1.  **Significance**: It converts a permanent capacity loss into a temporary interruption followed by reduced throughput. A pure data-parallel `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.job_gpus_str`-GPU job that loses `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.gpus_per_node_str` GPUs retains `{python} ElasticNodeLoss.retained_pct_str` of its device count and may resume if the remaining devices can hold the state. Tensor- and pipeline-parallel jobs additionally need a feasible partition and compatible group sizes; retained device count does not guarantee the same fraction of throughput. The recovery policy must either preserve the effective batch size through additional accumulation or validate the optimization changes caused by a smaller batch.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike fixed-size checkpoint-restart recovery, which waits for replacement hardware to restore the original allocation, elastic recovery can restart or resume with a different worker count. The optimization loop may pause while membership, ranks, and state are re-established.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that elasticity is "automatic." In reality, recovery requires coordinated adaptation: the training framework, the data loader, and the orchestrator must all synchronize their state to ensure that no data samples are lost or double-counted during the resize.

:::

A small example shows the lifecycle in three phases (@fig-elastic-flow). Execution begins with a balanced four-node AllReduce ring at full throughput. When Node 3 drops out, the survivors pause at a rendezvous barrier and reload the last consistent checkpoint. The group then contracts into a three-node ring in which each worker takes a one-third larger data shard, resuming productive training at 75 percent throughput if the per-worker rate remains unchanged.

::: {#fig-elastic-flow fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Elastic Training Recovery**: Read the three phases top to bottom. Rather than restoring the original worker count before resuming, elastic training pauses when a node fails, reloads the last consistent checkpoint, re-forms the ring over the $\DeviceCount-1$ survivors, and redistributes the failed node's data shards among them. The job resumes at reduced throughput (75 percent here, assuming an unchanged per-worker rate), turning a hard failure into a temporary slowdown." fig-alt="Three stacked phase panels joined by downward arrows, each with a ring of nodes at left, columns of data-shard tiles in the middle, and a throughput bar at right. Phase 1: nodes N0 to N3 in an amber ring, three shard tiles per node, throughput bar full at 100 percent. Phase 2: N3 is red, the ring links touching it are red and dashed, N3's three shard tiles are red, a violet box over the surviving columns reads rendezvous plus reload, and the empty throughput bar reads paused. Phase 3: N0, N1, and N2 form a three-node ring, each column holds four tiles with the new top tile in green, a label reads plus 1 shard each (plus 33 percent), N3's column is an empty dashed outline, and the throughput bar is three-quarters full at 75 percent."}

### Recovery adaptation mechanisms {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-elastic-training-mechanisms-49b1}

Shedding a lost node narrows the active ring instead of idling the whole allocation until replacement hardware arrives, so elastic recovery converts a job termination into a bounded capacity adjustment. The worker group may restart while the framework re-establishes membership, ranks, and state under the smaller resource allocation. When a failure reduces the worker count, the recovery path must adapt several training components before productive work resumes. Each adaptation addresses a specific consistency requirement that, if violated, would corrupt the model or waste computation.

Batch size adjustment comes first. With fewer surviving workers, either each worker must process more samples to preserve the global batch size, or the global batch size must shrink, which in turn may require recalibrating the learning rate to preserve convergence. Changing the global batch size changes the optimization regime as well as the amount of work per step. The linear and square-root learning-rate rules of @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-learning-rate-scaling-rules-fa26 are candidate policies for a resized job, with the worker-count ratio standing in for the batch ratio when per-worker microbatch size and accumulation count stay fixed [@goyal2017accurate]. For a shrink, the square-root rule reduces the learning rate less than linear scaling does; that arithmetic does not establish which policy is more stable, and either policy requires validation for the optimizer, schedule, and workload. Preserving the global batch instead can avoid introducing this change in optimization regime.

Gradient accumulation offers that alternative. Each surviving worker processes additional micro-batches before synchronization to maintain the original effective batch size. If worker count drops by half, doubling the accumulation steps preserves the number of examples per update and can retain the existing learning-rate schedule. Each worker then performs twice as much micro-batch computation per update, although communication and overlap determine the wall-time increase. Equal batch size does not imply bitwise-identical updates or identical behavior from operations that depend on micro-batch statistics.

Data loader redistribution must agree with the recovered training step and new membership. When workers are lost, the loader reassigns the remaining logical input stream so that the resize itself neither omits samples nor counts them twice in an update. Replaying work discarded by checkpoint rollback is expected; duplicating contributions within the resumed stream is a different error. The saved data position and sampling state distinguish those cases.

State resharding adds further complexity when using sharded model parallelism (ZeRO/FSDP). When parameters and optimizer states are sharded once across the entire job without replication, losing a worker removes the only live in-memory copy of its shard, so the job must reload a complete durable checkpoint generation before repartitioning the state across the smaller worker set. When the job instead uses hybrid sharding that replicates each shard across two or more data-parallel groups, a surviving replica group still holds a live copy in GPU memory and can supply the missing shard over the network without reading from storage. Only after the missing values are recovered from a peer replica or a durable checkpoint can the runtime redistribute shard ownership across the surviving workers. Changing shard ownership alone cannot recover missing values.

#### Spot instance preemption as a failure class {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-spot-instance-arbitrage-68ad}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: spot-recovery-prices
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SPOT RECOVERY PRICES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-spot-instance-arbitrage-68ad.
# │
# │ Goal: Quote the same spot and on-demand GPU-hour prices that the fleet
# │       orchestration chapter uses for its spot-versus-on-demand model.
# │ Show: $0.70 spot vs. $2.00 on demand per GPU-hour.
# │ How:  Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.{SpotGpuHourRef, GpuHourRef}.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Infrastructure
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_usd

class SpotRecoveryPrices:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    spot = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.SpotGpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude
    on_demand = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(0 < spot < on_demand, "spot capacity must be cheaper than on-demand capacity")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    spot_str = fmt_usd(spot, precision=2, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    on_demand_str = fmt_usd(on_demand, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
```

Hardware faults are not the only event that removes workers from a running job. Cloud providers often price preemptible ("spot") instances below on-demand capacity, with the caveat that they can be reclaimed with little warning. Once workers vanish, recovery faces the same missing-state and membership problems as a hardware failure. An advance notice, when available, can allow a coordinated save or drain before departure and therefore changes the recovery opportunity.

Both fixed-size and elastic jobs can recover from preemption using checkpoints, but a fixed-size job must regain its required allocation before restarting. An elastic job can instead resume at reduced scale if enough capacity remains and the training invariants survive the resize. Recovery still pays for detection, state restoration, and group reconstruction; repeated reclamations can erase the apparent price advantage. At the reference fleet prices of `{python} SpotRecoveryPrices.spot_str` for spot capacity against `{python} SpotRecoveryPrices.on_demand_str` for on-demand capacity, the savings can outweigh the lost work and resizing delays; @sec-fleet-orchestration-spot-instances develops the full spot-versus-on-demand cost model. Where spot capacity makes worker departure frequent, federated training makes it the default.

::: {#lhs-fault-tolerance-archetype-c-federated-mobilenet-client-dropout .callout-lighthouse title="Archetype C (Federated MobileNet): Dropout as the normal case"}

Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) makes worker departure an expected part of training. Its phone-class clients train while charging, idle, and connected, so a client that disappears mid-round is an ordinary event rather than a fault to repair. The coordinator therefore selects more clients than a round needs and closes the round at a deadline. The round tolerates departures as long as enough compatible updates arrive; otherwise the coordinator abandons it [@mcmahan2017communication; @bonawitz2019towards]. Model-version checks prevent updates computed against a replaced model from entering the current aggregate, the federated counterpart of fencing a stale epoch, while aggregation weights account for the examples contributed under the chosen learning algorithm. Version checks and weighting do not remove participation bias. Recovery must preserve the coordinator state needed to continue that algorithm, including the model, round position, and any persistent optimizer or sampling state, rather than assuming weights alone suffice. @Sec-edge-intelligence-client-scheduling-f675 develops the round design, including deadlines, participation requirements, and the bias that arises when some kinds of devices report less often than others.

:::

#### Framework support for elastic recovery {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-framework-support-elastic-training-8b75}

Whether worker loss comes from a hardware fault or a spot preemption, training frameworks differ in how many of the resize invariants (group membership, shard ownership, data loader redistribution, and batch-size or learning-rate adjustment) they enforce automatically after a failure. PyTorch Elastic\index{PyTorch Elastic!worker failure detection} (TorchElastic) uses agents to monitor workers and a rendezvous mechanism to establish group membership [@pytorchElasticDocs; @pytorchRendezvousDocs]. On a failure or membership change, it stops all surviving workers, forms a new worker group, and starts its workers with new `RANK` and `WORLD_SIZE` assignments. It handles rank reassignment and communication-group reconstruction while leaving batch size, learning rate, and checkpoint semantics to user code. DeepSpeed [@rasley2020] provides ZeRO-based distributed training and checkpointing building blocks for large models [@deepspeedCheckpointingDocs]. Recovery reloads from the last durable checkpoint, and Universal Checkpointing addresses portability across some changes in parallelism and topology [@deepspeedUniversalCheckpointingDocs], though elastic behavior still depends on the surrounding launcher and resource manager.

Ray Train, built on Ray's actor model, provides a checkpoint-oriented recovery path that restarts a worker group after a failure or preemption and resumes from the latest available checkpoint. The training function remains responsible for saving and loading sufficient state [@rayTrainFaultToleranceDocs]. Horovod Elastic similarly builds on Horovod's data-parallel training system [@sergeev2018horovod] with an elastic state API for worker additions and removals [@horovodElasticDocs]. The API resets ranks and reconstructs communication while leaving convergence-sensitive choices such as learning-rate or batch-size policy to the training script. Across these four frameworks, restarting the worker group is largely automated, while state resharding remains manual, deployment-dependent, or tied to a checkpoint reload (@tbl-elastic-training-comparison).

| **Framework**       | **Failure detection** | **Automatic recovery** | **State resharding** | **Cluster integration** |
|:--------------------|:---------------------:|:----------------------:|:--------------------:|:-----------------------:|
| **PyTorch Elastic** |   Rendezvous timeout  |          Yes           |        Manual        |        Kubernetes       |
| **DeepSpeed**       |        External       |    Checkpoint-based    | Deployment-dependent |   External schedulers   |
| **Ray Train**       |   Actor supervision   | Checkpoint retry path  |  Checkpoint reload   |       Ray Cluster       |
| **Horovod Elastic** |    Driver heartbeat   |          Yes           |        Manual        |    Slurm, Kubernetes    |

: **Elastic Recovery Framework Comparison**: Frameworks differ in how they detect worker failures and how much of the recovery sequence (group reconstruction, state redistribution, batch size adjustment) they automate. {#tbl-elastic-training-comparison}

### Model-specific training fault tolerance {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-modelspecific-training-fault-tolerance-4b70}

Restoring model weights alone does not guarantee a valid restart: an LLM that reloads its weights but loses its curriculum cursor trains twice on the same documents, and a continuous recommender that rolls back its embedding tables serves stale user preferences. The checkpoint and recovery mechanisms of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-restart-fundamentals-0ac2 and @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-recovery-0f54 must therefore adapt to the workload costs priced in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-modeltype-diversity-failure-impact-8ec0. The design question is not simply how often to checkpoint, but which state variable would make a restart mathematically or economically wrong. For recommendation workloads, incremental checkpointing\index{Checkpointing!incremental}\index{Incremental checkpointing|see{Checkpointing}}, tiered checkpointing, and embedding versioning can reduce the cost of preserving fresh state. Incremental storage can still reconstruct an exact generation from a base and its required deltas; accepting stale or approximate state is a separate choice. For each workload, the state at risk determines what its checkpoint must contain (@tbl-training-recovery-state-invariants).

| **Workload**   | **State at risk**                                                                                  | **Checkpoint implication**                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|:---------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| LLM training   | Optimizer state, curriculum position, document position, long-context schedule                     | Preserve the FP32 optimizer state where precision matters, shard writes with ZeRO/FSDP, move serialization off the critical path, and include the data-schedule position so the optimization trajectory resumes correctly. |
| Recommendation | Embedding freshness, feature-store version                                                         | Preserve fresh state with incremental checkpointing, tiered checkpointing, and embedding versioning; accepting stale or approximate state requires a separate recovery contract.                                           |
| Vision         | Augmentation seeds, shuffling order, batch-normalization statistics, progressive-resizing schedule | Capture the stochastic and normalization state that controls the input stream; weights alone are not enough to reproduce the training trajectory.                                                                          |
| Scientific ML  | Simulator state, search frontier, explored configurations, validation seeds                        | Treat the model, simulator, search process, and random state as one consistency unit so recovery does not duplicate exploration or invalidate comparisons.                                                                 |

: **Training Recovery State Invariants**: Workloads require different checkpoint contents because they make different state variables quality-bearing. The correct recovery policy starts from the state that would make a restart wrong, then chooses sharding, incrementality, or domain-state capture accordingly. {#tbl-training-recovery-state-invariants}

The common pattern is that recovery correctness is broader than weight restoration. LLMs can reload weights but resume with the wrong curriculum position.
