Recommendation models that train continuously can reload dense parameters but serve stale embeddings, so a failure that loses recent updates carries a freshness cost as well as a replay cost. The recovery budget must reflect the workload's measured sensitivity to stale state.[^fn-recsys-model-freshness] Vision models have smaller checkpoints, about `{python} FaultToleranceIntroRecap.vit_ckpt_str` for the ViT-Large example, which permit more frequent saves on the same storage path. Yet reproducing their input stream requires the augmentation configuration, random-number generator state, and data position rather than only the initial shuffling seed. Scientific models can reload a neural network while losing the simulator state that made the data meaningful, and an iterative search must also retain which configurations it has evaluated when those results choose its next candidates. In every case the checkpoint boundary must include whatever prior decisions affect future work, wherever that state resides. Once the trained model is deployed to users, however, the operational calculus shifts from protecting *weeks of batch computation* to protecting *milliseconds of real-time latency*.

[^fn-recsys-model-freshness]: **RecSys freshness**\index{Recommendation system!freshness fault tolerance}: Freshness makes recovery delay part of the model-quality budget. Its importance depends on how quickly useful user and item signals change and how strongly predictions depend on them. Comparing quality at different state ages establishes the permitted staleness; that measured limit determines how much checkpoint and replication overhead is justified.

## Serving Fault Tolerance {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-serving-fault-tolerance-5375}

When users ask a voice assistant to turn off the lights, they will not tolerate a five-minute pause while the inference server reloads from a checkpoint. Serving presents a different challenge, because users expect millisecond-level responsiveness even when backend GPUs crash. The C³ budget for fault tolerance shifts accordingly. Training pays for coordination in synchronization time so that a failure does not erase completed compute, while serving pays in standing redundant compute and in routing coordination so that a failure does not break a latency contract.

A serving replica is a runnable copy of the model that can accept requests; the routing layer chooses a replica, and a readiness check determines whether that replica can serve successfully. Replicas may share external state stores or keep request state in accelerator memory, so replacing compute does not necessarily replace the state a request needs. Serving fault tolerance asks how those mechanisms behave when replicas, GPUs, or state stores fail under live latency budgets. The focus here is narrower than a complete serving architecture: each mechanism is treated as a reliability boundary for real-time inference.

### Stateless vs. stateful serving {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-stateless-vs-stateful-serving-0a60}

The first serving decision is where request state lives, because that choice determines whether failover is a retry or a state-reconstruction problem. A stateless model worker retains no required per-session state between requests. It obtains the necessary context from the request or an external state store, so another ready worker can process the same request. A stateful application can therefore use stateless model workers, although its external store remains a reliability dependency.

The stateless pattern appears when the input itself carries all context: an image classifier processes one image, an object detector processes one frame, a single-turn text classifier processes one snippet, and an embedding service maps one input to one vector. Fault tolerance can then focus on replica health and request routing. Redundant replicas\index{Replication!redundant replicas} serve requests in parallel, load balancing\index{Load balancing!serving fault tolerance} sends traffic only to healthy replicas, health checks\index{Health check!serving failover} remove failed replicas from rotation, and automatic replacement starts a new replica when capacity falls. When a replica fails, in-flight requests to that replica can be retried elsewhere, because no quality-bearing session state has been lost.

Stateless serving offers the simpler architecture when the application permits it. However, many ML applications inherently require state across requests. Consider a chatbot: a single-turn question-answering system can operate statelessly, processing each question independently. A conversational assistant must preserve its history somewhere, but the model worker can still be stateless if each request carries the complete history or reads it from a durable external store. Worker-local state creates a stronger dependency when later requests rely on information available only at the selected replica.

Stateful serving appears when later work depends on retained session state. For a transformer, the key-value (KV) cache stores attention keys and values computed for earlier tokens so the worker can reuse them while generating subsequent tokens. This cache is derived state. If the authoritative token history and compatible model version remain available, a replacement can recompute it by processing that history again. Losing the history itself is a different failure because cache reconstruction no longer has its required input. Streaming speech recognition similarly maintains context from previous audio, recommendation sessions accumulate user context, and interactive editing maintains document state across edits. The fault-tolerance consequence is that failure loses quality-bearing state rather than serving capacity alone. KV cache loss requires reprocessing previous turns, session context loss forces users to repeat previous interactions, and accumulated user state loss degrades quality when context is unavailable. The mitigation choice follows the size, update rate, and quality value of that state. Session affinity routes a session to the same replica, state checkpointing periodically saves session state, state replication maintains a standby copy, and graceful degradation keeps the service available at reduced quality if state cannot be recovered. @Tbl-stateless-stateful-comparison contrasts how that state boundary reshapes routing, failure impact, and recovery complexity. Whether the architecture is stateless or stateful, maintaining availability under live latency constraints requires deploying redundant capacity.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How the KV cache grows with sequence length and concurrency until it fills accelerator memory is developed in @sec-inference-scale-kv-cache-wall.
:::

| **Aspect**               |      **Stateless serving**       |             **Stateful serving**            |
|:-------------------------|:--------------------------------:|:-------------------------------------------:|
| **Request routing**      |           Any replica            |            Session-affine replica           |
| **Failure impact**       |     Retry on another replica     |             Potential state loss            |
| **Recovery complexity**  |     Restart and load weights     |      Reload state + reconstruct context     |
| **Redundancy approach**  |      Active-active replicas      |          Replicated state + standby         |
| **Work after detection** | Route or retry to a ready worker | Recover required state, then route or retry |

: **Stateless vs. Stateful Serving Fault Tolerance**: State recovery adds work after failure detection. End-to-end failover also includes probe timeouts, routing, replacement readiness, and request retry; neither worker category implies a fixed latency. {#tbl-stateless-stateful-comparison}

### Redundancy and replication {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-redundancy-replication-2239}

Redundancy buys availability only when replica placement and spare capacity match the failure domain being defended against. Turning multiple model copies into uninterrupted service requires sizing the replica count to the availability target, choosing how live traffic is split across healthy and standby workers, and placing those replicas across independent failure domains.

#### Availability calculations {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-availability-calculations-ef0a}

Serving redundancy is the parallel composition of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-quantitative-analysis applied to interchangeable replicas, with availability in place of survival probability. For a single replica with availability $\ReplicaAvailability$ (probability of being operational at any given time), @eq-availability-redundancy quantifies how multiple independent replicas achieve higher system availability:

$$ \RedundantServiceAvailability= 1 - (1 - \ReplicaAvailability)^\RedundantReplicaCount$$ {#eq-availability-redundancy}

where $\RedundantReplicaCount$ is the number of replicas. For a service whose single replica is available 99 percent of the time, redundancy compounds as follows.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: replica-availability
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ REPLICA AVAILABILITY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-availability-redundancy worked values and the margin ladder.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute availability and annual downtime for one, two, and three
# │       independent replicas at 99 percent per-replica availability.
# │ Show: 3.65 days; 99.99 percent and 52.6 minutes; 99.9999 percent and 31.5 s.
# │ How:  A = 1 - (1 - a)^r; downtime = (1 - A) x hours per year.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class ReplicaAvailability:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    a_single = 0.99  # scenario: per-replica availability

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    a2 = 1 - (1 - a_single) ** 2
    a3 = 1 - (1 - a_single) ** 3
    down1_h = (1 - a_single) * HOURS_PER_YEAR
    down2_h = (1 - a2) * HOURS_PER_YEAR
    down3_h = (1 - a3) * HOURS_PER_YEAR

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(down1_h > down2_h > down3_h > 0, "each replica must cut downtime")
    check(3.6 < down1_h / 24 < 3.7, "margin ladder shows 3.65 days for one replica")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    a1_str = fmt_percent(a_single, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    a2_str = fmt_percent(a2, precision=2, commas=False, style="prose")
    a3_str = fmt_percent(a3, precision=4, commas=False, style="prose")
    down1_str = fmt_time(down1_h / 24, "day", precision=2, commas=False, style="word")
    down2_str = fmt_time(down2_h * 60, "minute", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    down3_str = fmt_time(down3_h * 3600, "second", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
```

For a single replica, availability of `{python} ReplicaAvailability.a1_str` corresponds to `{python} ReplicaAvailability.down1_str` of downtime per year. Adding independent replicas changes the tail of the failure distribution quickly: two replicas give `{python} ReplicaAvailability.a2_str`, or `{python} ReplicaAvailability.down2_str` of downtime per year, and three replicas give `{python} ReplicaAvailability.a3_str`, or `{python} ReplicaAvailability.down3_str`. The arithmetic assumes independent failures and enough capacity on any surviving replica to meet the service target; shared power, shared networking, and shared software bugs reduce actual availability below these theoretical values.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_fault_tolerance_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Time ladder showing annual downtime dropping from 3.65 days with one replica to 52.6 minutes with two and 31.5 seconds with three."}

*Redundancy turns days of downtime into seconds.*
:::

#### Replication strategies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-replication-strategies-aaa2}

The availability equation says how much redundancy can help; the replication topology determines how that redundancy behaves under normal execution and sudden hardware loss. Two fundamental designs make opposite bets (@fig-serving-redundancy). Active-active replication splits ingress traffic evenly across live replicas, one-third each for three, which keeps every device busy but requires spare headroom so the survivors can absorb a failed replica's share. Active-passive replication sends all traffic to a designated primary and keeps a pre-warmed standby whose weights remain loaded in accelerator memory, which makes failover fast at the expense of a device that serves nothing while the primary is healthy.

::: {#fig-serving-redundancy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Serving Redundancy Strategies**: Active-active (left) splits traffic across three replicas, each carrying about one-third, which uses every device but requires enough headroom for the survivors to absorb a failed replica's share. Active-passive (right) sends all traffic to one primary and keeps a warm standby with weights already loaded, which simplifies failover at the cost of capacity that serves nothing while the primary is healthy." fig-alt="Two panels divided by a dashed line. Each replica card holds a blue weights bar and a load gauge whose green fill shows traffic served. Left, active-active: a load balancer splits requests along three violet arrows labeled one third to replicas 1, 2, and 3; each gauge is one-third full, and a bracket under the empty part of the first gauge reads headroom absorbs a failed share. Right, active-passive: a load balancer sends a solid arrow labeled all traffic to a primary whose gauge is full and labeled traffic, and a dashed arrow labeled on failure to a dashed warm standby whose weights are loaded but whose gauge is empty and labeled idle; text below reads loaded, serves nothing."}
![](images/svg/serving-redundancy.svg)

:::

Geographic replication extends the same choice across regions. It protects against data-center or regional network failures, but requests routed to distant regions pay additional latency, and the active-active headroom problem reappears at regional scale. When a region fails, the surviving regions must absorb its traffic and, for stateful services, rebuild its sessions, so each region either carries spare capacity sized for the largest region it may absorb or accepts degraded latency during the failover. Traffic returns to a recovered region gradually, because its caches and warm replicas start empty and an abrupt shift back would overload it and trigger the same failover again. Multi-tier designs combine several replication policies at once: edge caches replicate for latency, regional serving clusters replicate for availability, and a global primary or coordination layer preserves consistency and freshness.

#### Replica placement and failure domains {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-replica-placement-failure-domains-73a7}

Effective redundancy requires placing replicas in independent failure domains. Different machines tolerate individual machine failures; different racks tolerate rack-level failures from power or top-of-rack switch issues; different availability zones tolerate data-center-section failures; and different regions tolerate entire data-center failures. The independence level should match the availability requirement and cost constraint: regional replication is expensive because it duplicates compute and network capacity, but it is necessary when regional failure must not become user-visible downtime. Placement alone, however, only creates the possibility of recovery; the serving system still needs a control loop that notices the failure, removes the affected replica from traffic, and preserves enough state that the user-visible service continues with bounded degradation.

### Failover mechanisms {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failover-mechanisms-5ddd}

When a replica fails, traffic must be redirected to healthy replicas, and the speed and reliability of that redirection determine how much of the failure users see. The mechanism decomposes into two questions: how the system decides that a replica can no longer serve, and what happens to stateful sessions already attached to it.

#### Health checking {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-health-checking-a604}

Health checks\index{Health check!liveness vs. readiness}\index{Health check!inference correctness probe} decide when traffic should move. The liveness and readiness probes of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-mechanisms-efed apply to a serving replica, where readiness means that its weights are loaded, its accelerator is initialized, warmup has completed, and dependencies such as feature stores (the services that supply precomputed model input features) are reachable. Serving adds an inference check, which runs a known input through the model and compares the output with the expected result, catching the silent failure in which the process is healthy but its answers are wrong. The load balancer acts on these signals.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ What each probe must test on an accelerator replica, from process liveness to a fixed-prompt inference check, is developed in @sec-inference-scale-health-checking-failover-070e.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: health-check-detection-budget
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HEALTH CHECK DETECTION BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-health-checking-a604
# │          failover-budget paragraph immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal: Show how probe interval, timeout, and failure threshold bound the time
# │       a crashed replica keeps receiving traffic.
# │ Show: 5 s interval, 2 s timeout, threshold 3 -> removal 12-17 s after crash.
# │ How:  Earliest removal = (threshold - 1) x interval + timeout (crash just
# │       before a probe); latest = threshold x interval + timeout (crash just
# │       after a successful probe). Probe settings are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_range, fmt_time

class HealthCheckDetection:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    interval_s = 5  # probe interval (scenario setting)
    timeout_s = 2  # per-probe timeout (scenario setting)
    fail_threshold = 3  # consecutive missed probes before removal
    success_threshold = 2  # consecutive clean probes before readmission

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    detect_min_s = (fail_threshold - 1) * interval_s + timeout_s
    detect_max_s = fail_threshold * interval_s + timeout_s

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(detect_min_s == 12, f"Expected 12 s earliest removal, got {detect_min_s}")
    check(detect_max_s == 17, f"Expected 17 s latest removal, got {detect_max_s}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    interval_str = fmt_time(interval_s, second, precision=0, commas=False)
    timeout_str = fmt_time(timeout_s, second, precision=0, commas=False)
    fail_threshold_str = fmt_int(fail_threshold)
    success_threshold_str = fmt_int(success_threshold)
    detect_range_str = fmt_range(detect_min_s, detect_max_s, unit=second, precision=0)
```

The probe parameters\index{Health check!trade-offs and thresholds} set the failover budget. With a `{python} HealthCheckDetection.interval_str` check interval, a `{python} HealthCheckDetection.timeout_str` timeout, and a failure threshold of `{python} HealthCheckDetection.fail_threshold_str` missed probes, a crashed replica leaves rotation `{python} HealthCheckDetection.detect_range_str` after it fails, depending on where the crash falls between probes. Every request routed to it in that window fails or waits for a client retry. Shortening the interval or lowering the threshold speeds failover but raises the false-positive rate, marking healthy replicas unhealthy during transient stalls and removing capacity exactly when load is high. A success threshold of `{python} HealthCheckDetection.success_threshold_str` clean probes applies the same caution in reverse, holding a recovered replica out of rotation until it has proved stable.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\Needspace{24\baselineskip}
:::

#### Session affinity and stateful failover {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-session-affinity-stateful-failover-27b2}

For stateful serving, session affinity\index{Session affinity!stateful failover} routes all requests within a session to the same replica. Load balancers maintain session-to-replica mapping through sticky sessions implemented with cookies, headers, or IP hashing. Affinity preserves locality but supplies no replacement copy when that replica fails. Checkpointing saves session state periodically, replication copies it to a standby, and external systems such as Redis or Memcached move it outside the model worker. The external store still needs its own availability and durability contract. Accepting state loss is valid only when the service can reconstruct derived state from retained history or explicitly begin a reduced-context session. Which option fits a workload depends on state size, update frequency, and the quality impact of state loss, as @tbl-stateful-failover summarizes across the four common approaches.

| **Approach**                | **Recovery latency** |              **State guarantee**               | **Operational complexity** |
|:----------------------------|:--------------------:|:----------------------------------------------:|:--------------------------:|
| **State loss**              |         Fast         |                      None                      |            Low             |
| **Checkpointing**           |        Medium        | Consistent snapshot; later updates may be lost |           Medium           |
| **Synchronous replication** |         Fast         |                     Strong                     |            High            |
| **Distributed state**       |         Fast         |                  Configurable                  |           Medium           |

: **Stateful Failover Approaches**: Recovery latency, state guarantees, and operational complexity distinguish four approaches to session-state failover. Checkpoint recovery may lose updates after the saved snapshot. Distributed storage can provide different consistency contracts, and synchronous replication provides its promised guarantee only under the specified acknowledgment and fault model. {#tbl-stateful-failover}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
{{< pagebreak >}}
:::

### Model-specific serving fault tolerance {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-modelspecific-serving-fault-tolerance-3245}

Retrying a failed image classification request on another replica loses no session state, whereas losing the replica that holds a multi-turn LLM conversation drops gigabytes of live attention state and losing a recommendation feature store leaves the ranker with stale user signals. Model-specific serving policies therefore start from a state-loss budget: which state can be rebuilt within the latency deadline, which state must be replicated in advance, and which state may be degraded temporarily without violating the product contract. Each of the three common serving regimes answers that budget differently, setting both its fault-tolerance policy and its degradation path (@tbl-serving-recovery-state-invariants).

| **Serving workload** | **State expensive to lose**                    | **Fault-tolerance policy**                                                                                  | **Degradation path**                                                   |
|:---------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| LLM conversation     | KV cache, conversation context, prefix state   | Replicate or checkpoint high-value session state; regenerate only when the latency budget allows.           | Rebuild from transcript, reuse cached prefixes, or ask for retry.      |
| Recommendation       | Fresh user features, item features, embeddings | Replicate feature stores, cache hot features, and monitor freshness as a reliability signal.                | Serve stale or default features with measured quality loss.            |
| Vision service       | Preprocessing state, device health, edge input | Retry stateless requests on healthy replicas and fail closed on preprocessing or accelerator-health faults. | Use a smaller local model, defer prediction, or return low confidence. |

: **Serving Recovery State Invariants**: Serving fault tolerance starts from the state whose loss changes user-visible quality. LLMs protect live context, recommendation systems protect feature freshness, and vision services protect preprocessing and device correctness. {#tbl-serving-recovery-state-invariants}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-cache-live-state
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KV-CACHE LIVE STATE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: [^fn-kv-cache-resilience] below (serving fault tolerance).
# │
# │ Goal: Size one full-context conversation's KV cache for a Llama-family 70B
# │       model with grouped-query attention.
# │ Show: 128K context; ~43 GB per conversation.
# │ How:  Models.Language.Llama3_70B.get_kv_cache_size at its context_length,
# │       BF16 (2 bytes). The sizing equation itself is owned by the inference chapter.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_text

class KvCacheLiveState:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    m = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    kv_bytes = BYTES_FP16  # BF16 and FP16 are both 2 bytes per element

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    kv_gqa = m.get_kv_cache_size(seq_len=m.context_length, batch_size=1, precision=kv_bytes)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(40 < kv_gqa.to(GB).magnitude < 45, "footnote quotes about 43 GB per conversation")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    context_k_str = fmt_text(fmt_int(m.context_length // 1024), "K")
    kv_gqa_str = fmt_memory(round(kv_gqa.to(GB).magnitude) * GB, unit=GB, precision=0)
```

The KV cache[^fn-kv-cache-resilience] can be substantial (gigabytes for long contexts across attention layers). Losing it requires recomputing attention state from the retained token history, which can take seconds to minutes; previously delivered text need not be generated again. During an in-flight response, recovery must also know which output tokens the client has already received so a retry does not silently duplicate or replace part of the response.

[^fn-kv-cache-resilience]: [offset=-34mm] **KV cache**\index{KV cache!serving fault tolerance}: Stores key and value projections for all previous tokens across all attention layers, with a per-token size derived in @sec-inference-scale-kv-cache-wall. For a Llama-family 70B model at its `{python} KvCacheLiveState.context_k_str` context in BF16, the KV cache is about `{python} KvCacheLiveState.kv_gqa_str` per conversation. Reconstruction can exceed serving latency service level agreements (SLAs) even when a replacement replica is already available.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/fault_tolerance_kv_live_state_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two rows. An image retry shows only a thin baseline mark labeled no state lost. An LLM conversation shows a full-width blue bar labeled 43 GB."}

*A retried image loses nothing; a lost conversation loses `{python} KvCacheLiveState.kv_gqa_str` of KV cache.*
:::

LLM serving choices trade KV-cache recovery latency against memory and storage overhead. The simplest strategy is to accept regeneration cost by rebuilding KV cache from conversation history after failure, but this can turn a long conversation into a multi-second or multi-minute restart. KV-cache checkpointing saves live state periodically and bounds the amount of regeneration, while KV-cache replication keeps a standby copy for fast failover at the cost of extra memory. Prefix caching\index{KV cache!prefix caching}, also offered as prompt caching\index{KV cache!prompt caching}, reuses state for common system prompts and shared context. A compatible cached prefix can reduce reconstruction work if it survives the failure and remains accessible to the replacement worker. Cache reuse alone does not establish a failover guarantee or preserve the session-specific history.

Recommendation serving protects freshness rather than conversational continuity. Recommendations depend on user and item features from feature stores, so feature-store unavailability can either degrade ranking quality or block recommendations entirely. The serving decision is the staleness budget. Replicated feature stores keep recent features available across zones, local caches cover hot features, fallback to stale features accepts measured quality loss, and default features let the service return a lower-quality result when lookup fails. Real-time features such as recent user actions make freshness monitoring part of fault tolerance, because a pipeline that keeps serving old features is available operationally but wrong semantically. Large embedding tables may also sit behind dedicated embedding services, which need their own replication and failover plan.

Vision serving is usually closer to the stateless end of the spectrum because each image or frame can be retried on another replica. That simplicity changes where the checks belong. Thermal throttling threatens latency, while uncorrected memory errors threaten numerical validity; health policy must distinguish those consequences. Preprocessing checks must also prevent invalid resize, crop, color conversion, or normalization from producing apparently valid predictions. At the edge, disconnection can require a validated smaller local model, delayed nonurgent work, or abstention when the available computation cannot meet the prediction contract.

When redundancy cannot preserve full service, the remaining choice depends on the application contract. A validated reduced-capability response can preserve useful availability; if no such response is acceptable, the system must reject or defer the work. Graceful degradation makes the permitted reduction explicit before failure occurs.

## Graceful Degradation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-graceful-degradation-9122}

During a major regional network outage, an e-commerce site suddenly loses access to its heavy, GPU-accelerated recommendation cluster. Rather than showing users empty pages or crashing, the site instantly switches to serving precomputed, generic popular items. The serving fault tolerance mechanisms developed in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-serving-fault-tolerance-5375 aim to maintain full service, but graceful degradation dictates what happens when those defenses are overwhelmed.

::: {#dfn-fault-tolerance-graceful-degradation .callout-definition title="Graceful degradation"}

***Graceful degradation***\index{Graceful degradation!definition} is a fault tolerance strategy in which a system responds to resource exhaustion or component failure by deliberately reducing service quality (falling back to a smaller model, serving cached results, or returning partial outputs) rather than failing completely, maintaining measurable availability at reduced capability.

1.  **Significance**: Graceful degradation converts total outage risk into a controlled quality reduction. A recommendation system can fall back from a large ranker to a collaborative-filtering model on GPU failure, maintaining request availability with a quality penalty that must be measured for that workload. The engineering calculation includes both the requests served and the utility lost during fallback.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike complete system failure (where the service returns errors to all requests), graceful degradation provides a managed transition through a predefined capability hierarchy in which each fallback level has known accuracy, latency, and resource characteristics that allow the system to continue satisfying SLOs at reduced quality.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that degradation is automatic in well-designed systems. Graceful degradation requires explicit preengineering. Fallback models must be preloaded or precomputed, switchover logic must detect the failure condition and trigger the transition without human intervention, and each degradation level must have been validated to satisfy its reduced SLO before it is needed in production.

:::

### Degradation dimensions {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-degradation-dimensions-4b25}

A degradation plan must name which service property will be sacrificed before an incident begins. The main levers in @tbl-graceful-degradation-dimensions form a pre-incident design checklist, not an outage-time brainstorming aid. Each sacrificed property needs a measured quality budget, an activation condition, and a recovery path before the failure occurs.

| **Dimension**        | **What the system sacrifices**    | **Typical fallback**                                                                           |
|:---------------------|:----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Quality              | Model accuracy or ranking quality | Use a simpler model, such as a collaborative-filtering fallback for a multi-tower recommender. |
| Latency              | Response speed                    | Batch more requests together to preserve throughput and model quality under high load.         |
| Coverage             | Result completeness               | Return top-10 search results instead of top-100.                                               |
| Freshness            | Recency of computed results       | Serve cached or stale candidates, such as hour-old news recommendations during an outage.      |
| Feature completeness | Input richness                    | Use content features when user history or real-time context is unavailable.                    |

: **Graceful Degradation Dimensions**: Degradation plans choose which service property can be reduced while still returning a useful answer. Naming the dimension in advance prevents the system from treating every failure as a binary serve-or-crash decision. {#tbl-graceful-degradation-dimensions}

These dimensions are not interchangeable. A search product may sacrifice coverage by returning fewer results while keeping freshness intact. A recommender may sacrifice freshness by serving cached candidates while preserving latency. An interactive assistant may sacrifice quality by using a smaller model while keeping the session alive. The correct fallback is therefore workload-specific. It follows the property whose temporary loss least harms the application and whose recovery path can be validated before the incident.

### Graceful degradation strategies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-graceful-degradation-strategies-e85e}

The dimensions in @tbl-graceful-degradation-dimensions become operational only when the service binds each sacrificed property to a specific fallback mechanism. The strategy ladder starts with model fallback when the primary inference path is too expensive or unavailable. It then moves to feature fallback when input quality degrades, and finally to load shedding when demand exceeds capacity and the system must preserve the highest-value requests first.

#### Model fallback {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-model-fallback-bc6e}

Model fallback turns quality into an explicit availability lever by maintaining multiple model versions with different resource requirements. The primary model\index{Graceful degradation!primary model} provides full capability at the highest resource cost, a secondary model\index{Graceful degradation!secondary model} reduces capability and resource demand, a tertiary model\index{Graceful degradation!tertiary model} preserves minimal capability, and a static fallback\index{Graceful degradation!static fallback} serves precomputed defaults with no inference at all. When the primary path is unavailable or overloaded, the policy descends only as far as resource pressure requires, then returns upward after the primary path is healthy again.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: model-fallback-cascade
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MODEL FALLBACK CASCADE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-model-fallback-bc6e prose below.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the three named vision models' sizes and ImageNet top-1 accuracy.
# │ Show: ViT-Large 307M / 88%; EfficientNet-B4 19M / 83%; MobileNetV3-Large 5.4M / 75%.
# │ How:  Models.Vision.*.parameters; Literature.Benchmarks.*ImageNetTop1.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature, Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent

class ModelFallbackCascade:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    vit_params_m = Models.Vision.ViT_Large.parameters.to(param).magnitude / 1e6
    effnet_params_m = Models.Vision.EfficientNetB4.parameters.to(param).magnitude / 1e6
    mobilenet_params_m = Models.Vision.MobileNetV3_Large.parameters.to(param).magnitude / 1e6
    vit_top1 = float(Literature.Benchmarks.ViTLargeImageNetTop1)
    effnet_top1 = float(Literature.Benchmarks.EfficientNetB4ImageNetTop1)
    mobilenet_top1 = float(Literature.Benchmarks.MobileNetV3LargeImageNetTop1)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    # (no derived values; each rung is a named registry entity)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(vit_params_m > effnet_params_m > mobilenet_params_m, "each fallback rung must be smaller")
    check(vit_top1 > effnet_top1 > mobilenet_top1, "each fallback rung must trade accuracy for cost")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    vit_params_str = fmt(vit_params_m, precision=0)
    effnet_params_str = fmt(effnet_params_m, precision=0)
    mobilenet_params_str = fmt(mobilenet_params_m, precision=1)
    vit_top1_str = fmt_percent(round(vit_top1 * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
    effnet_top1_str = fmt_percent(round(effnet_top1 * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
    mobilenet_top1_str = fmt_percent(round(mobilenet_top1 * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
```

An image classification cascade makes the trade-off concrete. The primary path might run a ViT-Large model with `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.vit_params_str` million parameters and `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.vit_top1_str` ImageNet top-1 accuracy. Under pressure, it might fall back to EfficientNet-B4 with `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.effnet_params_str` million parameters and `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.effnet_top1_str` accuracy, then fall back again to MobileNet-V3-Large with `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.mobilenet_params_str` million parameters and `{python} ModelFallbackCascade.mobilenet_top1_str` accuracy when only minimal classification remains affordable. If even that path cannot meet the SLO, the service can return cached labels, a coarse category, or "classification unavailable" rather than blocking the request indefinitely. For that ladder to be real rather than aspirational, the production system must keep multiple models deployed, route requests to the appropriate level, monitor fallback frequency, and measure the quality impact of each level.

Recommendation and ranking systems use the same pattern when a complex deep learning model falls back to a top-n popularity list, a linear ranker, or a cached response during primary serving failures. Complex models often fight for the last mile of accuracy while simple heuristics provide the bulk of the utility, so the fallback path must be monitored as a first-class quality signal rather than treated as a silent failover. Otherwise the product appears healthy while quality is silently traded for availability.

#### Feature fallback {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-feature-fallback-0730}

Feature fallback controls how much input quality the model may lose before the request must be blocked. When feature retrieval fails, validated population-level defaults or cached values can substitute for missing user or item features. A recommender might use genre-level item defaults for missing item attributes or the most recent cached value of a real-time signal. The model must have been trained or evaluated with those missing-feature semantics; an average embedding or a vector from another encoder is not automatically a compatible input. Approximate features are useful only when their representation and measured prediction quality satisfy the fallback contract.

The key design step is prioritizing features by their measured contribution to prediction quality. In a four-level policy, critical features block the request, important features use defaults, useful features use cached values, and optional features can be omitted (@tbl-feature-degradation-tiers). The table's quality-loss ranges are example policy budgets, not transferable properties of those feature categories. Deployment requires measurements showing that each permitted fallback meets its budget. When feature degradation alone is insufficient to maintain system stability under extreme load, the serving infrastructure must begin actively dropping requests.

| **Tier**      |      **Example features**     | **Missing action** |  **Quality impact**  |
|:--------------|:-----------------------------:|:------------------:|:--------------------:|
| **Critical**  |        User ID, Item ID       |   Block request    |     Cannot serve     |
| **Important** | User history, Item attributes |    Use defaults    | 5--10% quality loss  |
| **Useful**    |       Real-time context       |     Use cached     |  2--5% quality loss  |
| **Optional**  |       Secondary signals       |        Omit        | $< 2\%$ quality loss |

: **Graceful Feature Degradation Tiers**: Features classified by importance to prediction quality, with the corresponding response when each tier is unavailable. Critical features block the request entirely; lower tiers allow the system to fall back to defaults, cached values, or omission with bounded quality impact. The tiers convert a binary "feature available or not" question into a four-step degradation ladder. {#tbl-feature-degradation-tiers}

#### Load shedding {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-load-shedding-8476}

Load shedding protects the system by sacrificing selected requests before overload spreads to every request. Random shedding is the simplest policy: drop a fraction of incoming requests and preserve enough capacity for the rest. Its weakness is that it treats all requests as equally valuable. Priority-based shedding turns quality-of-service degradation into an explicit policy by serving premium users before free users, revenue-generating requests before analytics requests, and interactive traffic before background batch work. The system is still degrading, but it is degrading according to a predeclared service contract rather than whichever queue happens to fill first.

Admission control\index{Graceful degradation!admission control} applies the same idea at system entry points. It rejects requests that would exceed capacity rather than accepting work that will degrade every request already in the system. Circuit breakers\index{Circuit breaker!serving resilience} extend the same protection to individual dependencies by failing fast when a model replica, feature store, or supporting service is unhealthy, so that one failing dependency cannot exhaust connection pools across the fleet. @Sec-inference-scale-circuit-breakers-backpressure-e61c develops their states and the backpressure signals that accompany them.

#### Graceful degradation implementation {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-graceful-degradation-implementation-1aa5}

Implementation begins by turning the degradation ladder into a control loop. Tail-latency percentiles reveal delayed responses, dependency-specific error rates locate failed calls, resource utilization exposes pressure, and growing queues indicate a mismatch between arrivals and completions. These signals support entry and exit conditions for each degradation level: a trigger can justify load shedding before diagnosis is complete, even though the signal alone does not establish the underlying cause. Degradation triggers\index{Graceful degradation!triggers} define conditions that activate degradation; three common triggers watch tail latency, error rate, and feature store health, and each one activates its own fallback mechanism (@lst-degradation-triggers).

::: {#lst-degradation-triggers lst-cap="**Progressive Degradation Triggers**: Conditions that activate graceful degradation based on tail latency, error rate, and feature store health. Each trigger activates a different fallback mechanism appropriate to the detected problem."}

```{.python}
# Monitor tail latency for user-facing impact
if p99_latency > threshold:
    activate_model_fallback()  # Switch to faster, simpler model

# Track error rates to detect downstream failures
if error_rate > threshold:
    activate_circuit_breaker()  # Fail fast, prevent cascade

# Feature store slowdowns degrade recommendation quality
if feature_store_latency > threshold:
    activate_feature_fallback()  # Use cached/default features
```

:::

Degradation should increase progressively as conditions worsen rather than switch at one cliff. The system can raise the fallback percentage gradually as load increases, then require sustained improvement before traffic returns to higher-capability paths. Hysteresis prevents oscillation between primary and fallback modes when the service hovers near a threshold.

### Degradation monitoring and alerting {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-degradation-monitoring-alerting-87c2}

Because graceful degradation trades quality for availability, monitoring must make that trade visible rather than letting the system appear healthy while serving lower-fidelity results. The monitoring surface must expose how much service quality has been traded away. @Tbl-degradation-monitoring-action-map turns that surface into an action map: fallback share reveals how often model quality was reduced, default-feature share reveals input-quality loss, drop rate reveals capacity protection, and the primary-vs-fallback quality gap reveals whether the degraded path remains acceptable. Its escalation thresholds illustrate one policy; the service's permitted degradation duration and quality loss must determine the deployed thresholds.

| **Signal**                      | **Quality trade exposed**                       | **Escalation rule**                                                              | **Postincident question**                              |
|:--------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| Fallback-model request share    | Model capability reduced to preserve serving    | Sustained activation beyond 5 minutes becomes a warning.                         | Did the fallback preserve enough user value?           |
| Default-feature request share   | Input richness reduced because dependencies lag | Severe degradation affecting over 50% of requests becomes critical.              | Which feature dependency needs replication or caching? |
| Load-shed request rate          | Coverage reduced to protect the service         | Any growth after the circuit breaker opens triggers capacity investigation.      | Was admission control early enough to prevent cascade? |
| Primary-vs-fallback quality gap | Product quality lost during the incident        | Degradation beyond 1 hour escalates even when availability metrics look healthy. | Is the fallback path still a valid product experience? |

: **Degradation Monitoring Action Map**: Graceful degradation is safe only when the quality trade is observable. Each signal ties a degraded serving mode to the escalation and postincident question that prevent silent quality loss. {#tbl-degradation-monitoring-action-map}

After the event, postincident analysis should identify the root cause, evaluate fallback effectiveness, measure user and business impact, and define improvements that prevent recurrence. Implementing these fallback mechanisms safely requires deep visibility into the system's runtime state. When a complex recommendation pipeline begins degrading, operators must rapidly determine which microservice is failing, and that diagnosis depends on distributed debugging and observability.

## Distributed Debugging and Observability {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-debugging-observability-1a7f}

At 2:00 AM, latency on the flagship generative API spikes from 200 ms to 5 seconds, but CPU, memory, and network metrics all look normal. The latency breach can justify immediate mitigation under a predefined policy; choosing a targeted repair requires locating the stalled work across hundreds of microservices. Distributed debugging and observability provide the diagnostic capability required to locate these invisible bottlenecks.

### Diagnostic challenges in distributed ML systems {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-ml-systems-hard-debug-8d8a}

When a latency spike or stalled collective appears on one run and vanishes on the next, the evidence needed for recovery is split across timing, state, scale, and model behavior. Nondeterminism enters from multiple directions: network timing variations change execution order, thread scheduling differences alter race conditions, GPU kernel execution order varies across runs, and floating-point operation ordering changes numerical results. Consequently, a bug that manifests on one execution may not reproduce on subsequent runs, creating "Heisenbugs"[^fn-heisenbug-ml-concurrency] that appear to vanish when observed.

[^fn-heisenbug-ml-concurrency]: **Heisenbug**\index{Heisenbug!distributed debugging}: A pun on Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, popularized in @gray1986computers's analysis of why production systems fail. Instrumentation perturbs timing, so observing the bug changes it. In distributed ML training, inserting gradient logging alters collective timing and can mask the very race that caused the silent corruption.

Partial failures turn that nondeterminism into a recovery problem. A single machine can also suffer partial failures, but distribution adds independently progressing workers and communication paths: one component can stop while others continue, leaving peers uncertain whether it has failed or become unreachable. Scale then removes manual inspection as a viable debugging method. With thousands of components, automated tools must filter large telemetry streams and identify the few signals that explain the incident. ML systems add model behavior to the same diagnostic problem: silent accuracy degradation produces wrong results without errors, numerical issues like NaN and infinity propagate through computation, data-dependent bugs manifest only for specific inputs, and learning causes expected behavior changes that can resemble bugs. Isolating a fault across all four sources requires structured telemetry that links cluster-wide symptoms to individual requests and events.

### Observability pillars {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-observability-pillars-0e45}

Observability supports both immediate mitigation and investigation of the cause. Suppose a recommendation service suddenly violates its latency SLO while the model replicas still report healthy GPU utilization. Metrics establish the timing and scope of the symptom, traces show which service span consumes the request budget, and logs record events inside that service. @Fig-observability-three-pillars connects these streams to operational decisions. A single signal can justify an action, such as shedding load when a queue exceeds its budget. Joining request and trace context with model versions, deployment tags, and time windows strengthens the diagnosis when several causes could explain the same symptom. Correlated evidence narrows those possibilities; it does not by itself prove the physical or software cause.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How metrics, logs, and traces become a fleet-wide observability architecture that routes evidence across many models and owners is developed in @sec-ml-operations-scale-observability-architecture-ba87.
:::

::: {#fig-observability-three-pillars fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Three Pillars of Observability**: Diagnosis of fleet failures can combine three signal types. Metrics reveal *when* and *where* a problem occurs (for example, GPU utilization drops). Logs provide the *what* through event context (for example, an out-of-memory exception). Traces expose the *request path* by linking events across the distributed lifecycle (for example, identifying the request that triggered the memory spike). A single signal can justify immediate mitigation; joining signals on shared identifiers strengthens diagnosis without proving the cause." fig-alt="Three panels draw each signal in its native form. Metrics, labeled when and where: a GPU utilization time series that runs level and then drops sharply in red. Logs, labeled what happened: a stream of gray log lines with one red monospace line reading OOM exception. Traces, labeled request path: a waterfall of nested span bars with one long span outlined in red. In each panel a dashed violet connector leaves the red anomaly, the end of the utilization drop, the end of the OOM line, and the end of the red span, and runs down as an arrow into a bar reading correlate on shared identifiers, listing request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment, which leads to a recovery action box: shed load, restart, roll back, or degrade."}
![](images/svg/observability-three-pillars.svg)

:::

Metrics are the first evidence because they compress fleet behavior into time series that can trigger action. A metric stream becomes fault-tolerance infrastructure only when an alert maps to a recovery decision. High p99 latency may trigger load shedding, a falling cache hit rate may trigger fallback features, and a sudden prediction-distribution shift may block a rollout before it corrupts user-facing decisions.

Logs provide the event context that a metric intentionally discards. Structured logging\index{Structured logging!JSON format} uses formats such as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) with consistent fields, so incident tooling can search by service, request, model version, GPU, feature store, or trace identifier. A GPU memory allocation failure logged this way records both the local failure context and the trace identifiers needed to connect the event to distributed metrics and spans (@lst-structured-log-entry).

::: {#lst-structured-log-entry lst-cap="**Structured JSON Log Entry**: A structured log entry for a GPU memory allocation failure, including trace and span identifiers for correlation with distributed traces and resource metrics for diagnosis."}

```{.json}
{
  "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:23:45.123Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "inference-server",
  "trace_id": "abc123",
  "span_id": "def456",
  "message": "GPU memory allocation failed",
  "gpu_id": 3,
  "requested_bytes": 4294967296,
  "available_bytes": 2147483648
}
```

:::

For fault tolerance, the important logging property is consistent correlation rather than the particular backend. Log levels should map incidents to escalation consistently across components, but the recovery system depends more on whether operators can query events by the same request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment identifiers that appear in metrics and spans. Log aggregation is therefore useful because it preserves the join between local failure context and fleet-wide symptoms.

Traces show where latency or failure propagated across distributed components. A trace\index{Distributed tracing!trace} is the end-to-end journey of a request, a span\index{Distributed tracing!span} is one operation within that journey, and context propagation\index{Distributed tracing!context propagation} carries the trace identity across service boundaries. A trace through an ML inference pipeline illustrates how these spans compose:

```text
Trace: user-request-12345
|-- Span: api-gateway (5 ms)
|   `-- Span: auth-service (2 ms)
|-- Span: feature-service (15 ms)
|   |-- Span: user-feature-lookup (8 ms)
|   `-- Span: item-feature-lookup (12 ms)
|-- Span: inference-service (45 ms)
|   |-- Span: preprocessing (3 ms)
|   |-- Span: model-inference (40 ms)
|   `-- Span: postprocessing (2 ms)
`-- Span: response-formatting (1 ms)
Total: 66 ms
```

Standard distributed tracing\index{Distributed tracing!observability} APIs such as OpenTelemetry carry this context across services, and a tracing backend stores and visualizes the traces. The durable requirement is not the particular backend but enough preserved context to answer whether the fault lives in request routing, feature retrieval, model execution, postprocessing, or a dependency outside the model service.

### ML-specific debugging {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-mlspecific-debugging-27d5}

Operational signals alone are not enough when a process stays healthy while its tensors, inputs, or per-rank execution times drift outside the model's contract. ML systems therefore add specialized debugging across three surfaces: numerical health inside the computation, semantic validity across the data pipeline, and straggler attribution across distributed stages.

#### Numerical debugging {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-numerical-debugging-ee2a}

Numerical debugging targets failures where tensors remain valid objects but contain invalid values. NaN detection\index{Numerical debugging!NaN detection}[^fn-nan-gradient-propagation] exposes values that can propagate through later arithmetic without a process crash. A minimal diagnostic check only flags the invalid output (@lst-nan-detection), so the caller must act on the result and block its publication.

[^fn-nan-gradient-propagation]: **NaN propagation**\index{NaN propagation!training corruption}: Many IEEE 754 arithmetic operations propagate a NaN operand, so an invalid gradient can contaminate dependent updates without stopping the process. The affected scope depends on the computation's data dependencies. Zero divided by zero and the logarithm of a negative real value produce NaNs; division of a nonzero finite value by zero or floating-point overflow can instead produce infinity, which may cause a later invalid operation. Checking only for a process crash therefore misses numerical failures.

::: {#lst-nan-detection lst-cap="**NaN Detection**: This check flags NaN output for diagnosis. The caller must block publication or choose a fallback; a logged request identifier refers to an input retained by the application for replay."}

```{.python}
# Check tensor for NaN values
# (propagate from any corrupted computation)
if torch.isnan(output).any():
    log.error("NaN detected in output", request_id=request_id)
    # Caller must retain a replayable input reference and block or replace this output
```

:::

During training, per-step gradient statistics expose numerical faults before they corrupt the entire run. Tracking the global gradient norm catches sudden explosion or vanishing, histogramming the gradient distribution flags outlier spikes, and logging layer-wise gradient norms isolates which block in the network first destabilized. Mixed-precision training[^fn-mixedprecision-fault-tolerance] can introduce related numerical issues when narrow dynamic range interacts with unstable updates. A dynamic loss scaler reduces its scale after detecting nonfinite gradients, indicating overflow or another invalid operation rather than proving underflow. Gradient magnitudes, skipped updates, and comparison with a higher-precision replay help distinguish range problems from other causes; ordinary FP16 rounding differences are not themselves faults.

[^fn-mixedprecision-fault-tolerance]: **Mixed-precision numerical issues**\index{Mixed-precision training!numerical issues}\index{Mixed-precision training!numerical fault tolerance}: FP16's exponent range is far narrower than FP32's or BF16's, which is why mixed-precision training scales the loss before backpropagation and dynamic scaling skips nonfinite updates. The formats and the mixed-precision recipe are recapped in @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-training-memory.

#### Data debugging and validation {#sec-fault-tolerance-data-debugging-validation}

Data bugs surface as valid-looking but wrong inputs, so debugging must verify semantic correctness at each pipeline boundary in addition to numerical validity. Validation checks expected format, shape, value ranges, required fields, and encoding before data reaches the model, catching malformed examples while the failure is still local to the input path. Once the input passes those static checks, the system needs evidence about behavior over time. Distribution monitors track feature drift, null-rate changes, and outliers as they emerge, while transformation instrumentation logs intermediate shapes and statistics so teams can compare each stage against known-good data. Together, these signals separate a corrupted input path from a numerical failure inside the model.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The validation gates and response policies that run these data checks continuously across a production fleet are developed in @sec-ml-operations-scale-data-quality-operations-e77b.
:::

#### Straggler detection and analysis {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-straggler-detection-analysis-6925}

Perspective \ref{psp-fault-tolerance-straggler-or-failure} treated a straggler as a slow training rank that holds up a synchronous step. The same idea extends to serving once "peer" means any component on a request's path, so straggler diagnosis there asks which replica or service stage is slow enough to become a failure-equivalent bottleneck. A slow serving replica delays requests routed to it and can trigger retries under load; its effect on the service's tail percentile depends on its traffic share and the routing policy. A request that waits for several required parallel branches is instead bounded by the last required completion. Operation-level timing\index{Straggler!timing instrumentation} instrumentation measures time for each operation, enabling latency attribution across pipeline stages. Wrapping each operation in a context manager that emits per-span timing metrics makes performance directly comparable across replicas (@lst-timing-instrumentation).

::: {#lst-timing-instrumentation lst-cap="**Operation-Level Timing**: Context manager instrumentation attributes latency to individual pipeline stages, enabling straggler detection by comparing the same span across replicas."}

```{.python}
# Wrap operations in timing context managers for latency attribution
with timer("feature_lookup"):
    features = feature_store.lookup(
        ids
    )  # Often the latency bottleneck
with timer("model_inference"):
    predictions = model(features)  # Host submission time for asynchronous GPU work
```

:::

For asynchronous GPU execution, the host span around `model(features)` in @lst-timing-instrumentation measures only the CPU time required to enqueue kernels onto the GPU stream, not completed device work. Because kernel launches return to the host before the GPU finishes executing them, a naive host timer can report a fast inference span even on a thermally throttled GPU and misattribute the delay to whichever later stage first synchronizes the stream or copies predictions back to host memory. Measuring actual GPU execution time requires recording hardware events on the stream before and after the forward pass and reading their elapsed time after the stream completes. Like-for-like component timing is then compared across replicas with percentile analysis: p50 shows typical performance, while p99 shows tail latency, and comparing p99 across replicas identifies workers whose slow path has become a fleet-wide bottleneck. The diagnosis must then separate the causes that share this slow-worker symptom, which include the gray-failure causes of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distinguishing-stragglers-failures-285d and data skew, in which some inputs are slower to process.

### Serving failure patterns {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-common-failure-patterns-3306}

Serving failures require a symptom-to-action mapping under much tighter latency constraints than the training-loss signatures of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-mechanisms-efed. Common serving symptoms differ both in what each one reveals and in what the serving system must do first (@tbl-serving-failure-response-map). Cascade failures are hardest to diagnose because the root cause is obscured by the secondary timeouts and retries it generates, as example \ref{exmp-fault-tolerance-diagnosing-cascade-failure} traces across metrics, logs, and spans.

| **Symptom**                | **Likely interpretation**                                                               | **Immediate response**                                                                         |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Latency spikes             | Resource contention, garbage collection, cold caches, or model reloads                  | Check placement and capacity; repeated spikes usually mean the problem is no longer transient. |
| Rising error rates         | Dependency failure, data-format change, or model bug                                    | Investigate immediately because errors compound across dependent services.                     |
| Silent quality degradation | Model drift, feature degradation, or data-pipeline fault                                | Use quality monitoring beyond standard operational metrics.                                    |
| Cascade failure            | Timeout exhaustion, resource depletion, or error propagation from one failing component | Trip circuit breakers and preserve isolation boundaries before the failure spreads.            |

: **Serving Failure Response Map**: Serving incidents must be classified quickly because every diagnosis competes with a user-facing latency budget. The table ties each symptom to the first operational response rather than treating all serving failures as generic errors. {#tbl-serving-failure-response-map}

::: {#exmp-fault-tolerance-diagnosing-cascade-failure .callout-example title="Diagnosing a cascade failure"}

**Scenario**: A recommendation system experiences sudden latency spikes.

**Diagnosis**: The three observability pillars narrow the failure path. Metrics\index{Metric!observability} reveal the symptom: p99 latency jumped from 45 ms to 800 ms at 14:32, with error rate increasing from 0.1 percent to 15 percent. Traces\index{Trace!observability} locate the delay in the feature-service span, which consumes 700 ms instead of the normal 12 ms, while model inference remains at 40 ms. Logs\index{Log!observability} show repeated connection timeouts to the user embedding cache at 14:31, followed by requests bypassing the cache and reaching the embedding database directly. That evidence identifies cache unavailability and increased downstream demand; it does not yet distinguish a failed cache process from a network or resource problem.

**Systems lesson**: Cache unavailability can transfer enough demand to overwhelm the embedding database. A circuit breaker and a validated default-embedding path can limit that cascade while diagnosis continues. The fallback must also respect the quality budget and avoid sending the rejected demand to another saturated dependency.

:::

Observability and diagnostic maps help operators isolate a failure once it strikes, but verifying that detectors, circuit breakers, and recovery paths actually hold under fire requires triggering those failures deliberately before production traffic meets them.

## Fault Injection Tools and Frameworks {#sec-ft-fault-injection-tools-frameworks}

An injected failure is useful evidence only when it resembles the production failure the system must survive. A multi-node training cluster that claims to tolerate network partitions should have that connection severed in a staging environment so engineers can observe what the orchestration layer does. Fault injection\index{Fault injection!testing discipline}\index{Fault injection!tools and frameworks} is the engineering discipline of deliberately perturbing a system to empirically verify that robustness mechanisms work before production traffic discovers the gap. Fault-injection tools for tensors and accelerators cover bit flips, corrupted tensor values, and accelerator-oriented failures [@chen2020tensorfi; @tsai2021; @grafe2023], while network partitions, latency injection, dependency termination, and API-response faults belong to chaos and distributed-systems testing practice [@basiri2016].

An injection experiment is evidence only at the level where it injects. Its fault model\index{Fault model!abstraction} names the originating disturbance, such as a transient single-bit upset or a permanent multi-bit defect, and its error model\index{Error model!propagation} names the corrupted state that results. Results for transient single-bit faults therefore do not establish resilience to permanent multi-bit defects [@sangchoolie2017]. The injection level also decides which masking the experiment includes. Hardware absorbs many physical disturbances before software sees them, in unused units, overwritten values, and dead instructions [@mohanram2003; @ko2021]. Hardware-based injection through field-programmable gate array (FPGA) emulation or particle-beam exposure [@velazco2010] passes through that masking, while software tools such as PyTorchFI\index{PyTorchFI!fault injection} [@mahmoud2020] perturb weights, activations, and gradients directly. They cover many model states quickly, but by skipping the masking they can overstate how often a physical fault corrupts the model. Frameworks such as Fidelity\index{Fidelity!fault injection framework} [@he2020fidelity] narrow that abstraction gap\index{Fault injection!abstraction gap} by mapping hardware faults to the software-visible errors they produce. A tensor mutation still tests how the software responds to a corrupted value; on its own, it does not estimate production vulnerability.

For fleet recovery, the most valuable experiments inject faults at the level where recovery decisions are made. Killing a rank in the middle of a collective or delaying its heartbeat past the timeout exercises the detection layers of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-detection-mechanisms-efed. Partitioning a node from the rendezvous service exercises the membership and fencing rules of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-recovery-procedures-002d. Corrupting one checkpoint shard exercises the manifest check of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-checkpointing-5dcc. Each of these experiments tests one row of @tbl-software-faults-summary-ft. Running these experiments continuously in staging, and in controlled form in production, keeps rarely executed recovery code from decaying between real incidents [@basiri2016]. A recovery path is trustworthy only for the fault model it has been exercised against, which is why the case studies that follow report both the failures production fleets met and the machinery that absorbed them.

## Case Studies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-case-studies-927f}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: opt175b-case-study
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPT-175B CASE STUDY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Case-studies opener and
# │          @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-largescale-llm-training-fault-tolerance-f4aa.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the OPT-175B run's reported cluster size, restart counts, host
# │       churn, and sustained throughput to Literature.TrainingRuns.
# │ Show: 992 GPUs; at least 35 manual and ~70 automatic restarts; >100 hosts;
# │       147 TFLOP/s per A100, about 47 percent of A100 dense FP16 peak.
# │ How:  Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175B*; fraction = 147 / A100 peak_flops.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware, Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent

class Opt175BCaseStudy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpus = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BGpus)
    manual_restarts = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BManualRestarts)
    auto_restarts = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BAutomaticRestarts)
    hosts_cycled = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BHostsCycled)
    tflops_per_gpu = float(Literature.TrainingRuns.Opt175BTflopsPerGpu)
    a100_peak_tflops = Hardware.Cloud.A100.compute.peak_flops.to(TFLOPs / second).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    peak_fraction = tflops_per_gpu / a100_peak_tflops

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(0.45 < peak_fraction < 0.50, "prose says 'near 50 percent of FP16 peak'")
    check(manual_restarts < auto_restarts, "paper: more automatic than manual restarts")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    gpus_str = fmt(gpus, precision=0)
    manual_restarts_str = fmt(manual_restarts, precision=0)
    auto_restarts_str = fmt(auto_restarts, precision=0)
    hosts_cycled_str = fmt(hosts_cycled, precision=0)
    tflops_per_gpu_str = fmt(tflops_per_gpu, precision=0)
    peak_fraction_str = fmt_percent(round(peak_fraction * 100) / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
```

Training a 175-billion-parameter language model across `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.gpus_str` GPUs for two months, keeping a 4,096-chip supercomputer slice routable despite daily hardware faults, and serving low-latency recommendations across dozens of microservices each stress a different layer of the fault-tolerance stack. Public operational reports from Meta, Google, and Netflix show how production fleets combine failure detection, state preservation, topology reconfiguration, and chaos testing at scale. Their reported numbers are operational magnitudes that expose the design pressure on each system rather than universal hardware constants.

### Large-scale LLM training at Meta {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-largescale-llm-training-fault-tolerance-f4aa}

Over two months of training the Open Pre-trained Transformer (OPT-175B) on `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.gpus_str` NVIDIA A100 GPUs, Meta's engineering team reported at least `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.manual_restarts_str` manual restarts and estimated `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.auto_restarts_str` or more automatic restarts triggered by hardware failures including ECC memory errors, NCCL and InfiniBand network faults, and lost GPUs [@zhang2022opt]. Alongside these restarts, more than `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.hosts_cycled_str` hosts were cycled [@zhang2022opt; @opt2022logbook]. Numerical instability created a separate recovery problem. These counts establish repeated interruption, but cycling hosts and restarting jobs are different events; their totals do not directly measure one common MTBF. The recovery design had to preserve progress while distinguishing failed execution resources from suspect optimization state.

During the OPT run, the team monitored progress through train-log freshness checks. The public logbook records a 15-minute modified-file threshold, later relaxed to one hour, as part of restart monitoring [@opt2022logbook]. For a hang that raised no error, this threshold contributed to $\FailureDetectionTime$; polling and response delays could extend the wait before restart. The logbook illustrates the trade-off of @eq-timeout-calculation in operational form, since relaxing the threshold reduced sensitivity to delayed logs while allowing longer idle windows.

Recovery procedures also had to account for loss spikes associated with numerical instability. Unlike a fail-stop event, this symptom made recent model state suspect without identifying a failed device. The team combined rollback to an earlier checkpoint with a lower learning rate to recover from divergence [@opt2022logbook]. The paper separately reports approximately `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.tflops_per_gpu_str` TFLOP/s per A100 (about `{python} Opt175BCaseStudy.peak_fraction_str` of dense FP16 peak) [@zhang2022opt]; that execution-rate metric alone does not establish end-to-end useful throughput after interruptions and replay. The enduring lesson is the distinction between recovery paths. A failed device calls for replacement and restoration of valid state, while numerical divergence can require an older checkpoint and a changed optimization policy. Retaining checkpoint history makes that second path possible.

### Google TPU pod resilience {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-google-tpu-pod-resilience}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tpuv4-pod-cubes
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TPUv4 POD CUBES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-google-tpu-pod-resilience.
# │
# │ Goal: Derive the pod's cube count from the registry pod size.
# │ Show: 4,096 chips as 64 cubes of 64 chips; one chip = 1/4096 of capacity.
# │ How:  Systems.Pods.TPUv4_4096.chips / cube size (4x4x4, architectural constant).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math

class TpuV4PodCubes:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    pod_chips = Systems.Pods.TPUv4_4096.chips
    cube_chips = 4 * 4 * 4  # 4x4x4 cube, the OCS-switched building block [@zu2024tpuv4]

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    n_cubes = pod_chips // cube_chips
```
