```{python}
    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(n_cubes * cube_chips == pod_chips, "pod must be a whole number of cubes")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    pod_chips_str = fmt(pod_chips, precision=0)
    n_cubes_str = fmt(n_cubes, precision=0)
    cube_chips_str = fmt(cube_chips, precision=0)
    chip_share_math = fmt_math(rf"1/{pod_chips}")
```

Google's TPUv4 supercomputer combines configurable topology with recovery software. A pod contains `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.pod_chips_str` chips organized as `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.n_cubes_str` cubes of `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.cube_chips_str` chips, each arranged in a $4{\times}4{\times}4$ 3D mesh [@zu2024tpuv4]. Losing one chip removes `{python} TpuV4PodCubes.chip_share_math`th of pod capacity, but can interrupt an entire job that requires that participant. The recovery unit therefore exceeds the failed device.

War story \ref{ws-fault-tolerance-google-tpuv4-routing} traced the recovery mechanism, in which the OCS fabric assembles healthy cubes into job-sized slices, reallocating spare cubes after machine outages and routing around unavailable links for supported OCS outage patterns. The published study adds the software that runs that loop, components including `libtpunet` and `healthd` for topology setup and health monitoring. It also gives the operating statistics that show how often the loop runs. System availability was 99.98 percent, with hardware outages affecting approximately 1 percent of training jobs [@zu2024tpuv4]. Daily failure rates were 0.08 percent of TPU machines, 0.005 percent of ICI cables, and 0.04 percent of OCS units. Small daily fractions still add up across thousands of components, so the control plane absorbs a steady stream of reconfiguration events rather than an occasional emergency. The architectural lesson is to match each failure boundary to a feasible replacement or routing mechanism.

### Netflix chaos engineering for serving dependencies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-netflix-chaos-engineering}

While training resilience focuses on long-running batch jobs, Netflix's published work on Chaos Engineering\index{Chaos engineering!serving resilience} [@basiri2016] provides the serving-side contrast, and it is the production origin of the injection discipline that @sec-ft-fault-injection-tools-frameworks applied to training. The premise is simple but operationally demanding. Because production systems have many interacting dependencies, teams should validate steady-state behavior by deliberately injecting failures instead of waiting for real incidents to discover whether fallbacks work.

For ML serving, the same discipline applies to feature stores, model-serving dependencies, caches, and fallback paths. A model endpoint can be healthy while a feature service is slow, stale, or unavailable; if the system lacks a tested fallback, a local dependency problem can become user-visible latency or degraded recommendations. Chaos tests make those assumptions executable by injecting latency, terminating dependencies, or forcing fallback paths in controlled conditions.

The recovery procedure for these injected faults centers on fallback hierarchies. If the primary deep learning model fails or times out, the serving system can switch to a lighter model, cached response, or simple popularity-based default. The systems lesson is that resilience in ML serving is not a static property but a continuous practice of active verification. A fallback path that is never exercised is documentation, not fault tolerance.

Across these production case studies, three architectural patterns recur. First, detection speed\index{Fault tolerance!detection speed} belongs in the recovery budget. Meta's log-freshness threshold and Google's health monitors determine when recovery can begin, while Netflix's chaos experiments test detection and fallback for selected dependency failures. Checkpoint age and replication lag separately govern recoverable state. Second, the atomic unit of failure\index{Failure domain!atomic unit of failure} shapes the architecture. Google combines cube replacement with fault-tolerant routing, the OPT run restarted from durable checkpoints and kept their history for numerical rollback, and Netflix validates service-dependency fallbacks. Third, fault tolerance is a spectrum\index{Fault tolerance!spectrum} rather than a switch. Exact state recovery trades normal-operation overhead against lost work and recovery time; graceful degradation additionally trades service capability against continued availability. Those distinct trade-offs help identify the misconceptions that follow.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-fallacies-pitfalls-74b8}

An infrastructure team might spend weeks hardening their storage layer against disk failures, only to have their entire training run destroyed by a subtle software bug in their PyTorch distributed backend. Fault tolerance for distributed ML systems involves counterintuitive mathematics and subtle trade-offs where conventional data center wisdom often fails. Recognizing the fallacies and pitfalls below prevents engineers from optimizing for the wrong failure modes before the chapter closes with a synthesis of its core quantitative rules.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Hardware failures are the main concern.*

This intuition comes from traditional systems where disk failures, power outages, and network partitions dominate, whereas in ML systems hardware failures are only one part of a broader incident mix. Long-lived, stateful ML jobs expose failure paths that hardware redundancy cannot cover. A malformed checkpoint path can make recovery impossible, a mismatched collective library can hang all ranks, an undersized shared-memory limit can crash data loaders, and a stale feature schema can silently corrupt training. Their relative frequency depends on the deployment, but even an infrequent software or configuration fault can destroy the same multi-day job that hardware redundancy was meant to protect. Investing heavily in hardware redundancy while neglecting software robustness (input validation, gradual rollouts, configuration management) leaves many important failure modes unaddressed, which is why the most reliable ML systems treat software bugs as inevitable and design defensively.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Setting checkpoint interval by intuition.*

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: young-daly-intuition-fallacy
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ YOUNG-DALY INTUITION FALLACY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-fallacies-pitfalls-74b8
# │          ("Setting checkpoint interval by intuition") — the display equation
# │          and the slower-storage follow-up sentence.
# │
# │ Goal: Reproduce the two Young-Daly optimal intervals from a hypothetical
# │       1,000-GPU cluster at the chapter's own MTBF so the "intuition is
# │ Show: tau_opt = sqrt(2 * T_write * MTBF) for a 5-minute and a 15-minute write.
# │ How:  Work in minutes; tau = sqrt(2 * write_min * mtbf_min); round to whole
# │       minutes for display.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.core.units import minute
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_display_math, fmt_int, fmt_time

class YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    # The 1,000-GPU row of the chapter's cluster-MTBF table, plus two write times.
    cluster_gpus = ClusterMtbfScaling.sizes[3]  # the 1,000-GPU row of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling (scenario sweep)
    mtbf_min = round(float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours) / cluster_gpus * 60)  # cluster MTBF, minutes
    write_fast_min = 5  # checkpoint write time, fast storage
    write_slow_min = 15  # checkpoint write time, slower storage / larger model

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    arg_fast = 2 * write_fast_min * mtbf_min
    tau_fast_min = math.sqrt(arg_fast)
    tau_slow_min = math.sqrt(2 * write_slow_min * mtbf_min)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(165 < tau_fast_min < 180, "5-minute write at 50 h MTBF should give a ~173-minute interval")
    check(tau_slow_min > tau_fast_min, "slower storage must lengthen the optimal interval")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    tau_opt_fast_eq_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"T^\ast_{{\text{{ckpt}}}} = \sqrt{{2 \times {write_fast_min} \times {mtbf_min}}} = "
        rf"\sqrt{{{arg_fast}}} \approx {fmt_int(round(tau_fast_min))} \text{{ minutes}}"
    )
    tau_opt_slow_min_str = fmt_time(round(tau_slow_min) * minute, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    mtbf_h_str = fmt_time(mtbf_min / 60, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    write_fast_str = fmt_time(write_fast_min * minute, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    write_fast_attr_str = fmt_time(write_fast_min * minute, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word", attributive=True)
    write_slow_str = fmt_time(write_slow_min * minute, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
```

Organizations commonly set checkpoint intervals based on "feels right": "every hour seems reasonable" or "every 1,000 steps." The Young-Daly formula reveals these intuitions are often wrong. For the `{python} ClusterMtbfScaling.n3_str`-GPU cluster of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling, whose GPU-only MTBF is `{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.mtbf_h_str`, with a checkpoint write time of `{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.write_fast_str`:

`{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.tau_opt_fast_eq_math`

The intuitive "every hour" checkpoints nearly three times more often than the expected-waste optimum. It reduces potential lost work, but the added write overhead outweighs that benefit under this model. A tighter RPO can still justify the shorter interval. The same hourly policy was too infrequent in the Young-Daly notebook, and both verdicts follow from one rule. The optimum scales as $\sqrt{\CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}$, so an hour is too long when a `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.t_write_s_str` write meets a full-system MTBF of `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.mtbf_h_str`, yet too short when a `{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.write_fast_attr_str` write meets a GPU-only MTBF of `{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.mtbf_h_str`. If checkpoint time increases to `{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.write_slow_str` (larger model, slower storage), the optimal interval stretches to `{python} YoungDalyIntuitionFallacy.tau_opt_slow_min_str`, further still from the "every 15 minutes" that some teams adopt to "stay safe." The decision must balance expected waste with the recovery contract rather than treat either interval as universally correct.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Component MTTF values predict individual failure timing.*

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Fallacy — component MTTF values predict individual failure timing.
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_math, fmt_time

class FleetReliabilityFallacyRates:
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    fleet_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    fleet_rate_per_h = fleet_gpus / gpu_mttf_h
    hours_between = 1 / fleet_rate_per_h

    check(abs(hours_between * fleet_rate_per_h - 1) < 1e-9, "interval must be reciprocal of fleet rate")

    _fleet_tex = fmt(fleet_gpus, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    _mttf_tex = fmt(gpu_mttf_h, precision=0).replace(",", "{,}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    fleet_gpus_str = fmt_count(fleet_gpus, label="GPU")
    fleet_rate_eq_math = fmt_math(f"{_fleet_tex}/{_mttf_tex} = {fmt(fleet_rate_per_h, precision=1, commas=False)}")
    hours_between_str = fmt_time(hours_between, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
```

Engineers read a GPU MTTF of `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.gpu_mttf_str` and plan around a five-year replacement cadence per device. MTTF is a population mean, not a lifetime assigned to each component. A GPU with MTTF `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.gpu_mttf_str` might fail at 200 hours or last 100,000 hours. Under the chapter's independent constant-rate model, a fleet of `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.fleet_gpus_str` has an aggregate rate of approximately `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.fleet_rate_eq_math` failures per hour, or roughly one failure every `{python} FleetReliabilityFallacyRates.hours_between_str`. This planning model helps size recovery capacity and spare pools. It does not make device-health monitoring pointless: temperature, error history, and recurring anomalies provide condition-specific evidence that the population mean alone lacks.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Using MTBF calculations as if failures were independent.*

The reliability equation $\SystemMtbf = \ComponentMttf/\RequiredComponentCount$ assumes component failures are statistically independent, while production failures correlate through the shared power, switches, software, and cooling of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-correlated-failures-95e8.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: correlated-failure-pitfall
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CORRELATED FAILURE PITFALL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Pitfall "Using MTBF calculations as if failures were independent."
# │
# │ Goal: Show how a correlated hazard 10x the independent rate collapses MTBF.
# │ Show: 1,000 GPUs x 50,000-hour MTBF -> 50 h; adding a 10x hazard -> ~5 h.
# │ How:  MTBF = MTTF / N; combined rate = (1 + 10) x independent rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_time

class CorrelatedFailurePitfall:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    cluster_gpus = ClusterMtbfScaling.sizes[3]  # the 1,000-GPU row of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling (scenario sweep)
    hazard_multiple = 10  # scenario assumption: correlated hazard 10x the independent rate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    independent_mtbf_h = gpu_mttf_h / cluster_gpus
    effective_mtbf_h = 1 / ((1 + hazard_multiple) / independent_mtbf_h)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(4.0 < effective_mtbf_h < 5.0, "prose says the effective incident MTBF drops to 'about 5 hours'")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    cluster_gpus_str = fmt(cluster_gpus, precision=0)
    gpu_mttf_attr_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word", attributive=True)
    independent_mtbf_str = fmt_time(independent_mtbf_h, "hour", precision=0, style="word")
    effective_mtbf_str = fmt_time(round(effective_mtbf_h), "hour", precision=0, style="word")
```

Correlated failures change two quantities that the simple MTBF equation hides: incident frequency and blast radius. A cluster with `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.cluster_gpus_str` independent GPUs each with `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.gpu_mttf_attr_str` MTTF has a first-GPU-failure MTBF of `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.independent_mtbf_str`. If a shared power, cooling, or software hazard adds an incident rate 10 times larger than that independent first-failure rate, the effective incident MTBF drops to about `{python} CorrelatedFailurePitfall.effective_mtbf_str`. Separately, a correlated incident may take out 10 GPUs at once, increasing recovery cost even if the independent GPU failure rate itself has not changed. Reliability engineering must identify and mitigate correlation through diversity: different power feeds, different network paths, different software versions in canary deployments.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Every failure should be handled as a full restart.*

Engineers often treat all failures as "node crashed, restart from checkpoint," but different failure modes require different responses. Transient stalls such as network congestion can permit a bounded wait or safe retry when state and the communication group remain valid; a brief fault can still require recovery if it corrupts state or leaves the group unusable. Permanent device loss requires replacement or a feasible resize, together with restoration of the missing state. Silent corruption requires a trusted recovery point, which may precede the latest checkpoint and therefore motivates checkpoint history retention. Persistent resource exhaustion (OOM, memory fragmentation) needs reconfiguration before restart; otherwise the job can crash again immediately. As @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failure-taxonomy-e78c details, misdiagnosing failure type wastes compute. Restarting for a harmless stall discards useful work, while continuing from corrupted state can contaminate later updates.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Assuming checkpoints are consistent without validating state.*

Modern frameworks checkpoint transparently, creating the illusion of automatic consistency. In practice, distributed checkpoints require cross-node coordination that can fail subtly across multiple dimensions. Rank desynchronization\index{Checkpoint consistency!rank desynchronization} occurs when workers record different training steps, such as rank 0 snapshotting iteration 1000 while rank 1 captures iteration 1001. Similarly, transient storage failures can cause partial writes\index{Checkpoint consistency!partial writes} that leave behind truncated shards, sharded optimizer state lag\index{Optimizer!state lag} leaves optimizer states misaligned with model weights when captured asynchronously, and in-flight gradients\index{Checkpoint consistency!in-flight gradients} from incomplete AllReduce operations can produce ambiguous reduction boundaries. Production systems must therefore implement checkpoint validation: verify all shards exist, verify iteration numbers match, and verify optimizer state matches model state. The reason is that organizations that discover corrupted checkpoints during recovery from a failure have no recourse except restarting from a potentially much earlier checkpoint.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Overhead budgets are fixed fractions of training time.*

Reference tables that show "pipeline bubble: 10 percent, checkpoint overhead: 5 percent, failure recovery: 3 percent" are easy to read as physical laws and pass through as line items in capacity plans. They are engineering targets, not constants. Pipeline bubble overhead depends on the number of microbatches and the interleaved schedule, as its bubble fraction shows (@sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-pipeline-parallelism-8748). Elastic recovery can reduce waiting for replacement capacity while still restarting workers and restoring state. Checkpoint overhead is a function of model size, storage bandwidth, and whether checkpointing is synchronous or asynchronous. Treating these numbers as fixed percentages leads to passive acceptance of avoidable inefficiency, because each one is set by a design choice.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Using elastic training as a substitute for checkpointing.*

Elastic training adjusts parallelism degree when workers fail, but resizing still requires a consistent recovery state. Reducing the active worker count requires redistributing model shards, optimizer states, and data assignments, often through checkpoint reload. Below some minimum viable size, training becomes infeasible because the model no longer fits or the batch policy cannot be maintained; the job must wait for sufficient capacity before restoring. If a failure was caused by a software bug triggered by specific data, the bug persists in remaining workers. Elastic training is complementary to checkpointing, not a replacement. Resizing alone does not justify a lower checkpoint frequency, because the recovery contract, failure rate, and checkpoint cost still determine that choice.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Silent data corruption is negligible because hardware has ECC.*

GPUs and memory systems include extensive error correction\index{ECC!end-to-end limitation} (ECC, CRC, parity), creating the intuition that silent data corruption is negligible. Large-scale CPU SDC and memory-error studies show that silent corruptions and memory faults still occur at fleet scale and can escape ordinary error reporting [@dixit2021silent; @sridharan2015]. ECC and link CRCs remain necessary layers, but they protect stored and transmitted bits rather than arithmetic, so they are not an end-to-end correctness proof for a training run. A 10,000-GPU cluster executes enough arithmetic that even rare per-device corruption becomes an operating condition, which is why it needs the check-and-verify defenses of @sec-ft-sdc-verification in addition to hardware protection.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Adding GPUs without accounting for communication and recovery overhead.*

Capacity plans typically account for Amdahl's Law and AllReduce overhead but treat reliability as a fixed background condition. At extreme scale, each additional GPU increases the aggregate failure rate, which inflates the expected recovery and replay time per job. There exists a cluster size beyond which the time lost to failures and recovery exceeds the time saved by additional parallelism, and wall-clock training time increases rather than decreasing with $\AcceleratorCount$. This is the reliability version of diminishing returns, and it applies on top of the Amdahl ceiling, so the two effects must be modeled together. Whole-run useful goodput must count only retained progress and include recovery time in the denominator, and its reliability penalty generally grows with $\AcceleratorCount$ under the independent-failure model. @Sec-performance-engineering-goodput-factors composes that runtime loss with the scheduling and program losses without counting any of them twice.

:::

## Summary {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-summary-48b0}

Fault tolerance turns the statistical expectation of hardware failure into a manageable operational routine. Individual component reliability compounds across thousands of devices, driving system-level MTBF from years down to hours. At fleet scale, systems must bound lost work and recovery delay through recovery that is automatic, fast, and minimally disruptive to training or serving.

In training, progress is only as safe as the last state the fleet can prove it can restore. Checkpointing bounds lost work, and the Young-Daly interval (@eq-ft-young-daly-interval) prices that bound against write cost, shrinking only with the square root of a falling MTBF. RPO and RTO turn the expected-value optimum into a service contract. A manifest published last defines which generation exists, and fencing at the resource boundary decides who may still write to it. The retries that recovery triggers stay safe only when each operation is idempotent, inherits its caller's deadline, and draws on one shared retry budget, so the response cannot amplify the incident. Elastic recovery then trades capacity for continuity, valid only while the data, batch-size, and optimizer invariants survive the resize.

Serving inverts the budget. Training can spend minutes restoring state that satisfies its optimization contract; an interactive request has milliseconds, so serving buys availability with ready replicas and decides in advance which state it will rebuild, replicate, or abandon. The KV cache is the clearest case, derived state that can be reconstructed from retained history only when the latency budget allows. When neither redundancy nor reconstruction fits that budget, graceful degradation keeps the service useful by sacrificing a named property that was validated before the incident.

Recovery depends on evidence about both the failure and the state being restored. A loss spike can originate in hardware, data, numerical behavior, or synchronization. Suspect state can justify a pause or rollback while investigation continues; attributing the cause to a device requires corroborating telemetry, replay, or integrity evidence. Restore drills and fault injection then test whether the selected response actually preserves valid state and meets its recovery budget. Passing those tests establishes evidence for the exercised fault model, rather than a guarantee against every failure.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Failure is normal operation"}

* **Scale makes failure routine**: A `{python} FailureCascadeExample.fleet_gpus_str`-GPU cluster\index{Failure!inevitability at scale} encounters hardware failures every few hours under the chapter's component-rate assumptions; software must treat failure as a normal state.
* **Liveness is not correctness**: A gray failure keeps answering heartbeats while every peer waits on it, and silent data corruption passes ECC while feeding wrong gradients into a correct AllReduce, so detection needs progress measurements and check-and-verify evidence beside liveness checks.
* **Recovery is a contract**: RPO bounds lost progress, RTO bounds recovery delay, MTTR combines with MTBF to determine steady-state availability, a manifest identifies committed state, and fencing prevents an expired worker epoch from writing after replacement.
* **Checkpoint cadence balances two costs**: Under the first-order assumptions, $\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}$ balances checkpoint write overhead against expected rework; for the 175B running example on a `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster it lands near `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.tau_opt_min_str`. The selected interval must also meet limits on lost progress; recovery delay needs its own budget.
* **Elasticity enables persistence**: Designing training jobs to be "elastic"\index{Elastic training!resilience} (rebuilding communication groups and rebalancing data shards as traced in @fig-elastic-flow) can reduce waiting for replacement capacity. The runtime must preserve valid state and data coverage, and either preserve batch size or validate the changed optimization policy. Checkpoint cadence still determines how much work must be replayed.
* **Serving recovery follows the state budget**: Preserve authoritative history, then choose reconstruction, checkpointing, or replication for derived state according to the latency contract (@tbl-stateful-failover). A ready replacement provides useful service only when it can also recover the context the request needs.
* **Degradation is a designed mode**: When recovery cannot finish inside the latency budget, a fallback validated in advance (a smaller model, cached results, default features, or shed low-priority load) keeps the service useful, provided monitoring exposes how much quality was traded away.

:::

Fault tolerance makes the cost of coordination a deliberate part of the execution budget. @Sec-appdx-c3-taxonomy-case-3 works a complete coordination-bound diagnosis, attributing a large run's lost wall time to checkpoints, failures, pipeline bubbles, and scheduling. In the Fleet Law (@eq-fleet-law), checkpoint pauses, detection timeouts, and restarts all land in the synchronization term $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$, and in goodput accounting they are runtime losses. The chapter's mechanisms spend Coordination ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$) so that a failure does not erase completed Compute, and asynchronous checkpointing and warm restart earn their complexity by moving part of that synchronization cost into $\OverlappedTime$ or shrinking it outright. The useful comparison is between time spent preserving and validating state during normal operation and time lost reconstructing trustworthy execution after a failure. A cheaper recovery mechanism is valuable only when it still meets the workload's limits on lost progress, response delay, and degraded quality.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From resilience to resource management"}

Keeping the fleet running despite inevitable hardware failures requires three layers: checkpointing preserves progress, elasticity absorbs node losses, and redundancy protects stateful serving sessions. Each layer also assumed a decision made elsewhere: a spare pool deep enough to replace a drained node, a hot spare held idle, spot capacity that may vanish, and replicas placed across independent failure domains. Those are allocation decisions, made while many jobs compete for the same fleet, from month-long training runs to hour-long experiments. A fault-tolerant cluster therefore still needs orchestration to decide which jobs run where, when to preempt, and how to share capacity fairly among them.
